en: In the *Bhaiṣajyavastu*,
there is a summary verse (*piṇḍoddāna*) for the section on medicines.
The Chapter on Medicine consists of Mahāsena, Rājagṛha, the Bamboo Grove (Veṇuvana),
Icchānaṅgalā, Kampilla, Ādirājya, Kumāravardhana,
the Sick, and Kaineya; this is the well-arranged section.
The summary verse:
Medicine was permitted: fat, scabies, and ointment;
the madman, Pilinda, Revata, and with sour gruel.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.
At that time, the monks were afflicted by an autumnal disease.
Being afflicted by that autumnal disease, they became pale and sallow, emaciated, weak, withered, and physically unsteady.
The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are knowers who inquire; [as the MS adds:
"Knowing, they ask; not knowing, they do not ask.
To this extent, the Buddha, the Blessed One, questioned the Venerable Ānanda.
“Ānanda, why is it that nowadays the monks are so pale, wan, emaciated, weak, withered, and physically unthriven?
The Venerable Ānanda replied, “Venerable Sir,
at present the monks are afflicted by an autumnal illness.”
Now, being afflicted by an autumnal disease, they have become very pale, emaciated, weak, withered, and physically unwell.
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, Ānanda, I authorize that the monks should take medicine."

The Blessed One said, "Medicine should be consumed by the monks. The monks consumed it at the proper time, but did not consume it after the time had passed. Consequently, they became pale, emaciated, weak, withered, and physically unthriven.
The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are inquisitive and ask questions.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, asked the Venerable Ānanda:
"I have stated that medicine should be consumed by the monks."
Moreover, monks, they became exceedingly pale, emaciated, weak, withered, and physically unwell.
"Venerable Sir," it was said by the Blessed One, "medicines should be used by the monks.
Thinking, "We are those who eat at the proper time," they used them only at the proper time and did not use them when the time had passed.
Consequently, they became pale, extremely pale, emaciated, weak, withered, and physically unsteady.
Therefore, Ānanda, I authorize that monks should partake of four kinds of medicines:
those to be taken at the proper time (*kālika*), those for a watch of the night (*yāmika*), those for seven days (*sāptāhika*), and those for life (*yāvajjīvika*).
In that regard, the *kālika* [foods] are cream, boiled rice, boiled grain, meat, and cakes;
the *yāmika* [drinks] are the eight drinks:
coconut drink, plantain drink, and jujube drink.
The *aśvattha* drink, the *udumbara* drink, the *pāruṣika* drink, the *mṛdvīkā* drink, and the *kharjūra* drink.
This is the intermediate summary verse (*antaroddāna*).
Coca, moca, and kola, along with aśvattha and udumbara;
pāruṣika, mṛdvīkā, and kharjūra is considered the eighth.
Clarified butter, oil, molasses, honey, and sugar are permitted for seven days;
root-medicines, bulb-medicines, leaf-medicines, flower-medicines, and fruit-medicines, as well as the five resins, the five alkalis, and the five salts, are permitted for the duration of one's life.
Among these, the root-medicines are musta, vacā, haridrā, ārdraka, and ativiṣā.
Or furthermore, whatever else extends to the purpose of medicinal roots for the sake of medicine and not for the sake of food— namely,
medicinal applications for swellings such as sandalwood,
cavikā, padmaka, devadāru, guḍūcī, and dāruharidrā.
Or again, whatever else spreads for the purpose of medicinal decoctions and not for the sake of food—
namely, leaf-medicines such as the leaf of *paṭola*, the leaf of *vāśika*, the leaf of *nimba*, the leaf of *kośātakī*, or the leaf of *saptaparṇa*.
Or furthermore, whatever else spreads for the purpose of leaf-medicine and not for the sake of food—
flower-medicine consists of five flowers.
Vāśika flower, nimba flower, dhātukī flower, śaṭī flower, {MS śikā flower, nāgā flower,} and lotus filament;
or whatever other flowers there may be that serve for the purpose of medicine and not for the purpose of food.
Fruit medicines:
*harītakī*, *āmalaka*, *vibhītaka*, black pepper (*marica*), and long pepper (*pippalī*). Or whatever else serves for the purpose of fruit medicine, and not for the purpose of food.
There are five resins: asafoetida, resin of the *sarja* tree, *taka*, *takakarṇī*, and that which comes from them.
Among these, asafoetida is the exudation of the asafoetida tree.
Sarjarasa is the resin of the *sāla* tree.
*Takola* is lac; *takakarṇī* is beeswax; that which comes from other trees is [also] resin. What are the five alkalis?
Barley alkali, alkali from *yāvaśūka*, alkali from *sarjikā*, sesame alkali, and alkali from *vāsaka*.
What are the five salts? Rock salt (*saindhava*), biḍa salt (*viḍa*), black salt (*sauvarcala*), sea salt (*romaka*), and rock-salt from the ocean (*sāmudraka*).
What are the five astringent decoctions?
They are the astringent decoction of mango, the astringent decoction of neem, the astringent decoction of rose-apple, the astringent decoction of acacia, and the astringent decoction of *kośamba*.

In that regard, whatever is for the [current] day, whatever is for a watch of the night, whatever is for seven days, and whatever is for as long as life lasts—if that which is for the [current] day has been mixed together, it should be consumed at the proper time; once the proper time has passed, it should not be used.
It must not be consumed.

Regarding that which is for one night (*yāmika*), that which is for seven days (*sāptāhika*), and that which is for as long as life lasts (*yāvajjīvika*): if that which is for one night has become mixed with [other substances], it may be consumed within that one night; once the night has passed, it must not be consumed.

If that which is for seven days and that which is for as long as life lasts have become mixed with [other substances], it may be consumed within seven days; once the seven days have passed, it must not be consumed.
That which is for life-long use must be used after having performed the formal act of dedication (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for life-long use.
Furthermore, it should be dedicated in this manner:
having washed one's hands and received the object, standing before the monks, this should be said:
“Pay attention, Venerable One! I, [name], designate this medicine for as long as life lasts, for their sake and for the sake of my fellow celibates. Thus a second and a third time.
Just as one may determine [the use of] something for as long as life lasts, so too may one determine it for a watch of the night or for seven days.
The setting was Śrāvastī. Now, a certain monk fell ill with a wind-related affliction.
He approached the physician;
having approached him, he said,
"I am afflicted by a wind-disorder."
"I have fallen ill; prescribe a medicine for me. He replied, "Noble sir, consume some fat, and you will recover your health."
The monk said,
"Noble sir, am I a man-eater?
He replied:
"O monk, this is your medicine; it is not possible to become healthy otherwise.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"If a physician says, 'This medicine for the monk must be consumed by you; otherwise, it is not possible to become healthy,' then it should be used."
The monks did not know;
they questioned a physician, and he said:
"Noble ones, your very Teacher is omniscient; go to him and ask.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One said:
Five types of fat should be consumed.
Which five?
Fish fat, otter fat, porpoise fat, bear fat, and pig fat.
Thus, these five kinds of fat are not to be consumed if they are cooked at the wrong time, strained at the wrong time, received at the wrong time, or consecrated at the wrong time. Likewise,
they are not to be consumed if they are cooked at the right time, but strained at the wrong time, received at the wrong time, or consecrated at the wrong time.

"Those [medicinal substances] that have been cooked at the proper time, strained at the proper time, received at an improper time, and consecrated at an improper time are not to be consumed. Those that have been cooked at the proper time, strained at the proper time, received at the proper time, and consecrated at the proper time may be consumed for seven days by means of using them as oil. Then, that monk consumed the fat.
He recovered his health. Thinking, "I have become well," he discarded the remaining fat. Subsequently, another monk fell ill with exactly the same malady.
He too went to the physician and said, "O gentle-faced one, such an illness has arisen in me; prescribe a medicine for it. The physician prescribed marrow for him as well.
He went to that monk, who said:
"Venerable sir, you have used fat; the physician has also prescribed fat for me."
"Is there anyone remaining who might stay?
He replied,
"There was, but she was dismissed by me."
"This was not well done.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One,
and the Blessed One said:
A nun must not discard the residual fat that has been used. I shall prescribe the rules of proper conduct for the monk who is the keeper of the fat. By the keeper of the fat...
The fat remaining after being used by a nun should be given to this monk upon his request;
otherwise, it should be placed in the infirmary storehouse,
thinking, "Whoever shall need it will take it."
A monk who is a keeper of fat, if he does not conduct himself by undertaking the rules of customary conduct as they have been prescribed, becomes guilty of an offense.
The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.
At that time, a certain monk developed the disease of scabies.
He approached the physician and said, "Venerable sir, a disease of scabies has arisen in me; please prescribe a medicine. He replied:
"Noble one, partake of astringent decoctions;
you will recover your health.
"Worthy sir, am I a seeker of sensual pleasures?"
He said,
"This is medicine for you, O monk;
it is not possible to become healthy otherwise."
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
As before, up until: "The Teacher is omniscient; go to him and ask him."
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"There are five impurities."
The astringent decoctions were as before.
That monk, having prepared the decoction according to the rules, rubbed his body with it; it became a single solid mass.
The Blessed One said,
"It should be made into powder.
The monks powdered it while it was still moist.
It had become a solid mass.
The Blessed One said: "It must be dried."
They dry it in the sun,
and it becomes devoid of potency.
The Blessed One said:
It should not be dried in the sun;
they dry it in the shade,
yet even so, it becomes putrid.
The Blessed One said,
"They should be dried in the shade and the sun.
The monks, having smeared their bodies with a decoction, bathed.
They did not perform the function of the decoction.
The Blessed One said:
"It should be purified by hand-rubbing until [the impurity] is gone."
Then, having applied a decoction, he was to bathe;
thus he performed the function of the decoction.
Through the decoction, the monk’s illness was pacified.
He discarded the remaining decoction.
Subsequently, a similar illness arose in another monk;
he went to the physician.
As before:
"I have abandoned him; I have not done well."
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, I shall prescribe the rules of proper conduct for a monk who wears saffron-colored robes."
A monk who possesses a dye-vat should give the remaining dye to any monk who desires it,
or he should store it in the infirmary.
A monk who carries the kaṣāya robe but does not undertake and abide by the rules of customary conduct as they have been prescribed commits an offense. The setting was Śrāvastī.
At that time, a certain monk developed an eye disease.
He approached the physician and said,
"Good sir, an eye disease has appeared in me; please prescribe a remedy."
He said, "Noble sir, apply ointment;
you will recover."
"O gentle-faced one, are we indulgers in sensual pleasures?
Noble sir, this is your medicine;
it is not possible to become healthy otherwise."
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"The ointment should be used according to the physician's instruction."
They did not know;
they questioned the physician, and he said:
"Noble one, your Teacher is omniscient; go to him and ask. The monks then reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"There are five types of collyrium:
flower collyrium, juice collyrium, powder collyrium, pill collyrium, and Sauvīraka collyrium."
He used it and was restored to health;
however, he placed the remaining ointment here and there, and it was lost.
When another monk developed an eye disease,
he approached him and said,
"Venerable sir, an eye disease has also appeared in me."
"Do you have any ointment remaining? He searched for it, but did not find it.
He said, "Venerable sir, there was collyrium;
however, it is no longer obtainable now."
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"A monk must not place collyrium anywhere or everywhere."
I shall prescribe the rules of proper conduct for a monk who carries ointment.
Ointments must be placed by monks who carry them in this very manner:
flower-ointment in a bowl.
Liquid ointment should be kept in a small box;
powdered ointment, pill ointment, and *sauvīraka* should be tied in a small pouch and hung on a peg.
I have prescribed these rules of proper conduct for the monk who carries ointments.
If one does not cause these to be undertaken and maintained, one incurs an offense of transgression. The setting was in Śrāvastī.
The Venerable Saikata was insane and deranged; he wandered here and there.
When that brahmin householder saw him, he asked,
"Whose son is this venerable one?
Others said:
"Of such-and-such a householder.
They replied, "The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are without a protector; they have not even gone forth [into homelessness]."
"If he had not gone forth, his kinsmen would have provided medical treatment for him.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One,
and the Blessed One said:
This being the case, monks, the monk Saikata must be questioned regarding his illness.
Then they approached the physician and said, "Good sir, his illness is such and such."
"Prescribe a medicine;
let the noble one consume raw meat,
and he will recover."
“Noble sir, is that a man-eater?
“Venerable one, it is not possible to remain at ease otherwise.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"If it is thus, then medicine must be taken;
otherwise, it is not possible to become healthy."
"Meat should be given.
The monks gave it accordingly,
yet he did not eat it.
The Blessed One said,
"It should be given after binding the eyes with a cloth. They gave it accordingly.
The cloth was released very quickly;
he saw that his hands were smeared with it,
and he vomited.
The Blessed One said:
"He must not be released immediately.
However, if he is to be released immediately, then his hands should first be placed before him in very pure water, and only afterwards should the cloth be removed."
He recovered his health;
however, that same pregnancy craving arose in him again.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"When one has recovered, then, having undertaken this training, that state must be practiced.
If one practices otherwise, one becomes guilty of an offense."
The setting was Rājagṛha.
The venerable Pilindavatsa had been ill for some time since he went forth.
He was addressed by the monks:
"Venerable sir, is your illness like this?
He replied, "Venerable sirs, I have always been subject to much illness."
The section on departure does not exist.
They said,
"Elder, what was maintained previously?"
He said,
"The medicine is in a tortoise-shell box;
why do you not take it now?"
"It was not permitted by the Blessed One.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
This being the case, it is permitted:
monks should carry a medicinal pouch;
monks should carry medicines consisting of roots, flowers, stalks, and fruits.
They did not place all the medicines in a leather pouch.
The Blessed One said:
"Fruit medicines should be kept in a leather pouch."
Roots, flowers, stalks, and medicinal herbs should be tied in bundles and placed on pegs.
The Blessed One said:
They should be dried from time to time;
if they dry them in the sun,
they become devoid of potency.
The Blessed One said: "It should not be dried in the sun. They dried it in the shade.
Nevertheless, it was purified.
The Blessed One said:
"It should be dried in the shade and the sun."
Having set out, they depart;
when wind and rain come, they do not enter.
The Blessed One said:
"It should be brought in. The Blessed One said, "It should be brought in," but they did not know by whom it should be brought in.
The Blessed One said:
“... it does not come about by means of a novice monk.”
He is not yet a novice; he must be admitted by himself.
[The food] becomes mixed up;
thinking that the monks have touched it, they do not consume it.
The Blessed One said:
"Having examined it again and again, it should be consumed; one should not feel remorse in this matter."
The setting was Śrāvastī. Because the Venerable Revata had doubts regarding this or that matter, he became known as Kāṅkṣārevata, "Revata the Doubter."
Having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, he entered Śrāvastī for alms.
Proceeding by stages, he went to a sugar-mill and saw that the sugar was being bound together with chaff.
He said:
"Sirs, do not bind the molasses with husks.
"Noble one, do you know any other way to bind it?
"I know no other way to bind it."
"However, we eat at the wrong time.
Noble sir, eat either at the proper time or at the wrong time;
this is his bond, for otherwise he would not remain bound."
At another time, molasses and solid food were prepared for the Saṃgha,
but he did not eat it.
His co-residents and pupils said to him:
"Noble sir, hard molasses sweets have been prepared for the Saṅgha; please partake. He replied, "Friends, this contains meat."
They too did not eat.
They were addressed by other monks:
"Venerable ones, molasses and solid food have been provided for the Saṃgha; why do you not partake?"
They said,
"The preceptor says that this contains meat;
therefore, they too have not eaten it."
He had a large retinue;
"it was not consumed by them" means that for the most part it was not consumed by the entire Saṅgha.
The monks [reported] this matter to the Blessed One.
They reported this to the Blessed One, who said:
"It is not permitted to perform a service involving food with food that is not food.
Considering it to be pure as regards its origin, it should be consumed; no remorse should be felt in this matter."
The setting was Śrāvastī.
Then, in the forenoon, the venerable Revata adjusted his undergarment, took his bowl and robe, and entered Śrāvastī for alms.
He proceeded in due order along the street.
He saw a grocer who, having touched roasted barley flour, then touched molasses.
He said,
"Good sir, do not touch molasses after having touched roasted barley flour."
"We must eat out of season.
He said,
"Noble one, who is giving me hand-washing water so frequently?"
At another time, molasses and solid food were provided for the Saṃgha;
he did not consume it.
His co-residents and pupils said:
"Noble sir, molasses and solid food have been prepared for the Saṃgha; why do you not eat?
He replied, "Friends, this contains meat."
They, too, did not consume it.
They were told by the monks:
"Venerable ones, molasses and solid food have been prepared for the Saṃgha."
"Why do you not eat?
They replied,
"The preceptor says that this contains meat."
They, too, did not consume it;
for he had a great retinue,
and because they did not consume it, for the most part the entire Saṅgha did not consume it.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"It is not permissible to perform a service involving material goods by means of material goods."
Thinking, "It is pure with respect to the house," one should consume it;
no remorse should be felt in this matter.
The setting was Śrāvastī. A wind-related illness had arisen in the Venerable Śāriputra.
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana reflected:
"I have performed service for the Venerable Śāriputra many times, yet I have never once asked him about his illness.
Suppose now that I were to ask a physician.
He then approached a physician.
"O gentle-faced one, such-and-such an illness has arisen for the Venerable Śāriputra; prescribe a medicine that is suitable for it.
He replied, "Noble sir, salt and fermented gruel will serve as the medicine."
He prepared some fermented gruel,
but there was no salt;
he then began to search for salt.
The Venerable Pilindavatsa said to him, "Venerable sir, I have a horn-spoon of salt that has been empowered for as long as I live;
if the Blessed One permits it, I shall give it. This was heard by Śāriputra.
He said,
"Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, such a thought occurred to my mind:
it is not permissible to consume that which is for a limited time [kālika] as if it were for the duration of one's life [yāvajjīvika]."
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana informed the Blessed One of this matter.
The Blessed One said:
"It is not permitted, Maudgalyāyana, to consecrate that which is for a limited time, that which is for a watch of the night, that which is for seven days, or that which is for as long as life lasts."

In this regard, Maudgalyāyana, whatever is for a watch of the night, whatever is for seven days, and whatever is for as long as life lasts— if these are mixed with what is for the [proper] time, then considering them "mixed with what is for the time," they should be consumed within the [proper] time; once the time has passed, they should not be consumed.

Whatever is for a watch of the night (*yāmika*), whatever is for seven days (*sāptāhika*), and whatever is for as long as life lasts (*yāvajjīvika*), if these are mixed with that which is for a watch of the night, they should be consumed during that watch; once the watch has passed, they must not be consumed.
And whatever is for seven days and whatever is for as long as life lasts, if they are mixed with that which is for seven days, they are considered "mixed with the seven-day [allowance]."
Having determined this, it should be consumed for seven days; once the seven days have passed, it must not be consumed.
As for that which is to be used for as long as one lives, it should be consumed for as long as one lives.
If one consumes it otherwise, one incurs an offense of transgression (*sātisāra*).
The summary verse (*uddāna*) says:
Mahāsena, meat, hemorrhoids, the wind-disease, and Pūrṇaka. [...]
The Buddha, the Blessed One, while wandering on a tour through the country of Kāśī, arrived at Vārāṇasī.
He stayed at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana.
In Vārāṇasī lived a householder named Mahāsena, who was wealthy, possessed of great riches, and of vast enjoyments.
His wife was named Mahāsenā;
he, together with his wife, was faithful, auspicious, and of virtuous intent.
He heard [the following]:
The Blessed One, while wandering on a tour through the Kāśī country, arrived at Vārāṇasī and stayed there in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana. Upon hearing this, it occurred to him once again:

"Many times I have invited the Blessed One to my home, yet I have never offered him all the necessary provisions. What if I were now to offer the Blessed One all the necessary provisions for the three-month rainy season retreat? Having thought this, he approached the place where the Blessed One was, and having approached, he bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet and sat down to one side.
[The folios from 95 to 140 are missing. (Fol. 141r3 = GBM 6.950;
MSV I A) From afar, the Blessed One saw a dark-blue line of forest.
Having seen it, he addressed the yakṣa Vajrapāṇi:
"Do you see this dark-blue line of forest, Vajrapāṇi?
"I see it, Blessed One.
"This, Vajrapāṇi, is the region of Kaśmīra."
One hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there will be a monk named Mādhyandina, who was a co-resident disciple of the monk Ānanda.
He will subdue the wicked nāga Huluṭa;
then, having sat cross-legged, he will cause the teaching to enter the entire region of Kaśmīra.
The dwelling place suitable for insight (vipaśyanā) is the region of Kaśmīra;
it consists of sixty thousand villages, six thousand villages,
sixty villages, and three villages— this is the region of Kaśmīra.
In Bhraṣṭālā, the disciplined seer and the afflicted yakṣa along with his retinue were subdued;
in Kaṇṭhā, the yakṣiṇī and her retinue were subdued;
and he arrived at Dhānyapura.
In Dhānyapura, King Sena was established in the supreme truths;
he had not yet attained *nairātmya*.
In *nairātmya*, there was a certain potter.
He was exceedingly intoxicated with pride in his craft;
he was taking down dry vessels from the wheel.
The Blessed One, knowing that the time for his conversion had come, assumed the guise of a potter and began to converse with him.
"What kind of vessels do you take down from the wheel?
He replied,
"Dry ones."
I too shall bring down the dry [wood];
you are equal to me;
what is the use of this fragile thing?
"I even fashion things made of ivory;
you are more skillful than I,
not only in making those of ivory, but also those made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal."
Having gained faith,
the Blessed One then caused his disguise as a potter to vanish and stood in his own form; together with his retinue, he was established in the truths.
He arrived at Śādvalā;
there, together with his great retinue of yakṣas, he established Pālitakoṭa and Nāgapālaka in the taking of refuge and the precepts of training.
He then arrived at Nandivardhana.
In Nandivardhana, King Bhavadeva together with his retinue, as well as the yakṣa Bhūpa and his seven sons, were established in the truths.
There, Aśvaka and Punarvasuka were reborn in the womb of a nāga.
After the passing of twelve years, they became agitated and spoke thus:
"The Dharma was not taught to us by the Blessed One, whereby we have fallen and been born in the womb of a nāga."
"How shall we understand his teaching?
This thought occurred to the Blessed One:
"They possess great power."

Knowing that it was possible that his teaching might be reduced to ashes after he had passed into final nirvana, he went to the residence of Aśvaka and Punarvasuka. Having approached them, he taught them a Dharma discourse consisting of four lines, saying:
"You shall understand its explanation."
Thinking, "Who are we that we should be knowers of the True Dharma? they became immersed right there.
Then this thought occurred to them:
"The Dharma has been taught to us by the Blessed One."
"But we did not know this.
Then the Blessed One placed a single footprint in that very spot;
Aśvaka and Punarvasuka submerged themselves there once again.
Thinking, "The Blessed One still remains in that very place," [the Blessed One] converted the yakṣiṇīs Nālī and Udārī;
then he arrived at Kuntīnagara.
In the city of Kuntī, a yakṣiṇī known as Kuntī resided; she was full of wrath and fierce.
She devoured every child born to the brahmin householders of Kuntīnagara as soon as they were born.
The brahmin householders of Kuntīnagara heard that the Blessed One had arrived at Kuntīnagara.
Hearing that he was staying in that region, they gathered together and departed from the city of Kuntī. They approached the Blessed One,
and having approached him, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
As the Brahmins and householders of Kauśāmbī sat to one side, the Blessed One instructed, inspired, and gladdened them with a discourse on the Dharma as before, and then remained silent.
Then those faithful Brahmins and householders rose from their seats, draped their upper robes over one shoulder, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, said this to him:
"May the Blessed One, together with the community of monks, accept our invitation for a meal at our home tomorrow."

Then, perceiving that the Blessed One had finished his meal, had washed his hands, and had set aside his bowl while seated, he took a golden pitcher, stood before the Blessed One, and while making a request, spoke thus:
"The Blessed One has tamed those various wicked nāgas and wicked yakṣas."

"Venerable Sir, this yakṣiṇī Kuntī has for a long time been the co-wife of those who have no rival, and she has become a hater toward those who bear her no malice; she carries off our children as soon as they are born.
Oh, would that the Blessed One, out of compassion, might discipline the yakṣiṇī Kuntī!
At that very time, the yakṣiṇī Kuntī was seated and present in that same assembly.
There the Blessed One addressed the yakṣiṇī:
"Have you heard it, Kuntī?
"I have heard it, Blessed One."
"Have you heard it, Kunti?
"I have heard it, Sugata.
"Desist from this evil and unrighteous dharma!"
"Venerable sir, I shall desist on the condition that these people build a monastery for my sake.
Then the Blessed One addressed the brahmins and householders of Kauśāmbī.
"Have you heard this, brahmins and householders?
"We have heard it, Blessed One. "What do you think about this?"
“We shall do so, Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having disciplined the yakṣiṇī Kuntī along with her retinue, departed for Kharjūrikā.
Having arrived,
he saw young children playing with mounds of dust in Khajūrikā.
Having seen the young children playing with mounds of dust, the Blessed One—
Again, he addressed the yakṣa Vajrapāṇi:
"Vajrapāṇi, do you see those young children playing with sand stupas?
"I do, Blessed One."
Vajrapāṇi, four hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there will be a king named Kaniṣka of the Kuśāṇava lineage. He will establish a stūpa in this region,
and it shall be known by the name "Kaniṣka Stūpa."

"And after I have passed into parinirvāṇa, he will carry out the work of a Buddha. Then the Blessed One, having converted seven million seven hundred thousand living beings in the interval between the abode of Cāpalāla and Rohitaka, arrived at Rohitaka; entering his dwelling, he withdrew into solitary meditation.
In the evening, the Blessed One rose from his seclusion and addressed the venerable Ānanda:
"Come, Ānanda, let us go to Ādirājya.
Then the venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Blessed One, previously you spoke thus:
'In the northern region we shall convert the Naga king Apalāla;
there are five advantages to the northern region.'"
And yet again, the Blessed One said:
"Come, Ānanda, let us go to where the primordial kingdom is.
How is that so?
The Blessed One said:
"Ānanda, I went to the Northern Region accompanied by Vajrapāṇi;
I prophesied as far as the Tamasāvana forest."
The Sand-Stūpa has been prophesied. Ānanda, I have traveled as far as Rohitaka and as far as the realm of the Naga king Apalāla;
in this interval, seventy-seven hundred thousand living beings were disciplined by the Tathāgata.
There are five disadvantages in the Northern Region: stumps, thorns, trees, stones, and gravel; and women who behave with fierce dog-like ferocity and coarse conduct.
The summary verse (uddāna) says:
The first kingdom, Bhadrāśva, Mathurā, and Otalā.
Ārāmavairaṃbhya, Ayodhyā, the river Gaṅgā, and Pretāvelāmo are the western [cities].
Then the Blessed One, while wandering on a tour through the country of the Śūrasenas, arrived at Ādirājya.
There, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda:
"Ānanda, it was in this very place that King Mahāsammata was first consecrated with the royal inauguration."
Having been consecrated, he became the first of kings; because his kingdom was the first, the name "Ādirājya" came into being.
He arrived at Bhadrāśva.
There, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"In this place, Ānanda, the auspicious horse-treasure of King Mahāsammata appeared, from which his name Bhadrāśva came to be known.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: 'Come, Ānanda, let us go to Mathurā.'"
"So be it, Venerable Sir," the venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One set out for Mathurā.
Having seen from afar a row of forest that was intensely blue, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda once more.
"Do you see, Ānanda, that dark-blue line of forest?
Yes, Venerable Sir. Ānanda, this is the mountain named Urumuṇḍa."
"In this Mathurā, two brothers, Naṭa and Bhaṭa, will establish a monastery for me after I have passed into parinirvāṇa a hundred years hence;
therefore, it shall be known by the name Naṭabhaṭika, and it shall be preeminent. (MSV I 4)
"Ānanda, there will be resting places suitable for calm abiding and insight.
Today in Mathurā, there will be a young son of a perfumer named Gupta;
his son will be named Upagupta, a Buddha without the [major] marks."
After I have entered parinirvāṇa, he will go forth in my teaching after having lived there for a year;
known by the name Mādhyandina, he will be a co-resident of the monk Ānanda,
and he will cause Upagupta to go forth.
Upagupta will be the last of the instructors;
there will be a cave in the Grove of Trees,
eighteen cubits in length.
It will be twelve [yojanas] in width and seven in height. Whosoever shall realize arhatship through his instruction shall deposit a stone slab measuring four finger-breadths in that cave.
When that cave becomes full of the remains of Arhats, then Upagupta will pass into parinirvāṇa;
and having passed into parinirvāṇa, they shall gather those very remains of Arhats and cremate him.
The monks, filled with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts.
"Venerable One, it was prophesied by the Blessed One that even while still in the future, the Venerable Upagupta would be compassionate toward many people.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it is not only now; just as he has acted for the benefit of many people in the past, listen to that, and attend well and thoroughly to it, and I shall speak."
Long ago, monks, on three sides of this very Mount Urumuṇḍa there dwelt Pratyekabuddhas, sages, and monkeys;
on one side were five hundred Pratyekabuddhas, on the second five hundred sages, and on the third five hundred monkeys.
It was the habit of the leader of the monkey troop to kill every newborn monkey infant as soon as it was born.
Thereupon, those female monkeys, overwhelmed by grief for their young, began to converse with one another:
"Listen, you female monkeys!"
"This leader of our troop kills every young one as soon as it is born. Therefore, a strategic plan must be devised:
whichever female monkey among us becomes pregnant must not inform the leader of the troop."
Then, at another time, a certain female monkey became pregnant;
she was hidden away by them in a secluded place and nourished with roots and fruits,
and a male monkey cub was born.
He too was placed by them in a secluded spot, nourished, and raised.
When he had grown up, he then caused that leader of the herd to be driven away from his own herd to Mount Urumuṇḍa, here and there.
He began to wander about.
While wandering, he heard the sound of Pratyekabuddhas;
he went into their presence.
When they had become familiar with living together, he would provide them with roots, leaves, flowers, fruits, and tooth-sticks;
they, in turn, would dispose of the remnants from his alms-bowl.
It was the custom of those Pratyekabuddhas that after eating again and again, they would sit cross-legged.
That monkey, having observed their deportment, sat down cross-legged.
Then, at another time, it occurred to those Pratyekabuddhas:
"What is to be attained by us with this body of boiled flesh?"
"It would indeed be well if we were now to enter the peaceful realm of nirvāṇa.
Thereupon, having performed the miracles of blazing, heating, raining, and flashing lightning, they passed into final nirvāṇa in the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder.
This was their time of emergence.
"They do not rise during that night.
Not seeing them, the monkey could find no peace of mind;
eventually, that monkey entered the cave and began to rummage through the robes of those pratyekabuddhas.
The deity who resided in that cave thought to herself:
"Lest this monkey should disturb the robes of the Pratyekabuddha," and she remained there after blocking the door with a massive rock.
Then that monkey, having grieved, exhausted himself, and lamented, departed;
he wandered all around Mount Urumuṇḍa,
and finding no delight there and obtaining no stability, he listened intently for the sound of human voices.
He heard the sound of those sages' voices speaking,
and like a traveler who has lost his way, he approached them with great haste. There,
the sages were performing arduous austerities.
Some stand with their hands raised; some stand on one foot;
some perform the austerity of the five fires.
When that monkey had come to live with them in full confidence, he began to provide for those sages roots, leaves, flowers, fruits, and tooth-sticks;
they, in turn, would set aside the remains of their alms-food for him.
Disturbing their usual mode of conduct, he demonstrated to them the deportment of a Pratyekabuddha.
There, he lowered the hands of those who held their hands raised, made a *ricchaṭā* sound, and stood before them with his legs crossed in the *paryaṅka* posture.
He extinguished the fire of those who were practicing the five-fold austerity, made a *ricchaṭā* sound, and stood before them with his legs crossed in the *paryaṅka* posture.
Then, those sages informed the instructor of what had occurred.
"Preceptor, this monkey is creating an obstacle to our ascetic practice.
They reported this to him in detail,
and he said:
"Sirs, these monkeys are indeed possessed of mindfulness;
surely some sages must have been seen by him in this [ascetic] posture."
"You too should sit down, having assumed the cross-legged posture exactly as it was established.
They sat down, having likewise assumed the cross-legged posture;
their former roots of merit then became manifest before them.

Without a teacher and without an instructor, they produced through knowledge the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment and realized pratyekabodhi. In that monkey, they conceived a faith characterized by the Dharma.
Regarding those new crops—
Whenever they received alms-food from the countryside consisting of fresh fruits of the nine seasons, they would first give those to him and only then consume them themselves.
Later, at another time, that monkey passed away.
Thereupon, those Pratyekabuddhas had fragrant wood collected from various regions and locations; having built a funeral pyre with all that fragrant wood, they cremated him.
"What do you think, monks?
That very monkey who was nurtured by the Pratyekabuddhas is this very Upagupta.
Even then he was intent upon the welfare of many people; even now, he has been prophesied by me as one who is compassionate for the welfare of many."
Then the Blessed One, while wandering on a tour through the Śūrasena country, arrived at Mathurā.
The brahmins of Mathurā heard that the śramaṇa Gautama had arrived at Mathurā;
he exceedingly delights in, illuminates, proclaims, establishes, refutes, reveals, clarifies, and teaches the purity of the four castes.
"If he enters Mathurā, it will be an obstacle to our gains;
moreover, it is heard that he is afraid of disrespect.
If someone were to show him disrespect, he would not enter Mathurā at all—and what if some low-born man were to treat him with contempt? (MSV I 8)
He will enter [the city] and will not pay it special attention.
It would be well if some prominent person were to show him disrespect.
Who, then, is our prominent person?

At that time, in Mathurā, there was a brahmin named Nīlabhūti who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, who illuminated his own doctrines and was capable of refuting the arguments of others;
his speech followed the truth. Thereupon, the brahmins of Mathurā, having gathered and assembled together, approached Nīlabhūti.
"Preceptor, it is heard that the ascetic Gautama has arrived here;
he is said to be exceedingly afraid of a lack of respect, proclaiming— as previously described— the purification of the four castes, and so forth."
If someone were to show him disrespect, he would not enter Mathurā;
and if a low-born man were to treat him with disrespect, he would not take notice of it;
but if some person of high standing were to show him disrespect, that would be excellent.
"Therefore, who among us is a leading man except for the preceptor?
You must show him disrespect and revile him with verbal blows.
Nīlabhūti said:
"Gentlemen, this tongue of mine follows the truth:
if he should be worthy of abuse, I shall abuse him;
but if he is worthy of praise, I shall satisfy him."

Then the brahmin Nīlabhūti, escorted by the most venerable brahmins residing in Mathurā, approached the place where the Blessed One was. From afar, the brahmin Nīlabhūti saw the Blessed One adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man,
his body radiant with the eighty secondary characteristics, embellished by a celestial luster, and possessing a brilliance exceeding that of a thousand suns.
Seeing him seated at the foot of a certain tree with a peaceful deportment— like a moving mountain of jewels, auspicious on all sides—
he began to praise him, his eyes wide with wonder.
Having properly directed my mind, speech, and body along with my senses,
O ocean of great virtues who has become a source of excellence, I shall describe even a single portion of your qualities.
You are the most excellent among speakers, irreproachable, with senses perfectly composed;
you know the ultimate truth and are unshakable by all the striving proponents of other doctrines.
Your conduct is indeed fully perfected, O you whose vows are well-fulfilled, having accomplished your vows.
Your powerful and inexhaustible concentration is like Nārāyaṇa, the king of mountains.
O bull among men, you have no pain, no despondency, no fear, and no fatigue;
you have no calamity, much less strife, nor is there ever any lack of forbearance toward living beings.
You do not run forward, nor do you shrink back; you neither suffer distress nor do you rejoice.
Your mind is perpetually auspicious, ever as immovable as Meru, the lord of mountains.
O bull among sages, your vast wisdom, encompassing all elements, is fully unveiled.
Unobstructed and inexhaustible, you abide in various spheres of existence.
O Sage, you have no "how" or "why," no perplexity, and no doubt anywhere;
for you yourself, through your knowledge, have known all that is prior and posterior.
You delight in seeing what is pleasing, you delight in seeing the virtuous, you delight in the virtuous, and you delight in the wise.
For indeed, both the pleasant and the unpleasant are equal to you; you are always a bringer of joy and are thus honored.
You possess sweet eloquence, your speech is accompanied by smiles, and you are mindful and confident.
You speak what is approved by the wise, and your fame is spread throughout the three worlds.
O Sage, many humans, gods, asuras, yakṣas, and rākṣasas— those who are learned in this world— approach you again and again to question you, yet you are never weary of it.
O Great Sage, having been satisfied by your own words, the gods, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas among men depart with their doubts dispelled, after having paid homage at your feet.
Whether standing, sitting, coming, going, lying down, remaining silent, or speaking— [all these actions are observed].
Moreover, O Gautama, your manner of carrying the robe and bowl is entirely beautiful;
you speak at the proper time, O Best of Men, with speech that is neither too slow nor too hurried, even-paced, endowed with the qualities of sweetness of voice, and free from redundancy. (12–13)

You are powerful, world-renowned, a knower of men, a bull among men, and a lord; yet you neither pride yourself nor do you hold this entire world, including the gods, in contempt. You are never amazed by things, whether they be stable or unstable, remaining as they naturally are.
Toward friends and toward enemies, toward those who are hostile and those who are compliant—[he felt] lamentation with a voice that was not dejected, yet choked with flowing saliva;
it was joined with burning and consuming anguish, and was emaciated by fear, disease, fever, and grief. (15–16)
Having observed the world to be utterly agitated, oppressed by hundreds of various sufferings,
long deprived of a protector, restless, driven by the thirst for existence, and shrouded in darkness—
[he] brought down upon the Sage his great compassion and his manifold inherent power.

For you yourself, O Bull among the Śākyas, are intent on liberating those who are distressed. You have proclaimed this suffering of existence along with its cause, the total destruction of the suffering of existence, and the incomparable path leading to the cessation of the suffering of existence. (18–19)
O supreme among the great leaders of exceeding vigor, best of those who proclaim the truth!
There is no one equal to you; how could there be anyone superior? Such a person is not to be found even within the three worlds. [Free from] aversion and attachment. (Fol. 144v1 = GBM 6.957)

O Sage of excellent vows, those outflows do not exist for you, nor do they exist at all; likewise, O Sage, your attachments, aversions, and conflicts are never present. Having abandoned the pleasant and the unpleasant, as well as happiness and suffering, and the uneven and the even, you remain thus.
Transcending both aversion and attraction, you wander here in tranquility, self-restrained. Your mind is not indeed dejected in misfortune, nor do you exult in praise;
for you, infamy and fame are equal, as are abuse and veneration. (22–23)
Furthermore, you endure the excessive words uttered by wicked people against you, just as a tusker at the front of a battle endures arrows fiercely loosed [at him].
O Sage, you are one who speaks well and is patient with speech; even toward harsh words, you do not become resentful.
And you conduct yourself with equanimity, O Sage, toward both auspicious injunctions and words.
You are constantly honored, O worthy of the best offerings, by men, gods, asuras, yakṣas, and rākṣasas, as well as by the great-souled sages; yet your steadfast mind is not perturbed.
"You do not think of yourself as superior to this; you do not think of yourself as inferior to this;

you do not think of yourself as equal to this. These three types of conceit do not exist in you. You are steadfast, regarding a clod of earth and gold as the same, and viewing lapis lazuli, potsherds, and pebbles as equal."
O Great Sage, you indeed traverse this world with its gods as if it were mere grass and wood.
(28) Bearing a breeze that is cool and warm through contact with the rays of the snowy sun, you endure it like a king of mountains; your steadfast mind is not disturbed. (29)
O Sage, you who are free from outflows, having reflected upon this, you point out that these—beds, seats, drinks, food, and various upper and lower robes—are for the sake of those who need them.
Yet you do not grieve, O Protector; "it is not mine," and you have no possessions, O Sage.
You are unshaken, free from attachment to pleasant speech, and liberated from various misfortunes.
You do not rejoice upon gaining profit, nor do you fall into despondency from its lack;
you endure insult, and you do not delight in honor here.
Even when struck by sharp swords and arrows— those foremost sandalwoods produced on the slopes of Mount Mandara, fragrant and resembling blood— your mind was never once disturbed.
You did not engage in useless talk, nor in that discourse frequented by the wicked.
You do not speak of gain, nor of worldly things, nor of that which is disapproved by the great-souled ones.
You discourse on the topics of solitude that bring happiness, which proclaim nothing but tranquility.
O Supreme Deity, you speak those words which, when spoken, truly subdue all evil.
O Sage, you utter words that are sweet, coherent, well-composed, substantial, and definitive for the sake of the world;
yet there are those who are ignorant, possessed of perverted views, fickle, reckless, and attached to what they please. (36)

O Blessed One, you have no association with those who are slanderous, harsh, and deceitful. O Blessed One, your association is with those men who are honest, upright, pure, devoted to truth, masters of their senses, and who always act with circumspection.

O Knower of Dharma, Knower of Policy, Knower of Persons, I bow to you who possess the six super-knowledges at all times; O Sage, Knower of the Fields, Knower of the High and the Low, I bow my head to you, Knower of Right and Wrong Conduct. Though your virtues are vast, even this single portion of your qualities has indeed been recounted by me.
“O Noble One, no man in this world is able to reach the further shore of your ocean of virtues.
Thus was the Blessed One praised with these and other verses comprising five hundred hymns.

And to Nīlabhūti, who was thus inspired with faith, the Blessed One taught the Dharma in such a way that, while remaining seated on that very same seat, he attained the vision of the Truths. Then the brahmin Nīlabhūti, having praised the Blessed One, departed.
As he was traveling along the road, he was surrounded by the Brahmins of Mathurā,
who said to him, "Preceptor,
perform an act of disrespect toward the ascetic Gautama."
Having now come after offering praise, you say, "Sirs, I did not say this before;
my tongue speaks only the truth."
If he will be worthy of abuse,
he will be abused; if he will be worthy of praise, he will be praised.
"I shall praise him. "The ascetic Gautama, who is worthy of praise, has been praised by me.
Then, having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, the Blessed One entered Mathurā for alms.
Now at that time, the Festival of the Stars had arrived in Mathurā.
Then, a certain deity residing in Mathurā thought to herself:
"If the ascetic Gautama enters Mathurā..."
Knowing that he would create an obstacle for the Nakṣatrarātri festival, he stood naked before the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"O deity, even when not covered, a woman does not look beautiful, much less when she is naked."
Then that deity, feeling ashamed at being naked, withdrew to one side.
Thereupon the Blessed One stepped off the path and sat down on the seat prepared for him in front of the community of monks.
Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"Monks, there are these five disadvantages in Mathurā.
What are the five?
It is uneven with rises and hollows, and abounds in stumps and thorns."
"It is full of stones, pebbles, and potsherds; it is devoted to the worship of the moon; and it is crowded with many women.
Then the Blessed One, without even entering Mathurā, approached the abode of the yakṣa Gardabha.
Having approached and entered the abode of the yakṣa Gardabha, he sat down at the foot of a certain tree to dwell for the day.

The brahmin householders of Mathurā heard that the Blessed One had entered [the city] for alms but, being harassed by a deity, had not entered Mathurā at all and had instead gone to the abode of the yakṣa Gardabha. Upon hearing this, they each prepared a potful of pure and excellent hard and soft foods and loaded them onto carts.
Having mounted it, he approached the place where the Blessed One was;
having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
To the faithful brahmins and householders of Mathurā who were seated to one side, the Blessed One, with a discourse on the Dharma—as previously described—inspired them with joy and remained silent.
Then the faithful brahmins and householders rose from their seats, draped their upper robes over one shoulder, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, they said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, for the sake of the Blessed One, we have brought here a cart full of pure and excellent food, both hard and soft.
May the Blessed One accept it out of compassion."
Thereupon the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda:
"Go, Ānanda, to as many monks as there are who are staying near the abode of the yakṣa Gardabha."
"Summon all those who dwell there to the assembly hall;
they shall partake of the alms-food.
"So be it, Venerable Sir," the venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One, and having done so, he [gathered] as many monks as were at Gardabha...
Having gathered all those who were dwelling in dependence on the yakṣa’s abode, he brought them together in the assembly hall and approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, as many bhikṣus as there are dwelling in dependence upon the abode of the yakṣa Gardabha, they have all sat down and assembled together in the assembly hall.
Now, Blessed One, it is time for you to do as you see fit."
Then the Blessed One went to the assembly hall;
having arrived, he sat down on the seat prepared for him in front of the community of monks.
Then the faithful brahmins and householders of Mathurā [saw] him seated comfortably.

Having understood that the community of monks was headed by the Buddha, [they stood] as before, until—having washed their hands and set aside their bowls—they stood before the Blessed One and made this request:
"Venerable Sir, those various wicked nāgas and wicked yakṣas have been subdued by the Blessed One.
But this yakṣa Gardabhaka, Venerable Sir, has been an enemy for a long time to us who are ourselves without enmity."
He is an enemy of those who have no enemies; he is a betrayer of those who do not betray him;
he carries off children as they are born, one after another.
"O, would that the Blessed One, out of compassion, might discipline the yakṣa Gardabhaka!
At that time, the yakṣa Gardabhaka was seated and present in that very assembly.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the yakṣa Gardabhaka.
"Have you heard it, Gardabhaka?
"I have heard it, Blessed One.
"Have you heard it, Gardabhaka?"
"I have heard you, Sugata. I shall desist from this evil, unrighteous dharma.
Blessed One, I desist on this condition."
"If you are having a monastery built for the Saṅgha of monks from the four directions in my name," the Blessed One addressed the faithful Brahmins and householders of Mathurā:
"Have you heard this, Brahmins and householders?"
"It has been heard, Blessed One;
we shall have it built.
Thereupon, the Blessed One disciplined the yakṣa Gardabhaka along with his retinue of five hundred.
Faithful brahmin householders, dedicating [the merit] to them, had five hundred monasteries constructed.
In this way, the yakṣa Śara, the yakṣa Vana, and the yakṣiṇī Ālikāvendā Maghā were subdued.
Then, having entered Mathurā by means of his supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), the Blessed One subdued the yakṣiṇī Timisikā together with her retinue of five hundred.
For her sake as well, five hundred monasteries were constructed.
There, within and outside Mathurā, the Blessed One converted two thousand five hundred yakṣas;
for their sake, faithful brahmins and householders caused two thousand five hundred monasteries to be built.
Then the Blessed One arrived at Otalā and stayed there in Otalā,
in the Otalīya forest grove.
There lived a wealthy, affluent, and very prosperous brahmin householder named Oṭalāyana; such is the full account.
Then, having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, the Blessed One entered Oṭalā for alms.
In a certain place, there were about five hundred farmers.
With hair hanging down to their shoulders and dressed in hempen garments, they were plowing with a plow.
Those farmers saw the Blessed Buddha, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, his form radiant— so it is said in detail.
The Blessed One taught the Dharma to them,
until they became worthy of honor and salutation.
Then that thousand of oxen, having broken their yokes and thongs, approached the place where the Blessed One was.

Having approached and bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, they stood surrounding him. The Blessed One taught them the Dharma in three statements, whereby they were reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings.
Eventually, having realized the Truths, they returned to their own abodes.
The monks, overcome with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts: "Venerable Sir,
what karma was performed by these five hundred farmers and these oxen, as a result of which they became farmers born into poor households, and these [others] became oxen?"
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it was by these very individuals that such deeds were performed," and so forth in detail. These [monks] went forth in the teaching of Kāśyapa, the perfectly awakened one.
Because they were led there by laziness,
as the ripening of that karma, they became farmers.
And because those very oxen had gone forth as monks and showed disrespect toward the minor and secondary rules of training, [they have become oxen].
Through the ripening of that karma, they were reborn among the animals;

yet, because they went forth in the teaching of the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa, through the ripening of that karma, they have realized the vision of the Truths in my presence. Thus, monks, it is said: "Of those [deeds] that are entirely black," and so forth.

The brahmin Otalāyana heard that the ascetic Gautama had arrived at Otalā and was staying in the Otalīyaka forest grove. This is related in detail in the *Otalāyana-sūtra*, in the *Mārgavarga-nipāta* of the *Saṃyukta-āgama*.
{In the Saṃyuktāgama, in the Mārgavarga-nipāta} then this thought occurred to the brahmin Oṭalāyana:
"What further harm shall we do to him?"
He had previously heard that the ascetic Gautama, after feeding the community of disciples, makes a formal vow (*praṇidhāna*),

and that whatever he thinks of or whatever he prays for, all that he obtains. Then the brahmin Oṭalāyana rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows:
“May the Blessed One Gautama consent to take a meal at my home tomorrow, together with the community of monks.
[The rest follows] as before, until, having understood that the Blessed One had finished eating, washed his hands, and set aside his bowl, he took a lower seat and began to think of a false vow:
“May all these ascetics, sons of the Śākya, whom I have fed, become my oxen!”
Then the Blessed One, having understood with his own mind the thought in the mind of the brahmin Oṭalāyana, said this to the brahmin Oṭalāyana:
"Brahmin, the thought you have conceived is not fitting; it will not come to fruition."
For thus did the Blessed One say, "O monks, all these have exhausted further rebirth; generate another thought," and having given the instruction for the dedication of merit, he departed.
Then the Blessed One went to the monastery and sat down on the seat prepared for him in front of the community of monks.
Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"Monks, the brahmin Oṭalāyana has conceived an evil thought arising from a false resolution."
"After you have eaten, you should recite the verses of the Ṛṣis; thus,
your false vow shall not come to fruition."
Then, when that very night had passed, the Blessed One entered Oṭalā for alms with the Venerable Ānanda as his attendant monk.
At that time, in Oṭalā, there was an old woman named Kacaṅgalā;
she had gone to the riverbank seeking water.
The Blessed One, perceiving that the time for her conversion had come, addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"Go, Ānanda, and say to this old woman:
'The Blessed One is thirsty; offer him some water.'"
"So be it, Venerable Sir," the venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. He then approached the old woman Kacaṅgalā and, having approached her, said this to the old woman Kacaṅgalā:
"Kacaṅgalā, the Blessed One is thirsty; please give him some water."
She said,
"Noble one, I myself will bring it.
Then Kacaṅgalā, having filled a water jar, went very quickly toward where the Blessed One was.
Kacaṅgalā beheld the Blessed Buddha, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man,
his body radiant with the eighty minor characteristics, graced by a celestial luster, possessing a brilliance exceeding that of a thousand suns,
like a moving mountain of jewels, auspicious in every respect.
Upon seeing Kacaṅgalā together with him, maternal affection for her son arose within her.
With her arms raised, she began to embrace the Blessed One, crying out, "O son! O son!
The monks restrained her.
The Blessed One said:
"O monks, do not prevent this old woman.
For what reason? Because..."
For five hundred successive births, she has been my mother without interruption;
yet even so, she was prevented from embracing my body.
"Now she would surely vomit warm blood from her throat in an instant;
yet, recollecting her gratitude and seeing her longing for her son, I shall out of compassion and pity grant her the embrace of my body. Thus he spoke.
The Blessed One gave her an embrace around the neck;
having dispelled her maternal affection, she sat before the Blessed One to hear the Dharma.
Then, the Blessed One, knowing her disposition, latent tendencies, elements, and nature, [taught] such a discourse on the penetration of the Four Noble Truths.

He gave a teaching of the Dharma, hearing which Kacaṅgalā shattered with the vajra of knowledge the mountain of the view of a self-identity that rose up with twenty peaks, and realized the fruit of stream-entry.
Having seen the truth, she uttered this inspired exclamation three times:
"Venerable Sir, this was not done for us by our mother, nor by our father...
[as before] ...having shattered with the vajra of knowledge the mountain of the view of a self-identity accumulated since beginningless time, we have realized the fruit of stream-entry."
And he spoke this verse:
"That which ought to be done by a good son who seeks to benefit his mother has been performed by you today; my mind is now intent upon liberation."
Having rescued you from the miserable realms, I have established you with great effort in heaven and liberation; well done, you have performed a difficult task.
Having spoken thus, she bowed her head at the feet of the Blessed One and departed from his presence.
Then, at another time, Kacaṅgalā, having obtained permission from her husband, approached the Blessed One;
having approached and bowed her head at the feet of the Blessed One, she sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, Kacaṅgalā said this to the Blessed One:

"Venerable Sir, may I receive the going-forth and the full ordination in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, and may I attain the status of a bhikṣuṇī; may I lead the holy life under the Blessed One."
She was entrusted to Mahāprajāpatī by the Blessed One;
thereupon, she was ordained, received full admission, and given instruction.
By applying herself, striving, and exerting effort, she realized arhatship through the abandonment of all defilements.
She became an Arhatī;
free from passion for the three realms as before, she became worthy of honor.
Whenever the Blessed One would enter his dwelling to retire for meditation after giving a brief instruction to the bhikṣuṇīs, Kacaṅgalā would then explain it to them in detail.
Thereupon the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"Monks, this is the foremost among my female disciples, my bhikṣuṇīs, who analyze the sūtras—that is to say, the bhikṣuṇī Kacaṅgalā.
Then the monks, having conceived doubts, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts.
"Venerable Sir, what karma did Kacaṅgalā perform such that she went forth as a nun when she was old?
And what karma did she perform such that she became poor and a slave, yet the Blessed One was carried by her as her final dwelling in a womb,
and she realized arhatship after going forth?"
And the Blessed One declared her to be the foremost among those who compose analytical expositions of the sūtras.
The Blessed One said:
"By Kacaṅgalā alone."
"Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by this nun; having reached their full measure, they ripen for embodied beings, as previously described.
Monks, in the past, while I was engaged in the conduct of a Bodhisattva, she was my mother.
When I desired to go forth into the religious life, she would restrain me."
As the ripening of that karma, she became an elderly woman who had gone forth as a renunciant;
because she created an obstacle to my giving while I was bestowing gifts,
she has become poor.
Furthermore, she has not performed deeds conducive to great power and merit like those of Mahāmāyā, by which I was carried by her in my final residence in a womb;
nor did she, when she had gone forth as a nun—whether still in training or beyond training—under the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa, address them with the word "slave.
Because of that, she has become a slave.
Because she had there recited, studied, and mastered skill in the aggregates, skill in the elements, skill in the sense-bases,
skill in dependent origination, and skill in what is possible and impossible, she has now gone forth in my teaching and,
through the abandonment of all afflictions, realized arhatship.

The preceptoress under whom she had gone forth was designated by the Blessed One Kāśyapa, the Perfectly Awakened One, as the foremost among those who analyze the sūtras. At that time, at the moment of her death, she made this aspiration: "Although I have practiced the holy life for as long as I lived under the Blessed One Kāśyapa, the Perfectly Awakened One, the unsurpassed object of offerings, I have not attained any collection of virtues."
By this root of merit, may I go forth in the teaching of that very young brahmin named Uttara who was prophesied by the Blessed One Kāśyapa:
"Young man, when the lifespan of beings is one hundred years, you shall become a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha named Śākyamuni. May I go forth in his dispensation.
"Just as this preceptor of mine was designated by the Blessed One Kāśyapa, the Perfectly Awakened One, as the foremost among those who analyze the sūtras,
so too may that Blessed One Śākyamuni designate me as the foremost among those who analyze the sūtras.
By the power of that aspiration, I have now been designated as the foremost among those who analyze the sūtras.
Thus, monks, for actions that are entirely black, the ripening is entirely black;
as before, up to:
"effort must be made."
"Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
Having said this, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda:
"Come, Ānanda, let us go to Vairaṃbhya."
"So be it, Venerable Sir," the venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One set out and eventually arrived at a certain monastery,
where a brahmin was drawing water from a well.
He began to water the grove.
That brahmin saw the Blessed One from afar,
and having seen him, he reflected further:
"If the ascetic Gautama enters the grove,
he will defile our well," they said;
therefore, they remained there, guarding the rope and the water-skin.
Then the Blessed One entered the Ṛddhyārāma,
and the great yakṣa general Pāñcika flooded that well;
the entire park was inundated with water.
Then that brahmin, realizing, "This ascetic Gautama possesses great supernatural power and great majesty," became exceedingly pleased and said:
"Come, Blessed One Gautama!
Here is the rope; here is the water-pot."
"Take water as you please.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke this verse:
"What would one do with a well if there were water everywhere?"
Having cut the root of craving here in this world, whom would one go about seeking? Thus it is said.
Then that brahmin said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, may I receive the going-forth, the full ordination, and the status of a monk within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya," as before, up until:
he was ordained with the "Come, monk" formula.
When addressed by the Tathāgata with the words "Come," he stood there with shaven head and body wrapped in the saṃghāṭī robe;
his senses were immediately tranquil, yet he did not stand merely by the power of the Buddha's mental resolve.
By striving, exerting himself, and making an effort, he realized arhatship through the abandonment of all defilements.
He became an Arhat;

free from passion for the three realms, as previously described, he became one worthy of salutation. Then the Blessed One, wandering on a tour through the Śūrasena country, arrived at Vairaṃbhya and stayed at Vairaṃbhya at the foot of a neem tree belonging to Naḍera.
At that time, a brahmin king named Agnidatta was ruling in Vairaṃbhya— a realm that was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people and inhabitants.

King Agnidatta the brahmin heard that the ascetic Gautama, while wandering on a tour through the Śūrasena country, had arrived at Vairaṃbhya and was staying there at the foot of a *naḍera-picumanda* tree.
Having heard this, it occurred to him:
"The ascetic Gautama is honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by all the neighboring kings, and is regarded as an Arhat."
"If I do not pay honor to the ascetic Gautama, I shall be censured by the neighboring frontier kings:
'Sirs, King Agnidatta the Brahmin is truly a fool, for although the ascetic Gautama dwells depending upon his village and fields, he does not honor him.
What if I were to provide the ascetic Gautama, together with his community of disciples, with all necessary requisites?"
Thinking, "I shall invite [the Saṅgha]," and having understood this, he departed from Vairaṃbhya with great royal splendor and great royal majesty,
approached the Blessed One, and having approached him,
exchanged various greetings and pleasantries with the Blessed One face-to-face, and sat down to one side.

As the brahmin king Agnidatta sat to one side, the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dharma, as before, until he had made him joyful; then he remained silent.
Then the brahmin king Agnidatta rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One thus:
"May the Blessed One Gautama, together with the community of monks, accept from me for three months the requisites of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for the sick."
The Blessed One consented to the Brahmin king Agnidatta by remaining silent.

Then, the Brahmin king Agnidatta, understanding the Blessed One’s consent through his silence, rejoiced and delighted in the Blessed One’s words and departed from the Blessed One’s presence. Having gone to his residence, he gave an order to his ministers.

"Every day, cook eighteen kinds of sweetmeats and abundant food accompanied by various soups, juices, and side dishes. Furthermore, have a proclamation made by sounding a bell in Vairaṃbhya: 'No one else is to provide food for the ascetic Gautama for the three-month period.'"
"The punishment for whoever feeds him shall be death.
Having made this proclamation by ringing a bell,
he went to sleep at night and saw a dream.
He saw that the entire city of Vairaṃbhya was surrounded by his own entrails;
and having seen this, he became terrified, distressed, and his hair stood on end. Rising very quickly from his costly bed, he rested his cheek upon his hand and remained lost in thought, fearing:
"Could it be that because of this, I shall be deprived of my kingdom or face an obstacle to my life?"
When the night had turned to dawn, he informed his brahmin domestic priest:
"Preceptor, I have seen such a dream; how should I proceed in this matter?"
The brahmin domestic priest reflected:
"Even though the King has seen an inauspicious dream,
if I were to describe it to him, the ascetic Gautama will develop even greater faith."
Thinking, "I shall now cause him to change color," he said:
"Your Majesty, you have not seen an auspicious dream.
Preceptor, what will be the result of this?"
"Surely the king's fall from his kingdom will occur, or there will be an obstacle to his life.
The king reflected:
"Alas, may I not suffer the loss of my kingdom or an obstacle to my life! Having understood this, he spoke thus to his brahmin domestic priest:
"Preceptor, what might be the means by which there would be neither my fall from the kingdom nor any obstacle to my life?
He replied,
"If Your Majesty remains out of sight for three months, then there will be no fall from the kingdom for Your Majesty."
Nor does there come to be any obstacle to life.
King Agnidatta, the brahmin, reflected:
"If it is so easy..."
"I shall cause a proclamation by bell to be made in this manner.
Thereupon, he had a proclamation by bell made throughout the entire realm:
"No one at all must approach me for a visit during the three-month period."
"Whoever approaches him shall be punished with death.
Having made this proclamation by ringing a bell,
he remained out of sight for three months.
The Venerable Ānanda, having risen early in the morning, went to the residence of the brahmin king Agnidatta.
Upon arrival, he saw that the attendants of the brahmin king Agnidatta were standing about, having been made to wait with little concern.
Having seen this, he spoke again.
"Sirs, why do you remain so unconcerned?
They replied,
"Noble one, what shall we do?"

But the brahmin king Agnidatta has invited the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, for the three-month rainy season retreat with all necessary provisions. Why do you remain so unconcerned, neither preparing food nor arranging seats?
Will the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, undergo a lack of sustenance?
They said,
"Noble Ānanda, the King has given the command:
'Prepare excellent and abundant food for five hundred people.'"
But it was not said, "For the sake of so-and-so.
Sirs, go and announce:
"The Noble One has had a proclamation made by bell."
"No one should approach me for the purpose of seeing me;
whoever does so shall receive the punishment of death.
"Do we then have two heads? [they asked].
"We did not inform him.
Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One;
having approached, he reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One.
Thereupon the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"Go, Ānanda, taking the outer robe and accompanied by a junior monk, and announce in the streets, lanes, crossroads, and junctions of Vairaṃbhya:
'Sirs, whoever among you is able to feed the community of monks headed by the Buddha for the three-month period, let him do so.'"

"So be it, Venerable Sir," the venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. Taking his outer robe and accompanied by a junior monk as an attendant, he made an announcement in the streets, lanes, squares, and crossroads:
"Whosoever among you, sirs, is able to provide food for the community of monks headed by the Buddha for the three-month rainy season retreat, let him provide it.
Thus [he spoke] to the brahmins and householders of Vairaṃbhya.
They said, "Noble Ānanda,
each one of us is capable of providing food for three months;
however, this King Kali has caused a proclamation to be made by the ringing of a bell."
"No one else shall invite the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, for the three-month period;
whoever feeds them shall be punished with death.
Meanwhile, a caravan leader from the northern region arrived at Vairambhya, bringing five hundred horses as merchandise.
He reflected:
"If I go now, the horses' hooves will become sodden;
they will lose their traction."
"I shall remain right here.
He remained in that very place.
He then prepared two *prasthas* of barley for the noble steed.
"One horse each was allotted for the remaining horses. And this king heard that such and such an agreement had been made; thus it was announced by the Venerable Ānanda.
He reflected:
"I am not a resident of this king's realm;
what can the king do to me?"
Having understood this, he said this to the venerable Ānanda:
"Noble Ānanda, two measures of barley were assigned by me for the noble thoroughbred horse;
for each of the remaining horses, one measure was assigned."
"If the Blessed One is willing to eat barley, I shall offer two *prasthas* to the Blessed One and one each to the other monks.
Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the place where the Blessed One was.
Having approached, he reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One.
Then it occurred to the Blessed One:
"These very actions were performed and accumulated by me alone; their conditions have been gathered, their causes have ripened, and they have arrived like a surging flood."
"These actions were necessarily brought about and accumulated by me alone; who else shall experience their results?
For actions that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element."
Not in the fire element, nor even in the wind element;
as before, up until: "indeed, [karma] bears fruit for embodied beings."
He addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"Go, Ānanda, and distribute voting sticks (*śalākā*) among the monks, saying:
'Whosoever among you is able to consume barley with the Tathāgata at Vairaṃbhya for the three-month period, let him take a stick.'"
"So be it, Venerable Sir," the venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One, and began to distribute the voting sticks (*śalākā*).
When the Blessed One had taken a stick, as well as four hundred and ninety-eight monks,
the venerable Śāriputra said:
“Blessed One, I am afflicted by wind; I am not able to consume barley for the three-month period.
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana said, “I shall be his attendant.”
Then the Blessed One entered the rains retreat at Vairaṃbhya together with five hundred bhikṣus, excluding two bhikṣus.
The venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana went to Mount Triśaṅku and entered the rains retreat there;
subsequently, they were invited by Śakra, the lord of the gods, to partake of divine ambrosia.
Then the caravan leader presented two measures of barley to the Blessed One and one measure each to the other monks.
Thereupon, the Blessed One said this to the venerable Ānanda:

"Go, Ānanda, and prepare barley for the sake of the Tathāgata. "So be it, Venerable Sir," replied the venerable Ānanda; taking his portion from the Blessed One, he approached a certain elderly woman. Having approached her, (MSV I 31)
He said this to that woman:
"Sister, prepare some barley for the sake of the Tathāgata.
She replied:
"Noble sir, I am old and cannot do it; however, here is this young girl—
give it to her."
"She is preparing these," [the Buddha said].
The Venerable Ānanda approached her and asked,
"Sister, will you be able to prepare barley for the sake of the Tathāgata?"
She said,
"Noble sir, I will prepare myself on the condition that you grant me conversation."
He said,
"I will give it to you once it has been prepared.
She then began to prepare it.
And he asked,
"Noble one, who is this called 'Buddha'?
The Venerable Ānanda reflected:

"If I were to give her an illustration regarding the qualities of a Buddha, the Buddha-qualities are so profound that it is possible she would not understand them.
