Therefore, I shall provide her with an illustration concerning the qualities of the precious wheel-treasure. Having realized this, he said:
"Sister, upon the appearance of a universal monarch in the world, there occurs the appearance of the seven treasures in the world."
Of which seven? Namely:
the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the counselor-treasure as the seventh.
"Sister, with the appearance of a wheel-turning monarch in the world, what kind of wheel-treasure appears in the world?
Here, sister, when a consecrated Kṣatriya king, having bathed his head and observed the fast on the fifteenth day of the lunar month,
is adorned and seated upon the upper terrace of his palace surrounded by a host of ministers, a wheel-treasure appears in the eastern direction."
There appears a divine, all-golden wheel, thousand-spoked, with a hub and a rim, perfect in every aspect, auspicious, and not made by a smith;
and by means of this, he becomes auspicious.
When that very wheel, made entirely of gold, appears on the fifteenth day of the *poṣadha* for a consecrated Kṣatriya king— as described previously—
that king is a *cakravartin*. Thinking, "Truly, I am a *cakravartin* king," and desiring to examine the wheel-treasure, he rises from his seat and drapes his upper robe over one shoulder.
Having placed his right knee upon the ground and having grasped that wheel-treasure with both hands, he rests it in his left hand and turns it with his right hand,
saying: "Be victorious, O wheel-treasure, by which the noble one shall follow the ancient path of the universal monarchs!"
Then the wheel-treasure, set in motion by the universal monarch, rose up into the air and proceeded toward the east along the ancient royal path of the universal monarchs.
The universal monarch followed that wheel-treasure together with his fourfold army.
And in whatever region that wheel-treasure came to a halt, there the universal monarch established his residence together with his fourfold army.
Those regional kings who were in the eastern direction approached the wheel-turning monarch;
having approached, they spoke thus to the wheel-turning monarch: "May Your Majesty come!"
Welcome to Your Majesty!
These territories of Your Majesty are prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and teeming with many people; may Your Majesty govern them.
We shall be Your Majesty’s followers.

Therefore, village chiefs, govern each your own respective territories with righteousness and not with unrighteousness; and let no one who practices unrighteousness or acts perversely find pleasure in dwelling within your realm.
"You shall be followers in this manner.

Then that wheel-treasure, having conquered the eastern direction as before and having crossed back out to the great ocean, proceeded southward, westward, and northward, following the noble, ancient path of the universal monarchs. Then the wheel-treasure, set in motion by the universal monarch, rose up into the sky and turned northward, following the noble, ancient path of the universal monarchs.
The wheel-turning monarch follows that wheel-treasure together with his fourfold army.
In whatever region that wheel-treasure comes to rest, there the wheel-turning monarch establishes his residence together with his fourfold army.
Indeed, those frontier kings who dwell in the northern direction approach the presence of the wheel-turning monarch.
Having approached, they speak thus to the universal monarch: "Come, O Lord!
Welcome to the Lord!"
"These territories of Your Majesty are prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and teeming with many people and inhabitants.
May Your Majesty govern them;
we shall be Your Majesty's followers."
"Therefore, O village chiefs, govern each your own respective territories with righteousness and not unrighteously; let it not please any of you who act unrighteously to dwell within your realm.
Then the wheel-treasure, having conquered the northern direction, [reached] the northern great ocean.
Having crossed back over and returned to that very capital city, he stood upon it as if it were raised up for this administrative office.
Sister, through the appearance of a wheel-turning monarch in the world, there occurs the appearance of such a wheel-treasure in the world.
"Sister, with the appearance of a wheel-turning monarch in the world, what kind of elephant-treasure appears in the world?

Here, sister, the elephant of a wheel-turning monarch is entirely white, the color of a white water-lily, with seven limbs well-proportioned, firmly established, beautiful, handsome, and pleasing to behold;
seeing which, the mind of the wheel-turning monarch becomes serene."
"The auspicious, excellent jewel of an elephant will become tamed after only a single training session.
Then the Wheel-turning King summoned the renowned elephant trainer by messenger and said this to him:
"My good man, you must quickly make this renowned jewel of an elephant well-tamed and bring it before us."

"So be it, Your Majesty," replied the elephant trainer, acknowledging the command of the universal monarch (*cakravartin*). In a single day, he brought the elephant-treasure (*hastiratna*) under control through all the training methods. Being thus brought under control in a single day by all the training methods, the elephant received them in a single day;
just as other elephants, though many years old and tamed over many years, receive the training methods when they are applied.
In this way, this precious elephant-treasure is captured by all the trainers in a single day;
and knowing it to be tamed, he presents it to the universal monarch,
saying, "Sire, the auspicious precious elephant-treasure is tamed."

"If it pleases Your Majesty now, this is the time. Then the Wheel-turning King, desiring to examine that jewel of an elephant, mounted that jewel of an elephant at the time of sunrise and, having traversed this very great earth bounded by the ocean, [returned] to it.
Having thus arrived at the royal capital, he took his morning meal.
"Sister, it is because of the appearance of a wheel-turning monarch in the world that such a jewel of an elephant appears."
"Sister, with the appearance of a wheel-turning monarch in the world, what kind of horse-treasure appears in the world?
Here, sister, the king who is a wheel-turner has a horse that is entirely blue, with a black head, charming, swift, handsome, beautiful to behold, and pleasing.
Upon seeing it, the mind of the king who is a wheel-turner becomes serene."
"How wonderful it would be if this precious horse were to become well-trained even once!
Then the Wheel-turning King dispatched a messenger to a renowned horse-trainer and said to him:
"My good man, you must quickly bring this precious horse under perfect control and present it to us."
"So be it," replied the horse-tamer known as Saṃkhyāta to the universal monarch, and having given his promise, he brought that jewel of a horse to the presence of all the trainers in a single day.
Being brought before all the trainers in a single day, it was accepted by all the trainers in a single day;
just as other horses, though many years old and tamed over many decades, are accepted by all the trainers when they are brought before them.
In the same way, that horse-treasure, being approached by all the charioteers in a single day, receives all those charioteers in a single day;
and having recognized it as tamed, he presents it to the universal monarch, saying:
"Sire, the auspicious horse-treasure is tamed; now, Sire, do as you deem timely."

Then the wheel-turning monarch, desiring to examine the horse-treasure, mounted that horse-treasure at the time of sunrise and, having traversed this very great earth bounded by the ocean, returned to that same royal capital and took his morning meal.
Sister, with the appearance of a wheel-turning monarch in the world, there occurs the appearance of such a horse-treasure in the world.
Sister, with the appearance of a wheel-turning monarch in the world, what kind of jewel-treasure appears in the world?
Here, sister, the king who is a wheel-turner possesses a gem that is eight-faceted, made of beryl, beautiful, of pure birth, clear, serene, and unclouded.
Even all the lighting needs within the harem of the wheel-turning monarch were met by the radiance of that gem.

Then, the wheel-turning monarch, desiring to examine that precious gem, during a night of pitch-black darkness while rain was falling gently and softly and lightning was flashing, had the precious gem mounted upon the tip of a banner and set out for the pleasure grove.
He departs together with a fourfold army; indeed,
the entire fourfold army of the wheel-turning monarch is pervaded by the radiance of the jewel for half a yojana all around.
Sister, with the appearance of a wheel-turning monarch in the world, there occurs the appearance of such a jewel-treasure in the world.
Sister, with the appearance of a wheel-turning monarch in the world, what kind of woman-treasure appears in the world?
Here, sister, the queen of the wheel-turning monarch is beautiful, lovely to behold, pleasing, and not too fair.
She was neither too dark nor the color of a madgura fish; she was neither too tall nor too short, well-proportioned, neither too thin nor too stout, and her limbs were not excessively fleshy.
Indeed, sister, her limbs were warm to the touch in the cold and cool to the touch in the heat, as soft as the touch of Kalinga cloth.
Indeed, sister, sandalwood fragrance wafted from all her pores and the scent of a blue lotus from her mouth.
While the Venerable Ānanda was explaining the Jewel of a Woman, that girl prepared those two carts;
she prostrated at his feet and began to make a formal aspiration.
"Noble one, by this root of merit, may I become the jewel of a woman for a universal monarch (cakravartin) king.
Then the Venerable Ānanda, taking prepared barley, approached the Blessed One;
having approached, he offered the barley to the Blessed One.
The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are inquisitive and ask questions.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, asked the venerable Ānanda:
"Ānanda, by whom were these barley grains prepared?"
“By which brahmin girl, venerable sir? What was the conversation you had, Ānanda, with that brahmin girl?
Therefore, Ānanda, relate to us in detail everything that was the conversation you had with that brahmin girl.”
Then the Venerable Ānanda related in detail to the Blessed One everything that had been the subject of their conversation with that brahmin girl.
When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
"Ānanda, why did you not mention the praise of the Buddha to that girl?"
"Venerable sir, it occurred to me: 'Profound are the qualities of a Buddha; it is possible that this girl will not understand.
Therefore, I gave her the illustration of the appearance of a universal monarch."
"You have failed, Ānanda!
Had you uttered a praise of that Buddha, it is possible that she would have generated the irreversible mind set upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment."
"But rather, Ānanda, this girl will become the woman-jewel (*strīratna*) of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*).
[The Blessed One reflected:
'Monks, whatever disadvantage arises when a monk goes into a house wearing a robe made of strips of cloth (*paṭaplotika*), [it is because of this]. "
Therefore, a monk must not go into a house while wearing a cotton cloth;
if he goes, he commits an offense of transgression.
This report spread throughout the surrounding area.
"Such-and-such a brahmin girl has prepared barley for the sake of the Blessed One;
she has been prophesied by the Blessed One as the Woman-Jewel (*strīratna*) of a universal monarch (*cakravartin* king).
Having heard this, those five hundred young women—short by two—prepared barley for the five hundred monks—short by two.
They also made a vow,
saying, "May we be her attendants.
When the Blessed One began to eat the barley, the Venerable Ānanda became distressed and began to shed tears.

Thinking that the Blessed One, having given gifts such as the cutting off of hands, feet, and heads during those cycles of births, and having attained omniscience after three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), was now eating *koṭara-yava* grains, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"Ānanda, why are you distressed and shedding tears?"

"Bhagavān, born into the lineage of a noble universal monarch (cakravartin), you abandoned your kingdom and went forth as a renunciant; having given gifts such as your hands, feet, and head, and having attained omniscience after three incalculable eons (asaṃkhyeya-kalpa), why do you now eat the hollow barley? The Bhagavān said:
"Ānanda, do you wish to eat the barley grains that have emerged from between the Tathāgata’s teeth? "I do, Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One [offered] to the venerable Ānanda those [grains] that had emerged from between his teeth.
A single grain of barley was given;
for in this way, Ānanda, the Tathāgata’s taste-channel, which conveys the finest flavors, is perfectly purified.
Even if the Tathāgata partakes of ordinary food, it transforms for the Tathāgata into food of a hundred flavors.
The neighboring people spread the word:
"The Brahmin king Agnidatta, having invited the community of monks headed by the Buddha, has placed himself out of sight, [thinking], 'The Blessed One is eating barley in Vairaṃbhya.'"
The neighboring kings also heard of this, and they dispatched messengers to the brahmin king Agnidatta;
however, they were not granted entry and remained standing at the gate.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada heard of it as well, and he sent five hundred wagons filled with rice hidden beneath leaves.
Then this thought occurred to Māra, the Evil One:

"Many times have I harassed the ascetic Gautama, yet never have I found an opportunity. Even now, I shall strike at him. Having realized this, he manifested himself as the venerable Ānanda, stood before those five hundred carts, and said:

"Sirs, where are you going? They replied, "Noble Ānanda, King Agnidatta the Brahmin has invited the Blessed One together with the community of disciples and remains out of sight; the Blessed One is eating barley at Vairaṃbhya."
When the householder Anāthapiṇḍada heard this, he sent five hundred carts of rice covered with leaves for the sake of the Blessed One.
He said, "Sirs, the devas, nāgas, and yakṣas have placed their faith in him."
"If the Blessed One extends his bowl toward the sky, even the gods of the Trayastriṃśa heaven fill it with divine ambrosia.
For what purpose, then, does the Blessed One consume barley? Turn him back! (MSV I 40)
They said, "Noble Ānanda, we have already set out; why should we turn back now?
We shall go."
Māra reflected:
"It is not possible to turn them back;
a strategic device must be employed."
Having ascended into the upper air, he began to rain down streams of water as thick as axles;
by that means, he saw as far as those carts were submerged up to their hubs.
Then those carters unyoked the oxen and departed.
There, at Vairaṃbhya, the Blessed One consumed barley together with four hundred and ninety-eight bhikṣus.
Meanwhile, the Venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, having entered the rains retreat on Mount Triśaṅku, consumed divine ambrosia.
Then, at the conclusion of the three-month period, that caravan leader invited the Blessed One, along with the community of disciples, for a meal.
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.

That caravan leader, during that very night, prepared pure and excellent food, both solid and soft; as before, he waited until he knew the Blessed One had finished eating, his hands were washed, and his bowl was put away, and then [he stood] at the feet of the Blessed One.
Having prostrated, he began to make a formal vow:
"By this root of merit, may I become a universal monarch (*cakravartin*); may I have a noble steed as my son, the crown prince; and may those five hundred horses become five hundred sons.
May that girl whom the Blessed One designated as the 'jewel of a woman' (*strīratna*) be her attendant, and may those five hundred girls become her maidservants."
Then the Blessed One, knowing with his own mind the thought in the mind of that caravan leader, said this to him:
"Caravan leader, you shall become a universal monarch (*cakravartin*); a noble steed (*ājāneya*) shall be your son as crown prince; those five hundred horses shall be your five hundred sons;
and that girl shall be your jewel of a woman (*strīratna*)."
Those five hundred maidens, minus two, were her attendants.
Then, at the end of the three-month period, having finished his robes and completed his sewing, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"Go, Ānanda, and inform King Agnidatta, the brahmin."
And speak thus:
"O Great King, we have dwelt in your realm;
please look upon us with favor."
"Let us go. "Very well, venerable sir," the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One and, having taken his leave, went to the residence of the brahmin king Agnidatta.
At that time, the brahmin king Agnidatta was waiting for an auspicious day.
Then the Venerable Ānanda addressed a gatekeeper:
"Come, my good man, go to where the brahmin king Agnidatta is."
Having approached King Agnidatta, the brahmin ruler, speak thus to him:
"The monk Ānanda stands at the gate, desiring to see Your Majesty. "Very well, noble sir," the doorkeeper replied to the venerable Ānanda and went to where King Agnidatta, the brahmin ruler, was.
Having approached, he said this to Agnidatta, the king of the brahmins: "Noble sir, the monk Ānanda is standing at the gate, desiring to see the king.
He replied:
"O man, I am waiting for an auspicious day.
The monk Ānanda is one of great merit and renown; let him himself be that auspicious day."
And he possesses five excellences:
excellence of name, excellence of form, excellence of complexion, excellence of eloquence, and excellence of practice.
Let him enter! Who would prevent the venerable Ānanda?
The gatekeeper informed the venerable Ānanda accordingly, and the venerable Ānanda entered.
Those messengers from the neighboring kings also entered along with him.
Then the venerable Ānanda, having inquired after the health of the brahmin king Agnidatta, sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the venerable Ānanda said this to the brahmin king Agnidatta:
"The Blessed One, Great King, greets you and asks after your health.
We have dwelt, Great King, in your realm for the three months of the rains."
"Be looked upon;
let us go. "I pay homage to the noble Ānanda and to the Buddha, the Blessed One."
"Venerable Ānanda, I hope the Blessed One has spent the rains retreat happily among the Vairaṃbhya country and has not been exhausted by lack of alms-food?
Thus was he addressed by those envoys from the neighboring kings.
"O King, you who have not personally witnessed the kingdom, having invited the Blessed One together with the community of disciples for the three-month rainy season retreat, you remain out of sight;
for three months, you have subsisted on nothing but hollow barley.
He replied:
"It is true, Ānanda, that the Blessed One consumed barley for three months.
It is true, Great King.
He fainted.
Having fallen to the ground, his life returned through a great sprinkling of water; he summoned his ministers and asked:
"Sirs, did I not give you this command:
'Every day, prepare food for five hundred'?"
"It is excellent and abundant," they said.
"The King has indeed given such an order."
However, no order had been given that it should be given to such-and-such a person;
rather, the food was still prepared even now.
Then the brahmin king Agnidatta approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
As Agnidatta, the brahmin king, was seated to one side, the Blessed One instructed, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dharma, as before, until finally remaining silent.
Then Agnidatta, the brahmin king, prostrating himself at the feet of the Blessed One, said this to the Blessed One:

“Transgression, Blessed One! Transgression, Sugata! Just as a child, just as a fool, just as one who is unrefined, just as one who is unskilled—namely, I—who having invited the Blessed One together with the community of disciples for the three-month rainy season retreat, remained out of sight;
O Blessed One, since I recognize my transgression and see my transgression, please accept my transgression as a transgression out of compassion.”

"It is true, Great King, that you have acknowledged your transgression as a transgression, just as a child, a fool, one who is unrefined, and one who is unskilled would do— namely, you who, having invited the Tathāgata for three months, remained out of his sight. Since you, Great King, recognize your transgression, see your transgression, and having seen it, confess it, only growth is to be expected for you."
There was no decline in his wholesome qualities.
Then the brahmin king Agnidatta said this to the Blessed One:
"May the Blessed One, together with the community of monks, accept from me for as long as life lasts the requisites of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for the sick."
The Blessed One said: "Great King, the Tathāgata was born at a time when the lifespan was short, yet there was much work to be done, and it was the time of his final nirvāṇa."
He did not consent.
[The king said: "If that is so, may the Blessed One consent for me for seven years, seven months, and seven days.
Even so, the Blessed One did not consent.
The brahmin king Agnidatta said this to the Blessed One:
"May the Blessed One, together with the community of monks, accept my invitation for a meal at my home tomorrow.
The Blessed One reflected:

"If I do not accept even a single meal from him, it is possible that Agnidatta, the brahmin king, will vomit hot blood and pass away. Having understood this, the Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
Then, King Agnidatta, the brahmin, perceiving the Blessed One’s consent through his silence, departed from the presence of the Blessed One and went to his own residence.
Having approached, he addressed the ministers: "Sirs, what means might there be by which all this food could be consumed by the community of monks headed by the Buddha?
They replied:
"Your Majesty, let all this food on the earth be measured out."
"The monks will tread upon it with their feet;
thus it will be consumed.
With this thought, he gave an order to his attendants.
"Sirs, scatter all this food everywhere upon the ground.

They scattered it all around. Then King Agnidatta, the brahmin, having prepared pure and excellent hard and soft foods that very night, [proceeded] as before until the Blessed One was seated before the community of monks on the prepared seat.
While he was seated on that very seat,
a certain elderly man, having become indignant and thinking, "For three months we have subsisted on hollow barley,
yet now this King Kali displays his wealth," realized this and struck a blow with his heel upon the food, both hard and soft, scattered upon the ground.
The brahmins and householders reproached, reviled, and censured [the monks],
saying, "Noble ones, they touch with their feet the solid and soft foods that are to be consumed by the mouth.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One reflected:
"Whatever fault there may be,
it arises from the fact that monks eat solid and soft food [at improper times]."
Knowing that [the monks] were touching with their feet food intended for consumption by the mouth, he addressed the monks:
"Monks, a certain elder monk, having become indignant, struck his heel upon the ground over which hard and soft food intended for consumption by the mouth had been scattered.
Brahmins and householders are reproaching, censuring, and speaking ill of this."
"Therefore, a monk must not step upon hard or soft food intended for consumption with his foot; if he does so, he commits an offense.
Then King Agnidatta, the brahmin, perceiving that the community of monks headed by the Buddha was comfortably seated,"
With pure and excellent food, both hard and soft, he personally satisfied him by hand, as described previously, until the Blessed One had washed his hands and set aside his bowl.
Then, taking a lower seat, he sat before the Blessed One to hear the Dharma.
Thereupon, the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened Agnidatta, the brahmin king, with a discourse on the Dharma.
Having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them with a discourse on the Dharma in many ways, he rose from his seat and departed.
Then, after the three months of the rainy season had passed, a great number of monks—having finished their robes and completed their sewing—took their bowls and robes and approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, a great number of bhikṣus said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, we have dwelt at Vairaṃbhya for the three-month rains retreat."
The Vairaṃbhya-sūtra is found in detail in the Catuṣka-nipāta of the Ekottarikāgama.
There, the monks, having become doubtful, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts.
"Venerable One, what karma was performed by the Blessed One such that, through the equipment of giving— including the severing of hands, feet, and head—
and having satisfied destitute people for as long as three incalculable eons, he exhausted himself for the sake of sentient beings until all his worldly tasks were finished,
and finally ate the hollow barley at Vairambhya together with four hundred and ninety-nine bhikṣus?"
"The venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana [have eaten] divine ambrosia," [they said].
The Blessed One said:

"Monks, these very deeds were performed and accumulated by the Tathāgata himself in other previous births; having reached their full measure, as previously stated, they indeed bear fruit for embodied beings.

Long ago, monks, when the lifespan of humanity was eighty thousand years, a perfectly awakened Buddha named Vipaśyin appeared in the world—one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher."
The Buddha, the Blessed One, the awakened one among gods and humans,
was dwelling in dependence upon the royal capital of Bandhumatī with a retinue of eighty thousand monks.
At that time, in the royal capital of Bandhumatī, a certain brahmin who was a leader of a group was teaching the mantras of the brahmins to a group of five hundred.

Vipaśyin, the perfectly enlightened one, was exceedingly honored, revered, esteemed, worshiped, and regarded as an Arhat by the entire world; yet, from the very moment he arrived at the royal capital of Bandhumatī, no one honored him, revered him, esteemed him, or worshiped him.
He reflected upon this.
He became exceedingly envious toward the Tathāgata and his community of disciples.
Eventually, many monks— both those in training and those beyond training— having dressed in the morning and taken their bowls and robes, arrived at the royal capital of Bandhumatī.
Then, having filled their bowls with rice accompanied by various soups and sauces, they went out. That brahmin saw them and asked:
"O monks, let me see what kind of alms-food you have obtained."
They pointed him out as being upright;
thereupon, the young brahmins, provoked by his nature of envy, said:
"These shaven-headed śramaṇas do not deserve to consume rice-gruel accompanied by various soups, sauces, and side dishes."
"But they are worthy to consume *koṭarayava* beans.
They also confirmed this, saying, "It is so, preceptor; it is so."
"These shaven-headed ascetics are certainly not worthy to enjoy rice-gruel accompanied by various soups, sauces, and side dishes;
they are only worthy to eat hollow barley.
Now, in that place there were two young brahmins who were faithful, noble, and of virtuous intent.
The two of them said,
"Preceptor, do not speak thus;
these are great-souled ones who are indeed Arhats, fit to enjoy divine ambrosia, not mere groats from hollowed-out barley."
What do you think, monks?
That brahmin who was the leader of the assembly under the Tathāgata Vipaśyin was none other than myself at that time and on that occasion;
and those five hundred young brahmins minus two were these very same five hundred monks.

Those two young brahmins who were faithful, noble, and of virtuous intention are none other than these two monks, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana. Because I harbored a corrupt mind toward the disciples— both those in training and those beyond training— of the Perfectly Awakened One Vipaśyin and uttered harsh verbal karma, and because this was rejoiced in by two hundred and fifty of those young brahmins, but not by the other two.
However, that [act] was not approved by him; as the ripening of that karma, the Tathāgata now consumed hollow barley at Vairaṃbhya together with four hundred and ninety-nine monks,
whereas Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana consumed divine ambrosia.
"Thus, monks, for actions that are entirely black, the ripening is entirely black; as before, up until: one should apply oneself only to actions that are entirely white.
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves."
Thereupon the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda:
"Come, Ānanda, let us go to Ayodhyā.
"So be it, Venerable Sir," the venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, wandering on a tour through the country of Dakṣiṇapañcāla, arrived at Ayodhyā and stayed there by the bank of the river Gaṅgā.
Then a certain monk approached the Blessed One;
having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, that bhikṣu said this to the Blessed One:

"It would be well, Blessed One, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dharma in brief, so that having heard the Dharma in brief from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, heedful, ardent, and resolute."

Dwelling alone, withdrawn, heedful, ardent, and resolute, may I— having personally realized, witnessed, and attained through direct knowledge in this very life that supreme goal for which sons of good family shave off their hair and beard, don saffron robes, and out of right faith go forth from the home to the homeless state— declare that unsurpassed consummation of the holy life.
"Exhausted is birth for me; the holy life has been lived; what was to be done has been done; I know no further state of existence beyond this.
When this had been said, the Blessed One looked toward the river Gaṅgā.
Looking out, the Blessed One saw a great log of wood being carried along by the current of the river Gaṅgā.
Having seen him, he addressed that monk:
"Do you see, monk, that great log being carried away by the current of the river Gaṅgā? "I do, Venerable Sir. "If this [log] does not get stranded on the far bank," [he continued].
It will not stick to the far shore;
it will not stick in the middle;
it will not arise on dry land.
It will not be seized by humans; it will not be seized by non-humans;
it will not be seized by whirlpools.

"It will not become rotten within. In this way, O monk, this log of wood will gradually incline toward the ocean, slope toward the ocean, and tend toward the ocean. Even so, O monk, if you do not wash yourself on the further shore..."
As before, up until:
"You shall not come to internal putrefaction.
For in this way, O monk, you will gradually become inclined toward nirvāṇa, sloping toward nirvāṇa, and leaning toward nirvāṇa."
"Venerable sir, I do not know what is the hither shore, what is the further shore; what is the sinking in the middle, and what is the rising on dry land?"
What is the human-grasping? What is the non-human-grasping?
What is the whirlpool-grasping?
"What is internal putrefaction?

It would be well if the Blessed One would teach me the Dharma in brief, so that having heard the Dharma in brief from the Blessed One—as before—up until: 'I understand there is no further state of existence beyond this.'"
"O Bhikṣu, 'this shore' is a designation for the six internal sense-bases;
'the further shore' is a designation for the six external sense-bases;
and 'sinking in the middle' is a designation for delight and lust."
"Scraping on dry land" is a designation for the conceit "I am.
"The human grasp" refers to how some person here dwells in association with householders and renunciants.

Sharing in joy and sharing in sorrow, he will be happy among those who are happy and sorrowful among those who are sorrowful; and regarding whatever duties arise, he will take them up and follow through to their completion.

Regarding the phrase "seized by a non-human," it refers to one such as this here who, having made a vow, practices the holy life [thinking]: "By means of this morality, or vow, or austerity, or practice of the holy life, may I become a deva."
"Or one of the gods," he says.

"A whirlpool-grasper" refers to how someone here, having renounced the training, turns back toward decline. "Internal putrefaction" refers to how someone here is of bad character and evil nature—putrid within, leaking, born of a rotten core, with conduct like that of a conch-shell.
"One who is not a śramaṇa yet claims to be a śramaṇa, one who does not lead a life of celibacy yet claims to lead a life of celibacy—

if you, O monk, do not thus cling to the hither shore, as previously described, up until being inclined toward Nirvāṇa. Then that monk, having rejoiced and delighted in the words of the Blessed One, bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and departed from the presence of the Blessed One.
Then that monk, having been instructed by the Blessed One with this parable of the log of wood,

dwelt alone, secluded, heedful, ardent, and resolute; and he attained that goal for the sake of which sons of good family shave off their hair and beard, don saffron robes, and out of right faith go forth from the home into the homeless state.
Having personally realized, witnessed, and attained that unsurpassed culmination of the holy life in this very life, he declared:
"Birth is exhausted for me; the holy life has been lived; what was to be done has been accomplished; I know no further state of existence beyond this.
Thus he became one who has known.
That venerable one became an Arhat with a mind well-liberated.
At that time, Nanda the cowherd was standing not far from the Blessed One;
leaning on his staff, he was tending the cows.
Pinned down by that staff, as his skin was being torn away and his joints were being severed, he formed this thought:

"If I were to move my body or utter a word, it would cause an interruption in the conversation of Nanda the cowherd on account of this. Knowing this, and having conceived a mind of serene faith toward the Blessed One, he passed away.
He was reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings.
Then Nanda the cowherd, having set aside his staff to one side, approached the Blessed One;
having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, Nanda the cowherd said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, I shall not be swept away on this shore,
nor shall I be swept away on the far shore."
I shall not discharge it into the middle;
I shall not discharge it onto dry land;
I shall not become subject to capture by humans.
"May I not be seized by non-human beings, may I not be caught in a whirlpool, and may I not undergo internal putrefaction.

Venerable Sir, may I receive the going-forth and the full ordination in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya; may I attain the state of a monk and practice the holy life (brahmacarya) in the presence of the Blessed One.
Thereupon, Nanda gave his masters' cattle as a gift.
"No, Venerable Sir. For what reason?
Venerable Sir, cows with young calves will recognize their own respective herds."
They will go to their respective homes.
"Venerable Sir, may I receive the going-forth and the full ordination in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya;
may I attain the status of a monk and practice the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One."
Moreover, Nanda, even though the young cows with their calves will recognize their respective cow-pens and go to their respective dwellings,
nevertheless, this must be done by the cowherd, just as it is required by a master who accepts food and clothing from his dependents.
Then Nanda the cowherd, having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, departed from the Blessed One's presence.
Then, crying out "Fear! Fear! in a loud voice, he began to run.
On the way, he was seen by five hundred of his own cowherds.
They said,
"Of what is there fear?
"Of the fear of birth, the fear of old age, the fear of sickness, and the fear of death."
They too began to run after him.
Seeing them, other cowherds, horse-keepers, grass-gatherers, wood-gatherers, and men who subsist on the highway or off the highway also began to run.
Those traveling along the road saw them crying out in that manner and questioned them.
"What is this, sirs?
They replied,
"It is fear."
"Of what is there fear?
Of the fear of birth, the fear of old age, the fear of sickness, and the fear of death.
Having heard this, they too turned back.
When they had reached the vicinity of the village,
the inhabitants of that village, seeing that great multitude of people, became terrified from all sides;
some fled.
Some were guarding their goods; some remained standing in full armor;
and other heroic men, having gone out to meet them, were questioned by them.
"Sirs, what is this? They replied, "It is fear."
"Of what is there fear?
Of the fear of birth, the fear of old age, the fear of sickness, and the fear of death.
Thereupon, that multitude of people residing in the mountain stronghold was comforted.
Now at that time, the Venerable Śāriputra was seated and present in that very assembly.
Then, perceiving that Nanda the cowherd had been gone for a long time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Venerable Sir, why has the Blessed One sent back Nanda the cowherd—who desired to go forth in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya—to his home once again?"

"It is impossible, Śāriputra, it is out of the question that Nanda the cowherd should ever again enter the life of a householder and dwell in a home, or enjoy sensual pleasures through the possession of stored wealth;
such a thing cannot occur."
Now Nanda the cowherd will return after having returned the cows to his masters.

He has seen that unsurpassed culmination of the holy life for the sake of which sons of good family, having shaved off their hair and beards and donned saffron robes, go forth from the home to the homeless state with perfect faith.

"Having personally realized, witnessed, and attained this very Dharma, he will declare: 'Birth is exhausted for me; the holy life has been lived; what was to be done has been accomplished; I know no further state of existence beyond this.
Then, at another time, Nanda the cowherd, having returned the cattle to his masters, approached the Blessed One with a retinue of five hundred.
Having approached the Blessed One, he said this to him:
"Venerable Sir, my cattle have been entrusted to my masters.
Venerable Sir, may I receive the going-forth and the full ordination in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya; may I lead the life of a monk."
"I shall lead the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One.
Thus did Nanda the cowherd, with a retinue of five hundred, obtain the going forth, the full ordination, and the status of a monk within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya.
Having thus gone forth, that venerable one—just as before—became one whose mind was perfectly liberated.
It is the nature of things that as soon as a son of the gods or a daughter of the gods has been reborn, three thoughts arise:
"From where have I passed away? Where have I been reborn?"
"By what karma?
A son of the gods who had previously been a frog saw:
"Having passed away from among the animals, he was reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings because he had conceived a serene faith in the presence of the Blessed One."
This thought occurred to him:
"It would not be fitting for me to approach the Blessed One for a visit while my probation is still unfulfilled;
rather, I shall approach the Blessed One for a visit even before my probation has been fulfilled."

Then the son of the gods Maṇḍūkapūrvī, wearing shimmering and stainless earrings— as described previously— illuminated the entire bank of the Gaṅgā with a magnificent radiance and, having scattered flowers over the Blessed One, sat before him to hear the Dharma. Then the Blessed One, having understood the disposition, latent tendencies, elements, and nature of the son of the gods Maṇḍūkapūrvī, delivered a discourse on the Dharma that leads to the penetration of the Four Noble Truths.

Having heard this, as before, up until: having shattered with the thunderbolt of knowledge the mountain of the view of a self-identity accumulated since beginningless time, he realized the fruit of stream-entry. "I have transcended, O Venerable One; I have truly transcended! I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha of monks."
"And consider me a lay follower from this day forward, for as long as life lasts, endowed with vitality, having gone for refuge and being full of faith.

Then the divine son formerly a frog— like a merchant who has gained profit, like a farmer whose crops have ripened, like a hero who has won a battle, or like a sick man freed from all disease— approached the Blessed One with such splendor as he had come with.
He returned to his own abode with that very same splendor.
The monks, dwelling devoted to the practice of vigilance during the first and last watches of the night,
saw a magnificent radiance in the presence of the Blessed One.
Seeing this, they became doubtful and asked the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, did Brahmā Sahāmpati, Śakra the lord of the gods, and the four world-protectors approach the Blessed One for a vision during this night?
"Monks, it is not Brahmā Sahāmpati, nor Śakra the lord of the gods, nor the four world-protectors who have approached me for a vision."

However, the frog, being held down by the staff of the cowherd Nanda, remained motionless and silent as the skins were being cut and the joints were being severed, thinking, "May there be no obstacle to the religious practice of the cowherd Nanda.
Having thus developed a serene mind toward me, he passed away and was reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings.
"He approached me this very night;
I taught him the Dharma,
and having seen the Truth, he has returned to his own abode."

The monks, having conceived a doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts: "Venerable Sir, what karma was performed by Nanda the cowherd, together with his retinue of five hundred, by which he was reborn among the cowherds, yet having gone forth in the teaching of the Blessed One and abandoned all defilements, attained arhatship?"
"It has been directly realized. What karma was performed by the son of the gods who was formerly a frog, such that he was reborn among frogs and yet attained the vision of the Truths?
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, those very actions were performed and accumulated by him; having reached their full measure, they bear fruit for embodied beings, as previously described.
Long ago, monks, in this very Fortunate Eon, when the lifespan of humanity was twenty thousand years, a perfectly awakened Buddha named Kāśyapa appeared in the world.
As before, he eventually arrived at the city of Vārāṇasī and dwelt in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana."
In his teaching, Nanda the cowherd went forth as a monk.
He became a master of the Tripitaka, a preacher of the Dharma, possessed of ready and liberated eloquence, and was accompanied by a retinue of five hundred. He was skilled in settling disputes;
whatever disputes arose within the Sangha, he brought them to pacification.
In that place, there were two monks who were stubborn and arrogant;
they never once approached him.
At a later time, a dispute arose between those two.
Seeking their respective objects, the two approached him, prostrated at his feet, and said,
"Please settle this and that legal dispute which has arisen between us.
He reflected:
"If I were to settle this legal dispute today, these two seekers of wealth would not come back again.
Therefore, having assembled the entire Saṃgha and placed that dispute before them in the midst of the community, he did not resolve it definitively.
Consequently, on the following day as well, business arose for him in that market town.
He went there;
then, because he was delaying, those two convened the Saṃgha and presented that legal case to them.
Thereupon, it was settled by the Saṃgha.
When that monk, a master of the Tripitaka, had returned from that mountain village and his fatigue from the journey was dispelled, he asked his co-residents and pupils: "Have those two—
the plaintiff and the defendant— not yet arrived?"
They said,
"Preceptor, that legal dispute between those two has been settled.
By whom was it settled?"
By the Saṃgha. How was it related by them in detail?
He uttered harsh words.
"Venerable ones, it is known by the cowherds that the legal case has been settled. They too have confirmed to me, 'Upādhyāya, it is exactly as the cowherds say; that legal case has been settled.
What do you think, monks? That monk who was Tripiṭaka at that time and on that occasion was none other than this Nanda the cowherd."
Those five hundred disciples and resident pupils of his are none other than these five hundred cowherds.

Because he addressed the community of disciples of the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa with the term "cowherds," and because this was subsequently praised by his own disciples and resident pupils, as the ripening of that karma, for five hundred births—
Having been reborn among cowherds with a retinue of five hundred,
even now he has been reborn among cowherds with a retinue of five hundred.

Whatever he had studied and recited— skill in the aggregates (*skandha*), skill in the elements (*dhātu*), skill in the sense-bases (*āyatana*), and skill in what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna*)— [remained with him].
And by him, now accompanied by a retinue of five hundred, having gone forth in my teaching,
arhatship has been realized through the abandonment of all afflictions.
Furthermore, the son of the gods formerly a frog was a monk in the dispensation of the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa.
While wandering on a journey through the countryside, that practitioner of ascetic exertion arrived at a monastery in a certain small town.
During the first watch of the night, he sat cross-legged and began to apply his mind to mental cultivation.
While the monks engaged in recitation were reciting, [the practitioner] thought:
"Meditations have sound as their thorn;
because of that sound, he does not attain one-pointedness of mind."
He reflected, "These [monks] are reciting;
I shall sit in meditation during the middle watch.
Having risen, he sat in the middle watch while the other monks continued their recitation.
He reflected, "I shall sit in meditation during the final watch.
Having risen, he sat in the final watch until others began their recitation.
Because he had not yet transcended passion, a powerful outburst of affliction arose within him.
He said, "These Śramaṇas of the Kāśyapīya school have been croaking all night like frogs.
"What do you think, monks? That monk who was the forest-dweller is none other than this son of the gods who was formerly a frog."

Because he addressed the disciples of the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa with the word "frog," as the ripening of that karma, he was reborn among frogs for five hundred births, and even until now he has been reborn among frogs. However, because he produced a mind of faith toward me, he has been reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings.
"Because the holy life was practiced under Kāśyapa, the perfectly enlightened one, the vision of truth has now been achieved.
Thus, monks, for actions that are entirely black, the ripening is entirely black; as before, up to: "effort must be made.
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves. Thus he spoke.
Then the Blessed One descended into the river Gaṅgā; there he was surrounded and circumambulated by five hundred swans, fish, and tortoises.
To them, the Blessed One taught the Dharma in three verses:
"Thus, O gentle ones, all conditioned phenomena are impermanent."
All phenomena are without self;
nirvana is peace.
Set your minds with deep faith upon me.
"Perhaps you will thus become disenchanted with the animal realm.
Then this occurred to them:
"It would not be fitting for us to take food after having heard the Dharma from the Blessed One in these three verses."
They undertook the practice of non-eating.
A fierce fire broke out among those born in the animal realm;
having passed away, they were reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings.
It is indeed the natural law that as soon as a son of the gods or a daughter of the gods has been reborn, three thoughts arise:
"From where have I passed away? Where have I been reborn?"
"By what karma? They see that they have passed away from among the animals.
They were reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings.

As before, up until having filled their laps with *mandāraka* flowers, they illuminated the river Gaṅgā in the vicinity of the Blessed One, scattered flowers over the Blessed One, and stood surrounding him.
Knowing their intentions, latent tendencies, elements, and natures, the Blessed One performed a teaching of the Dharma that leads to the penetration of the four noble truths, as described previously.
Having shattered with the vajra of knowledge the mountain of the view of a self-identity accumulated since beginningless time, they realized the fruit of stream-entry.
Having seen the truths, they said:
"We have gone for refuge, O Venerable One; we have truly gone for refuge."

We here go for refuge to the Buddha, to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha of monks. Regard us as lay followers (*upāsaka*), who from this day forward, for as long as life lasts, have gone for refuge with our very lives and are full of faith.
Then those sons of the gods, who had previously been fish, tortoises, and swans—like merchants who have gained their profit—went to their own abodes as before.
The monks, overcome with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, what karma was performed by these swans, tortoises, and fish, such that they were reborn among swans, tortoises, and fish, and yet also attained the vision of the Truth?"
The Blessed One said:

"Monks, these very same swans, fish, and tortoises performed and accumulated these actions; their provisions were gathered and the conditions have ripened. As before, [the results] bear fruit for embodied beings. Long ago, monks, in this very Fortunate Eon (*bhadrakalpa*), when the lifespan of human beings was twenty thousand years—"
A teacher named Kaśyapa appeared in the world, as described previously, until he dwelt near the city of Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana.
They had gone forth into homelessness under his teaching.
In that regard, these monks violated the minor and lesser rules of training;
as the ripening of that karma, they were reborn among the swans, fish, and tortoises.
Because they had directed a mind of serene faith toward me, they were reborn among the gods.
"Because the holy life was lived under Kāśyapa, the perfectly enlightened one, the vision of truth was thereby achieved.
Thus, monks, for actions that are entirely black, the ripening is entirely black; as before, up until: 'effort must be made.
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves. Thus he spoke.
Then the Blessed One, having crossed the river Gaṅgā, was surrounded by about five hundred pretas who were shaped like burnt pillars,
held together like skeletons, covered with their own hair, possessing bellies like mountains and mouths like the eye of a needle;
they were blazing, glowing, and fully aflame.
Having become a single mass of flame, they joined their palms in reverence and said to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, we are hungry ghosts with bodies fallen into ruin; due to the obstruction of our past karma, we cannot obtain even water."
"How can there be a sight of the One who possesses compassion? You are the Greatly Compassionate One; please grant us water. The Blessed One showed them the Gaṅgā.
For this Bhāgīrathī flows with cool water and abundant currents, available for the enjoyment of all people;
she satisfies the villages, provinces, and cities, as well as the rice fields, lotus ponds, and the white and blue lotuses.
The pretas say:
"This Bhāgīrathī, whose waters were once dry for us, now flows as something to be enjoyed by all people;
yet we see her full of blood and filth, and they guard her with axes and staffs in their hands."
The Blessed One said to the goddess of the Gaṅgā:

"O you who satisfy the villages, kingdoms, and cities with your waters, why do you not satisfy the rice fields, the śāli rice, and the white, blue, and red lotuses? Are you not overcome by intense thirst? Have you no compassion for the sufferings of these foolish people?"
The goddess Gaṅgā said:
"Neither out of fear, nor because of a man, nor even through deceit toward people, do I abandon my domain, the water."
"But this water, having reached a state of desiccation for those shrouded by the great obstruction of evil deeds— what fault of mine is there in this?
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
"Satisfy the hungry ghosts, Maudgalyāyana.
"So be it, Venerable Sir," the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana replied to the Blessed One and began to satisfy the hungry ghosts.
There, because their mouths were like needles, the hungry ghosts were unable to open their mouths.
Then the Blessed One opened their mouths by means of his supernatural power,
and the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana gave them water;
being afflicted by thirst, they drank it in great abundance.
Their bellies burst open;
then, having conceived a serene faith in the presence of the Blessed One, they passed away.
As before, having realized the Truths, they returned to their own abodes.
The monks, having conceived doubts, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, what karma was performed by these hungry ghosts such that they were reborn among the hungry ghosts?
What karma was performed such that they were reborn among the gods?"
"And the vision of the truth has been attained.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, these very actions were performed and accumulated by them; having reached their full measure, as previously described, they bear fruit for embodied beings."

Monks, in the past, in this very Fortunate Eon, when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, a Teacher named Kāśyapa appeared in the world; as before, he dwelt near the city of Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana.
His disciples, having made a request for alms, perform services for the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. At that time,
when the teaching of the Blessed One, Kāśyapa the Perfectly Awakened One, was not yet widespread,
there were few monks who requested alms.
But when it had spread widely, there came to be many monks who were solicitors for consent.
Eventually, in a certain assembly hall, five hundred lay followers (*upāsaka*) were seated together, having gathered for some particular business.
And a great many monks who were solicitors for consent approached them, desiring to obtain their consent.
With intense obsession, they uttered harsh words of action:
"These ascetics of the Kāśyapīya school are like those reborn as pretas, with their hands perpetually outstretched.
What do you think, monks? Those five hundred lay followers were none other than these five hundred pretas.
Because they addressed the disciples of the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa with the term "pretas," as the ripening of that karma, they were reborn among the pretas for five hundred births;
even now, they have been reborn among the pretas.
However, because they produced a mind of faith toward me, they have been reborn among the gods.
"Because he had taken refuge and received the precepts under the perfectly enlightened Buddha Kāśyapa, he has thereby realized the vision of truth.
Thus, monks, for actions that are entirely black, the ripening is entirely black; as before, up to the point where effort must be made.
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves. Thus he spoke.
Then the Blessed One, having crossed the river Gaṅgā, gazed at the river Gaṅgā with a rightward "elephant-look.
The monks asked the Buddha, the Blessed One:
"For what purpose, Venerable Sir?"
The Blessed One turned back and looked toward the river Gaṅgā.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, do you wish to hear about the origin of the river Gaṅgā?"
"Blessed One, this is the time; Sugata, this is the occasion for the Blessed One to teach the origin of the river Gaṅgā, which the monks shall hear.
Once upon a time, monks, there was a king named Piṇḍavaṃśa;
he was righteous, a king of Dharma, who ruled his kingdom according to the Dharma."
His realm was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people; its trees were always laden with flowers and fruit, and the rain fell in due season.
The earth was rich in crops, and it was free from strife, quarrels, tumult, civil unrest, thieves, and disease.
The people were constantly devoted to the Dharma.

When the spring season had arrived and the trees were in full bloom, while the forest groves resounded with the cries of swans, cranes, peacocks, parrots, mynas, cuckoos, and jīvañjīvakas, that king set out for the pleasure gardens surrounded by his harem. At that time, a certain man appeared— his head covered in wrinkles and grey hair, his bodily limbs utterly decayed, his sense faculties fully ripened [with age], emaciated, with little strength, moving very slowly due to his infirmity.
He goes along leaning on a staff.
Then the king asked his ministers:
"Sirs, who is this man with a head covered in wrinkles and grey hair, [and so on as before] up to: who is he going along leaning on a staff?"
They replied,
"Your Majesty, because his conditioned formations have completely decayed, this man is called 'worn out' and 'old'.
The king said:
"I too, sirs, shall be subject to such a nature.
They replied,
"Your Majesty, this nature is common to all."
Then the king, dejected in mind, set out.
Once again he saw a man who was extremely pale, with cracked and coarse limbs, and a belly as large as a mountain;
his major and minor limbs were covered with bandages bound over wounds from which pus was oozing, and he was sighing deeply.
Seeing him set out, leaning upon a staff and walking with a limping gait, he addressed his ministers once more:
"Sirs, who is this man, so exceedingly pale— [as described previously]— who has set out walking with a limping gait?"
They said,
"Your Majesty, this one is called 'the sick man'.
The king said:
"I too, sirs, shall become subject to such a law.
The ministers replied, "Your Majesty, this law is common to all; it arises for those who have committed evil deeds due to the transgression of their past karma."
The king reflected:
"In every way, evil must not be committed. Having understood this, he set out;
yet once again, he saw [the same thing].

A palanquin adorned with blue, yellow, red, and white cloths, crowded with parasols, banners, flags, conchs, drums, women, men, boys, and girls, was being carried aloft by four men; a torch was being led before it, followed from behind by men holding pieces of wood in their hands, while cries of "Alas, father! Alas, brother! Alas, father! Alas, master! resounded on all sides.

Having heard the sound of weeping, he addressed his ministers again: "Sirs, why is this palanquin being carried with blue, yellow, red, and white cloths? [The description continues] as before, up to the sound of weeping.
The ministers replied:
"O Lord, this one is called 'dead'.
The king said,
"Sirs, I too shall be subject to such a law."
They said, "Your Majesty, this too is a common lot.

Then, having seen the sight of the aged, the sick, and the dead, his mind became deeply agitated; thinking that such enjoyments must be renounced, he turned back, entered a chamber of mourning, and remained there.
Now, in his realm, there was a brahmin named Velāma, wealthy, possessing great riches and vast enjoyments, who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
He heard that the king, having become distressed by the sight of the old, the sick, and the dead, had entered the chamber of sorrow and remained there.

Upon hearing this, surrounded by many hundreds of thousands of brahmins, he mounted a chariot drawn by mares that was entirely white; holding a golden staff and water-pot, he approached King Piṇḍavaṃśa.
The ministers informed the king:
"Your Majesty, the brahmin Velāma is standing at the gate.
Thereupon the king went out and sat down in the court of justice.
The brahmin Velāma, having greeted him with wishes for victory and long life, sat down and asked,
"For what reason, O King, have you entered and remained in the chamber of sorrow? The king related everything exactly as it had happened in detail to the brahmin Velāma.
He said,
"Your Majesty enjoys the fruits of your own karma;
there is no need for grief in this matter."
There are beings who perform good deeds, there are those who perform evil deeds, and there are those who perform both kinds of deeds.
However, wheel-turning monarchs, always performing good deeds, are reborn among the gods;
even a god may become a wheel-turning monarch.
"Having experienced happiness superior to that of humans, he shall experience divine happiness.
Furthermore, "Your Majesty, a sacrifice must be performed, for it serves as a staircase to heaven.
Thereupon, the king issued a command to his ministers.
"Sirs, cause a proclamation by the ringing of bells throughout the entire realm:
'The King is performing an unrestricted sacrifice;
you must come and partake of it.'"
Then a hall for giving was prepared;
let food be given to those seeking food, and drink to those seeking drink.
There, a trench was formed by the overflowing of the rinsing water.
Wherever he was heated, there he became cooled;
thus, it came to be known as "Anavatapta" (the Unheated). As it was being filled with its own froth and rice-water for twelve years, its increase occurred.
Then this river flowed forth from his mouth, and it became known by the name "Ācāmanadī" (the Washing River). The summary verse (*uddāna*) is as follows:
Kumāravardhana, Krauñca, Aṅgadikā, Maṇivatī, Sālabalā, Sālibalā, Suvarṇaprastha, and Sāketa.
Peyā, Toyikā, and Śrāvastī; Anavatapta, Nagara-bindu, and Vaiśālī is the last.
Then the Blessed One arrived at Kumāravardhana.
At Kumāravardhana, he addressed the venerable Ānanda:
"Ānanda, it was in this very place that the king named Upoṣadha was born."
He grew up right here; therefore, this city became known by the name Kumāravardhana, "The Increaser of the Prince. He arrived at Krauñcanam.
Thereupon the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda:
"Ānanda, in this place Krauñcana, a sound was made by the king Upoṣadha’s elephant as it trumpeted like a curlew; thus the name 'Krauñcana' came to be established."
He arrived at Aṅgadikā;
in a certain place in Aṅgadikā, he manifested a smile.
The detailed account of the four Buddha-seats is as before.
He arrived at Maṇivatī.
In Maṇivatī, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"Ānanda, in this Maṇivatī, a Bodhisattva performed a sacrifice with many jewels."
The name Maṇivatī became established for her. He arrived at Sālabalā;
in a certain place in Sālabalā, he manifested a smile.
In detail, the fourfold seat of the Buddhas was as before.
He arrived at Sālibalā;
in a certain place in Sālibalā, he manifested a smile.
In detail, the fourfold seat of the Buddhas is as before.
He arrived at Suvarṇaprastha.
Ānanda, it was here in Suvarṇaprastha that the Bodhisattva performed the Bahusuvarṇaka sacrifice.
Now, the Brahmins divided the gold by weight;
thus it became known as "a prastha of gold" (suvarṇaprastha),
and he arrived at Sāketa.
In Sāketa, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"Ānanda, in this Sāketa there is a king named Upoṣadha who rules over a kingdom that is prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people.
At a later time, a tumor grew on his head—soft, very soft, like a tuft of cotton or a tuft of silk-cotton—and it caused him no affliction whatsoever."
Because it had reached full maturity, it burst open and a boy was born.
He was handsome, beautiful to behold, pleasing, fair-skinned, with a golden complexion— as previously described— endowed with all major and minor limbs.
Because he was born on the head [of the bed], the name Mūrdhāta—meaning "Born on the Head"—became established for him.
King Upoṣadha had sixty thousand women;
when the prince was born, he was brought into the inner apartments.
At the mere sight of him, the breasts of all the women flowed with milk;
each one said, "Let me nurse him! Let me nurse him! and thus the name Māndhātṛ arose.
Regarding this, some understood the name as Mūrdhāta, while others understood it as Māndhātṛ.
While Prince Māndhātṛ was away in his territories, King Upoṣadha fell ill. He was attended with medicines consisting of roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, and fruits;
nevertheless, he continued to decline.
He gave this command to the ministers:
"Sirs, quickly consecrate the prince with the royal inauguration. "So be it, Your Majesty," the ministers replied, and they dispatched messengers.
King Upoṣadha was ill;
he gave this command: "Summon the prince so that he may receive the consecration for the kingship."
"Therefore, it is fitting that the prince should come quickly.
He set out, but King Uposadha passed away.
Then the ministers again dispatched a messenger to him.
"Prince, your father has passed away;
come and accept the kingdom.
Prince Māndhātṛ reflected:
Thinking, "If my father has passed away, what is the use of going there?", he remained right where he was.
The ministers, having gathered once more, dispatched the chief minister.
He went and said to him:
"O prince, come and accept the kingdom.
He replied,
"I have obtained the kingdom through righteousness."
"Let the royal consecration come right here! Thus was it communicated by the ministers:
"Your Majesty, much is required for the royal consecration."
"The royal consecration is performed with a jeweled stone, a lion throne, a parasol, a turban, and a crown,
in the midst of the consecration hall.
Therefore, it is fitting that the prince come here at once."
He said,
"If my kingdom was obtained through righteousness,
then let everything come right here."
Prince Māndhātṛ had a yakṣa named Divaukasa who was his forerunner;
by him a lion-throne made of precious stone was brought right there.
Furthermore, the presiding deities themselves arrived, bringing the parasol, the headband, and the crown.
Because the consecration had come of its own accord, the place came to be known as Sāketa, Sāketa. There, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda:
"Come, Ānanda, let us go to Śrāvastī."
"So be it, Venerable Sir," the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One set out on a journey toward Śrāvastī, and as he proceeded, he arrived at a certain place where a brahmin who had missed his meal was plowing with a plow.
For his sake, a young girl had come carrying a bowl of gruel.
And the Blessed One arrived at that place;
the brahmin beheld the Buddha, the Blessed One, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.

His body was radiant with the eighty secondary marks, adorned with a fathom-wide halo, and possessed a splendor exceeding that of a thousand suns; like a moving mountain of jewels, he was auspicious in every respect.
Upon seeing him, faith in the Blessed One arose within him.

Twelve years of practicing *śamatha* do not produce such flexibility of mind as the first sight of a Buddha does for a sentient being who has accumulated roots of merit— just as a sonless man gains a son, a poor man discovers a treasure, or one who longs for a kingdom receives the royal consecration.
Taking that rice-gruel, he approached the Blessed One with all possible speed.
Having approached, he said this to the Blessed One:
"O Gautama, here is rice-gruel; it is at my disposal."
Out of compassion, O Blessed One Gautama, drink this rice-gruel.
Thus, out of compassion, the Blessed One said:
"Then the Blessed One showed the well to that brahmin:
'If these [water pots] are to be discarded by you, O brahmin, throw them into this old well.'"
He threw them into that old well;
the old well, steaming, became filled with broth, through the power of the Buddhas and the power of the deities.
Then the Blessed One addressed that brahmin:
"O Brahmin, distribute the rice-gruel," he said.
He began to distribute it,
and the Blessed One empowered it in such a way that the rice-gruel was served by the entire Saṅgha.
The dilapidated well, steaming with vapor, remained filled with broth as before.
Then that brahmin, with even greater faith, prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down before him to hear the Dharma.
Having understood his disposition, latent tendencies, elements, and nature, the Blessed One [taught him].

Such a Dharma teaching, which penetrates the Four Noble Truths, was given as before, until— having shattered the mountain of the view of a self-identity accumulated over beginningless time with the vajra of knowledge— he realized the fruit of stream-entry.
"I have transcended, O Venerable One; I have truly transcended.
I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha of monks.
Pray, accept me as a lay follower from this day forward, for as long as life shall last, one who has gone for refuge with deep faith."

Then that brahmin, like a merchant who has gained profit, like a farmer whose crops have ripened, like a hero who has won a battle, or like a sick man freed from all disease, rejoiced and delighted in what the Blessed One had spoken; he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and departed from the Blessed One's presence, eventually reaching his field.
In that field, he saw golden barley fully ripened;
and having seen it, his eyes wide with wonder, he spoke this verse:
"Oh, what a field composed of virtues, entirely free from all defects!"
"Today itself I have sown the seed; today itself it shall yield fruit.
Then that brahmin quickly approached the presence of the king.
Having approached and greeted him with wishes for victory and long life, he said to the king:
"Your Majesty, the barley seeds I scattered have turned into gold. May Your Majesty grant favor regarding this matter. Thus addressed, the king dispatched an official to oversee the situation.
The Brahmin piled them together and divided them;
the king's share turned out to be ordinary barley.
The superintendent reported this to the king.
The king commanded,
"Divide it again!
and so it was divided again.
In the same way, the king's share turned into natural barley. This happened up to seven times of dividing [the crop].
Likewise, the king, filled with curiosity, went there himself and saw it.
In the same way, he said to that brahmin:
"Brahmin, this is produced by your own merit;
enough with the king's share."
"Give me whatever you intended for yourself.
Then, because that brahmin was satisfied, those [seeds] he gave turned into golden barley.
Thereafter, the Blessed One set out until, in a certain place, he saw five hundred farmers who were extremely pale, with cracked hands and feet, dressed in hempen rags, and holding plows.
They were driving them along;
those oxen, their bodies mangled and wounded by goads that pierced through the pus of their sores, were pulling while gasping for breath again and again.

Those farmers saw the Blessed Buddha, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man—as described previously—[and they thought: "This is the first sight of a Buddha for a being who has accumulated roots of merit."
Then they approached where the Blessed One was.
The Blessed One saw those farmers from afar;
having seen them, out of consideration for their discipline, he stepped off the path and sat down on the seat prepared before the community of monks.
Then those farmers bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.

Thereupon, the Blessed One, having understood their inclinations, latent tendencies, elements, and dispositions, delivered a discourse on the Dharma conducive to the penetration of the Four Noble Truths, as before, until— by means of the thunderbolt of knowledge— he shattered the mountain of the view of a self-identity accumulated since beginningless time.
Having burst through [the veil of ignorance], they realized the fruit of stream-entry.
Having seen the truth, they bowed with palms joined toward where the Blessed One was and addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Venerable sir, may we receive the going forth and the full ordination into the state of a monk within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya; may we lead the holy life under the Blessed One.
They were granted the going forth by the Blessed One with the "Come, monk" formula, as before, until they stood [in their places].
[cf. nepacchitā -] *Pravṛ-v* III, fol.
47r6: By the Buddha’s wish, the Blessed One gave them instruction.
Through their exertions, as described previously, they became worthy of salutation.
Those oxen, having broken their yokes and thongs, approached the Blessed One;
having approached and bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, they stood surrounding him on all sides.
The Blessed One taught the Dharma to them in three statements,
as previously described, up to the point where— just as in the case of the swans, fish, and tortoises at the descent into the Ganges— they perceived the Truths and returned to their own abodes.
The monks, having conceived doubts, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts.

"Venerable One, what karma was performed by these monks who were formerly farmers, such that they became farmers and, having gone forth in the teaching of the Blessed One, realized arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions?
And what karma was performed by those sons of gods who were formerly oxen, such that they were reborn as oxen and yet attained the vision of the Truths?"
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, these very actions were performed and accumulated by them; having reached their full measure, as previously described, they bear fruit for embodied beings.
Long ago, monks, in this very Fortunate Eon, when the lifespan of humanity was twenty thousand years, a Teacher named Kāśyapa appeared in the world."
As before, [the Buddha] eventually arrived at the city of Vārāṇasī and dwelt in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana.
Under his teaching, these five hundred farmers had gone forth as monks.

However, they neither studied nor recited, nor did they apply themselves to mental cultivation; instead, having repeatedly consumed offerings given out of faith, they spent their time in socializing and through laziness.
"What do you think, monks? Those five hundred monks were these five hundred farmers.

He who was the owner of the monastery was this very householder. As for these farmers, because they consumed the gift of faith belonging to the owner of the monastery but did not recite [the scriptures], [they became farmers]."
They did not engage in recitation, nor did they practice mental attention; rather, delighting in social company, they spent their time in laziness.
Because of that karma, for five hundred births they became farmers belonging to that monastery’s owner. Even now, they have been born as his very farmers.

Because they had gone forth and practiced the holy life under the teaching of the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa, they have now gone forth under my teaching and, through the abandonment of all defilements, attained arhatship—even those sons of the gods who were formerly oxen.

They had indeed gone forth under the teaching of the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa, but there they violated the minor and lesser rules of training; as the ripening of that karma, they were reborn among oxen.
Because they had conceived a mind of serene faith toward me, they were reborn among the gods;
because they had practiced and maintained the holy life under Kāśyapa, the Perfectly Awakened One, they have now, having become sons of the gods, attained the vision of the Truths.
"Thus, monks, for actions that are entirely black, the ripening is entirely black; [as stated] previously, up to: 'effort must be made.
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
Having said this, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda.
"Ānanda, go to Toyikā.
"So be it, Venerable Sir," the venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One arrived at Toyikā.
And in that place, a brahmin was plowing with a plow.
Then he saw the Blessed Buddha, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man, his body radiant with the eighty minor characteristics, embellished by a fathom-wide halo,
possessing a splendor exceeding a thousand suns, like a moving mountain of jewels, auspicious in every respect.
He reflected:
"If I approach the Blessed Gautama and pay him homage, there will be a loss of my ritual merit;
but if I do not approach and pay homage, there will be a loss of my spiritual merit."
"What might be that skillful means by which there would be neither a loss of my [lay] duties nor a loss of my merit?
Such a thought arose in him:
"I shall perform my salutation while remaining right here."
"In this way, there will be neither a loss of karma nor a loss of merit.
Therefore, with that very goad-stick he had taken up, while remaining right where he was, he performed a salutation, saying:
"I pay homage to the Buddha, the Blessed One."

Thereupon the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, this brahmin has missed his opportunity. Had he approached this spot and offered a salutation, a personal realization of knowledge and vision would have arisen within him."
"In this place lies the undisturbed collection of bones of the perfectly enlightened Kāśyapa. Having approached it, I would pay homage;
in this way, he would have paid homage to two perfectly enlightened Buddhas.
For what reason?
"Ānanda, in this place remains the undisturbed collection of bones of the perfectly enlightened Kāśyapa.
Then the Venerable Ānanda quickly prepared his upper robe folded fourfold and said this to the Blessed One:
"May the Blessed One sit upon this very seat that has been prepared.
In this way, this spot of earth will have been used by two perfectly enlightened Buddhas: both by the perfectly enlightened Buddha Kāśyapa and now by the Blessed One.
The Blessed One sat down upon the very seat that had been prepared.
Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"Monks, do you wish to see the uncorrupted mass of relics of Kāśyapa, the Perfectly Awakened One?
