"Blessed One, this is the time; Sugata, this is the occasion for the Blessed One to show the uncorrupted mass of relics of Kāśyapa, the Perfectly Awakened One, to the monks."
Upon seeing this, the monks will develop serene faith, thinking, "The Blessed One has generated a worldly thought.
Desiring to see the uncorrupted physical remains of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, the Perfectly Awakened One, they behold them; for such is the nature of things (dharmatā).
Then, he raised up the undisturbed collection of the bodily relics of the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa.
There, the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"Monks, take note of this sign!"
"It will disappear" means it has disappeared.
King Prasenajit heard that the Blessed One had not disturbed the relics of the Perfectly Awakened Kāśyapa in order to allow his disciples to see them.

Having heard that "the body has been raised up," Virūḍhaka, filled with curiosity, set out together with the women of the harem, the princes, the ministers, the army commanders, and the merchants and countryfolk.
Likewise did Anāthapiṇḍada the householder, Uṣidatta the former carpenter, and Viśākhā, mother of Mṛgāra.
Many hundreds of thousands of living beings set out, filled with curiosity and impelled by their own past roots of merit. When he had vanished,
they heard that the physical remains of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, the Perfectly Awakened One, had disappeared.
Upon hearing this, they felt grief and dejection, thinking, "Our coming here has been in vain. Then,
a certain lay follower circumambulated that spot and formed this thought in his mind:
"How much merit will arise for me from this step of mine?

Then the Blessed One, desiring to produce a state free from regret in that great multitude of people and having understood with his own mind the thought in the mind of that lay devotee, spoke this verse:
"A hundred thousand gold *niṣkas* of Jāmbūnada gold are not equal to the merit of a wise person who, with a devout mind, takes even a single step at the stūpas of the Buddha. Thus it was said.
Then, a certain lay follower (*upāsaka*) offered a lump of clay at that spot.
Having formed such a thought, he wondered:
"The Blessed One has declared that the merit of merely taking a single step is this great;
but how much merit will there be from this mere lump of clay?"
Then the Blessed One, knowing his mind with his own mind, spoke this verse:
"A hundred thousand lumps of gold from the Jambū river are not equal to that person who,
with a devout heart, places even a single lump of clay upon the shrines of the Buddha."
Having heard that, many hundreds of thousands of living beings performed the act of depositing lumps of clay; others scattered loose flowers there, and formed such a mental resolve.
"The Blessed One has stated that such is the merit of a single footprint and of a lump of clay;
but how much merit will there be for us who have offered these loose flowers?
Then the Blessed One, knowing their thoughts with his own mind, spoke this verse:

"A hundred thousand chests of Jāmbūnada gold are not equal to the heap of loose flowers that one with a devout mind might offer at the shrines of the Buddha. Thus it was said. Others there made garland-arches.
And with a mind that has been fully prepared,
the Blessed One has declared such great merit for these loose flowers; what then shall be said of our monastery adorned with garlands?
"How much merit will there be?
Then the Blessed One, knowing their thoughts with his own mind, spoke this verse:
"A hundred thousand loads of Jāmbūnada gold would not equal it."
"The wise one who, with a devout mind, constructs a flower-grove at the shrines of the Buddha"—
thus [it was said]. Others there offered garlands of lamps and cultivated their minds.
"The Blessed One has described such great merit for the Mālāvihāra;
how much merit will there be for our gift of lamps?
Then the Blessed One, knowing their thoughts with his own mind, spoke this verse:

"A hundred thousand loads of Jāmbūnada gold are not equal to the wise man who, with a devout mind, offers a lamp at the shrines of the Buddha. Thus it was said. Then others there offered a consecration of perfumes.
And with a mind thus conditioned, they wondered:
"The Blessed One has stated that the merit of giving a lamp is this great;
how much merit will there be for our perfumed consecration?"
Then the Blessed One, knowing their thoughts with his own mind, spoke this verse:
"A hundred thousand heaps of gold from the Jambū river would not equal [the merit of] that wise man who, with a devout heart, performs a fragrant consecration at the shrines of the Buddha."
Others there offered the raising of umbrellas, banners, and flags, and they formed a mental resolve.

The Blessed One has stated that such is the merit of taking a single step, offering a lump of clay, scattering loose flowers, offering a garland, giving a lamp, and performing a consecration with perfumes.
"How much merit will there be for us in erecting parasols, banners, and flags?
Then the Blessed One, knowing their thoughts with his own mind, spoke this verse:
"A hundred thousand mountains of gold equal to Mount Meru would not be equal to this."
Whoever, with a mind full of faith, should offer parasols, banners, and flags at the shrines of the Buddha;
"For this is declared to be the sacrificial gift (dakṣiṇā) for the Tathāgata who is immeasurable, like the ocean, the unsurpassed caravan leader toward perfect enlightenment.
Then it occurred to them: "The Blessed One has stated that even for one who has entered final nirvāṇa, the merit resulting from [making offerings] to the Blessed One is of such magnitude."
"How much merit will there be for those who remain?
Then the Blessed One, knowing their thoughts with his own mind, spoke this verse:
"One should worship him who remains, and likewise one who has entered final nirvāṇa."
Having pacified the mind with equanimity here, there is no distinction in merit.
For thus the Buddhas are inconceivable, and the Buddha-dharma is also inconceivable;
for those who have faith in the inconceivable, the maturation [of that faith] is likewise inconceivable.

"It is not possible to reach the limit of the qualities of those inconceivable, unimpeded Turners of the Wheel of Dharma, the Perfectly Awakened Ones. Then the Blessed One gave such a teaching of the Dharma to that great multitude of people that, upon hearing it, many hundreds of thousands of living beings attained a great distinction.
Some generated the aspiration for the enlightenment of a śrāvaka, some for the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, and some for unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Some attained the stage of heat (uṣmagata), some the summits (mūrdhan), some the stages conforming to the truths (satyānuloma), and some the stages of patience (kṣānti).
Some realized the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattiphala), some the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmiphala), and some the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala).
Some, having gone forth, realized arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions.
For the most part, that assembly was established as being inclined toward the Buddha, leaning toward the Dharma, and gravitating toward the Saṅgha.
Thereupon, faithful brahmins and householders established a festival in that place.
The festival of Toyikā became known by the name "Toyikāmaha. Then the Blessed One, while wandering on a tour through the Kosala country, arrived at Śrāvastī.
He stayed at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.

The householder Anāthapiṇḍada heard that the Blessed One, while wandering on a tour through the Kosala country, had arrived at Śrāvastī and was staying in Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, our very own monastery.
Having heard this, he approached the place where the Blessed One was.
Having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.

To the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, who was seated to one side, the Blessed One taught the Dharma with a discourse; he instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him as before, until finally becoming silent.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada rose from his seat, and as before, having bowed with palms joined toward where the Blessed One was, he said this to the Blessed One:
"May the Blessed One, together with the community of monks, accept my invitation for a meal at my home tomorrow.

As before, having prepared pure and exquisite solid and soft foods, he rose early in the morning, arranged the seats, set out water-jars, and announced the time to the Blessed One by means of a messenger.

“The time has come, Venerable One; the meal is ready. Now, Blessed One, please do as you deem timely. He then addressed the gatekeeper: “O man, no others belonging to rival sects are to be admitted until the community of monks headed by the Buddha has finished eating.”
"After that, I shall give them to the non-Buddhist teachers.
"Very well, Noble One," the doorkeeper replied to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.
Then, in the forenoon, the Blessed One dressed himself, took his bowl and robe, and was surrounded by a company of monks.
Honored by the community of monks, as described previously, until he had washed his hands and set aside his bowl, he took a lower seat and sat before the Blessed One to hear the Dharma.
Then the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, coming from a certain forest dwelling, went to Jetavana with long hair and beard and worn-out robes.
He saw that Jetavana was empty.
He asked the superintendent of the monastery, "Where is the community of monks headed by the Buddha? and he was informed by him.
Having been invited by the householder Anāthapiṇḍada,
he reflected:
"I shall partake of almsfood right there and attend upon the community of monks headed by the Buddha."
He went to the residence of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada. The gatekeeper said to him,
"Noble sir, you shall not enter."
For what purpose?
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada gave this command:
"Do not allow the entrance of the heretics until the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, has finished their meal."
After that, he thought, "I shall give [this] to the non-Buddhist ascetics.

The Venerable Mahākāśyapa reflected: "It is a great gain for me that these brahmins and householders do not know me as a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas. I shall go; I will show compassion for the wretched people. Having realized this, he went to the park.
He reflected:
"Whom should I favor today?
Then he saw a certain city-dweller, overcome by leprosy, afflicted with disease, her limbs putrefied, wandering for alms.
He approached her,
and she had obtained some rice-gruel for alms.
She saw the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, who was serene in body and serene in mind, with a tranquil deportment.
She reflected:
"Surely it is because I have not performed acts of service toward such a worthy recipient of offerings that I am in this condition.
If only the noble Mahākāśyapa would show compassion toward me..."

"Having taken it, one should receive the rinsing water [thinking], 'I shall give this to him. Then, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, knowing her thought with his own mind, held out his bowl and said, 'Sister, if it has been relinquished by you, let it be given into this bowl.'"
Then, having developed faith in her heart, she gave [the food] into that bowl; a fly fell into it, and she began to remove it. As she was doing so, her finger fell into that rinsing water.
She reflected:
"Even though the Noble One did not throw it away, it was because he was protecting my feelings."
"But he will not eat it.
The Venerable Mahākāśyapa, knowing her thought with his own mind, sat down against the base of a certain wall right before her and ate.
She reflected:
"Furthermore, the Noble One has eaten out of consideration for my feelings; he will not perform the function of food with this meal.
Then the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, knowing her thoughts with his own mind, said to that female scavenger:
"Sister, be joyful! I shall spend the day and night on the food provided by you."
An intense sense of rapture arose within her:
"The noble Mahākāśyapa has offered almsfood to me and accepted it. Having developed a mind of serene faith toward the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, she passed away and was reborn in the Tuṣita host of gods.
She was seen by Śakra, the lord of the gods, as she was offering the rinsing water and passing away; however, he did not see where she had been reborn.
He began to survey the realms, but he did not see her among the animals, the hungry ghosts, humans, or the gods of the Four Great Kings or the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
For such is the nature of the gods' vision and knowledge: it extends downward, but not upward.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, approached the Blessed One;
having approached, he asked the Blessed One a question by means of a verse sung:
"While the great-souled Kāśyapa is indeed wandering for alms..."
Where does that woman rejoice, she who gave the rinsing-water to Kāśyapa?
The Blessed One said:
"Those gods are called Tuṣitas, where all desires are fulfilled;
there that woman rejoices, she who gave alms-food to Kāśyapa."
Then this thought occurred to Śakra, the lord of the gods:

"These humans, who do not have direct perception of merit, nevertheless give gifts and perform meritorious deeds. I, however, am one who has direct perception of merit and am established in the very fruit of my own merit.
Therefore, I too shall give gifts or perform meritorious deeds."

"This noble Mahākāśyapa is compassionate toward the wretched, the helpless, the poor, and beggars; what if I were to provide him with alms? Having thought this, he created a house on a street of the destitute. Having transformed himself into a weaver of very coarse robes, one who was haggard like a crow and not at all handsome, with disheveled hair, clad in a garment of hemp, and with cracked hands and feet, he [offered] cloth...
He began to weave;
Śacī, too, the celestial maiden, assuming the guise and dress of a weaver-woman, began to ply her shuttle.
And by his side stood prepared divine nectar.

Then the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, who was compassionate toward the wretched, the helpless, and beggars, arrived at that house in due course. Thinking, "This man is suffering," he stood at the door and extended his alms-bowl.
Śakra, the lord of the gods, [perceived this].
A vessel was filled with divine nectar.
Then, this thought occurred to the venerable Mahākāśyapa:
"This food is divine nectar, and yet this house is so vast."
"Knowing this to be utterly contradictory, doubt has arisen in my heart.
For such is the nature of things:
the knowledge and vision of the Arhats does not function without focused attention.
He began to reflect and saw Śakra, the lord of the gods.
He said,
"Kauśika, why do you create an obstacle for suffering people?"
The Blessed One has completely uprooted the thorn of doubt and uncertainty that had followed him for a long time, just as it was done by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One.
Noble Mahākāśyapa, why do you create an obstacle for these suffering people?
These humans, though they have not seen [the results] with their own eyes, nevertheless give gifts and perform meritorious deeds.
Since I am as if a direct witness to the fruits of merit, why should I not give gifts or perform meritorious deeds?
Has it not been said by the Blessed One:
"Meritorious deeds must be performed, for there is suffering for one who has not performed them"?
"For those who have performed meritorious deeds rejoice both in this world and in the next.
From that time forward, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa began to enter households for alms after having reflected upon them.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, standing in the sky, filled the bowl of the Venerable Mahākāśyapa with divine ambrosia.
The venerable Mahākāśyapa also turned his alms-bowl face downwards, and the food and drink were spilled.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One,
and the Blessed One said:
"Therefore, I authorize that an alms-bowl support should be carried.
This report spread throughout the vicinity:
"The noble Mahākāśyapa has been provided with rinsing water by such-and-such a female city-dweller."
And she was reborn in the Tuṣita host of gods.
When King Prasenajit of Kosala heard this,
having heard it, he approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
As King Prasenajit of Kosala was seated there, the Blessed One instructed, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dharma,
as described previously, until finally remaining silent.
Then King Prasenajit of Kosala rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"May the Blessed One, for the sake of the noble Mahākāśyapa, accept my invitation for a meal for seven days.
The Blessed One accepted King Prasenajit of Kosala’s request by remaining silent.
Then King Prasenajit of Kosala, understanding the Blessed One’s acceptance through his silence, bowed his head at the Blessed One’s feet and departed from his presence.
Then King Prasenajit of Kosala, having prepared pure and excellent food, both hard and soft, that very night, rose early in the morning, arranged the seats, set out water-jars,
and announced the time to the Blessed One by means of a messenger.
As before, up until he personally gratifies and serves [the monks].
Now, a certain beggar stood at the edge of the assembly with a mind full of serene faith, thinking:
"This king is as if visibly manifesting the fruits of merit; established in his own karmic rewards, he remains insatiable for meritorious deeds, bestowing gifts and performing acts of merit."

Then King Prasenajit of Kosala, in many ways, having personally satisfied and served the community of monks headed by the Buddha with pure and exquisite food both hard and soft, and knowing that the Blessed One had finished eating, had washed his hands, and set aside his bowl, took a lower seat and sat before the Blessed One to hear the Dharma.
Then the Blessed One said to him:
"O King, in whose name shall I assign the merit-offering?
Is it yours, or that of someone from whom a much greater merit has been produced?"
The king reflected:
"The Blessed One partakes of my alms-food;
who else could generate greater merit than I? Having understood this, he said:

“Blessed One, may the Blessed One designate the dedication of merit by name for whoever has generated more abundant merit than I. Thereupon, the Blessed One designated the dedication of merit by the name of Koṭṭamallaka;
and so it continued for six days.
On the sixth day, the king sat with his cheek resting on his hand, lost in thought:
"The Blessed One partakes of my almsfood,
yet he assigns the merit to Koṭṭamalla."
He was seen by his ministers, who said,
"Your Majesty, for what reason do you stand lost in thought, resting your cheek upon your hand?"
The king said,
"Sirs, why do I not remain absorbed in anxiety?
For now the Blessed One consumes my alms-food, yet he assigns the dedication of merit in the name of Koṭṭamalla."
Thereupon, one of the senior ministers said,
"Your Majesty, please do not be anxious.
We shall act in such a way that tomorrow the Blessed One will assign the merit-offering in Your Majesty's own name."
He gave this order to his attendants:
"Tomorrow you must prepare excellent and abundant food;
it should be served in this manner."
"Half [of the food] falls into the monks' bowls, and half on the ground.
On the following day, the ministers prepared abundant and exquisite food.
Then they began to serve the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, as they sat comfortably.
(MSV I 86) They dropped half [of the food] into the monks' bowls and half onto the ground.
Then the scavengers ran forward, thinking, "We shall take what has fallen on the ground!
and they were stopped by the servers.
Then that Koṭṭamallaka said:
"If this king possesses abundant wealth and property,
there are others like us who are suffering and who desire it."
"Why is this not given to them? What is the use of throwing it away so that it cannot be used?
At these words, a distraction of mind arose in that beggar.
He was not able to gladden the mind [of the Buddha] as he had done before.

Then the king, having fed the community of monks headed by the Buddha, realized that the Blessed One had not dedicated the merit in his name; thus, without even hearing the dedication of merit, he departed.
Thereupon, the Blessed One dedicated the merit in the name of King Prasenajit of Kosala in this way:

"You behold one who travels by means of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, enjoying a city together with its merchants; yet such power comes from a mere lump of boiled rice, devoid of salt and lacking fat.
Then the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One:
"Venerable One, many times the Blessed One has eaten in the residence of King Prasenajit of Kosala and assigned a dedication by name;
yet I do not recall ever before having been assigned such a dedication.
The Blessed One said:
“Ānanda, do you wish to hear the narrative of karmic connections concerning King Prasenajit of Kosala and a lump of saltless boiled beans?

Now is the time, Blessed One; now is the occasion, Sugata, for the Blessed One to describe the narrative of karmic connections concerning King Prasenajit of Kosala and that lump of saltless boiled beans.
Having heard it from the Blessed One, the monks will remember it.”
Thereupon the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"In the past, monks, there lived a householder in a certain mountain village."
He brought home a wife from a family of equal status;
he played, dallied, and enjoyed himself with her.
While he was playing, dallying, and enjoying himself, a son was born to him.

As before, [the child] was raised and grew until he became a great man. Then that householder addressed his wife: "My dear, we have had born to us one who shall pay our debts and take over our wealth."
"I am going to another country taking my merchandise," he said.
She replied, "Noble sir, do so.
Taking his merchandise, he went to another country.
And there, having fallen into misfortune through his own misconduct, he possessed little means; the wealth in his house was completely exhausted,
and his son became distressed.
That householder had a friend,
and he said to him,
"You are my son as well."
"Look after my field;
I shall provide for your sustenance with food.
He then began to perform the work of that field.
He, too, provided him with the requisites for his practice out of devotion.
Then, at another time when a festival had arrived,
the boy’s mother reflected:
"Today the householder’s wife will be busy providing a meal for friends, relatives, kinsmen, and mendicants;
I shall go at the proper time and bring food for that boy.
Having gone at the proper time, she informed the householder’s wife of this matter.
Enraged, she said:
"I will not give anything to śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas yet;
I will give it first to my kinsmen or to a servant."
"For now let it wait;
tomorrow I shall give you double.
Then the boy's mother reflected:
"Lest the child become hungry,
I shall take this ball of unsalted boiled beans belonging to me.
Having taken it, she went to the field.
Having related in detail everything that had been said by the householder’s wife regarding her son, he said:
"I have brought this lump of saltless boiled beans belonging to myself;
please eat it."
He said,
"Leave it and go.
She left it behind and departed.

When Buddhas do not appear in the world, Pratyekabuddhas arise in the world; they are compassionate toward the lowly and the wretched, devoted to remote lodgings and seats, and are the sole objects of veneration for the world. Eventually, a certain Pratyekabuddha arrived at that place, and he was seen by him.
Radiant in body and radiant in mind, he conducted himself with a peaceful deportment.
He reflected:
"Surely, it is because I have not performed acts of service toward such a truly worthy recipient of offerings."
"By whom has my condition become such?
If this man would take from me a lump of saltless boiled beans, I would give it to him.
Then the Pratyekabuddha, knowing the thought of that poor man with his own mind, extended his alms-bowl.
"If it has been relinquished by you, let it be given into this bowl.
Then, with intense faith, she offered that lump of saltless boiled rice to the Pratyekabuddha.
"What do you think, monks? That poor man at that time and on that occasion was none other than King Prasenajit of Kosala."
Because he offered this saltless lump of boiled beans to a Pratyekabuddha,
by that karma he exercised sovereignty and lordship among the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven for six times;
and by the remainder of that very same karma, he became a consecrated Kṣatriya king in this very Śrāvastī for six times.
Even now, he has become an anointed Kṣatriya king;
that alms-offering of his has ripened. It is with reference to that ripening that I speak.
"You behold the city with its merchants, where elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry march about,
all because of that coarse, saltless lump of boiled beans.
Thus the report spread throughout the surrounding area.

King Prasenajit of Kosala heard that the Blessed One had explained the unfolding of karma concerning a lump of unsalted boiled beans belonging to King Prasenajit of Kosala. He then approached the place where the Blessed One was staying.
Having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
As King Prasenajit of Kosala sat there to one side, the Blessed One gladdened him with a discourse on the Dharma as before, and finally became silent.
Then King Prasenajit of Kosala rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"May the Blessed One, together with the community of monks, accept from me for three months the requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for the sick.
The Blessed One accepted King Prasenajit of Kosala's request by remaining silent.
Thereupon, King Prasenajit of Kosala provided the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, with food of a hundred flavors for three months.
Each individual monk was covered with a garment worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold], and having procured ten million jars of oil, they were prepared to offer a garland of lamps; there,
during that meal and worship, a great clamor arose.
At that time, a certain female dependent of the city was in extreme distress.
While she was wandering for alms with a broken bowl, she heard that loud and great noise.
Having heard it, she asked again:
"Sirs, what is this loud noise, this great clamor? Others replied,
"King Prasenajit of Kosala has fed the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, for the three-month rainy season retreat."
Each individual monk was clothed in a garment worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold], and having procured ten million jars of oil, he was prepared to offer a garland of lamps; then,
this thought occurred to that female street-sweeper of the city:

"This King Prasenajit of Kośala, unsatiated by his merits, is today giving gifts and performing meritorious deeds. What if I were also to prepare something from somewhere and offer a lamp to the Blessed One? Thinking thus, she requested a small amount of oil from a broken bowl, lit a lamp, and placed it on the Blessed One’s walking path.
And falling at his feet, he made this aspiration:

"By this root of merit, just as this Blessed One Śākyamuni has appeared in the world as a Teacher when the lifespan of beings is one hundred years, may I too become a Teacher named Śākyamuni when the lifespan is one hundred years."
Just as Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana were his foremost pair, his auspicious pair; Ānanda the monk was his attendant;

Śuddhodana his father; Mahāmāyā his mother; Kapilavastu his city; and Rāhulabhadra his son—likewise may Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana be my foremost pair, my auspicious pair, and Ānanda the monk my attendant.
"Śuddhodana was my father, Mahāmāyā my mother, Kapilavastu the city, and Prince Rāhulabhadra my son.
Just as this Blessed One, having divided his relics, will enter final nirvāṇa, so too may I, having divided my relics, enter final nirvāṇa.
When all those lamps had gone out, the lamp lit by her continued to burn.
It is indeed the natural law (*dharmatā*) of the Blessed Buddhas that the attendant does not retire until the Blessed Buddhas have retired.
The Venerable Ānanda reflected:
"It is impossible, it is out of the question, that the Blessed Buddhas would resort to a bed in the light; what if I were to extinguish the lamp?"
He began to extinguish it with his hand, but he was unable; then with the corner of his robe, and then with a fan, yet even so he was unable.
The Blessed One said, "Do not fall into despair, Ānanda."
Even if the Vairambha winds were to blow, they would not be able to extinguish it, let alone a hand, the corner of a robe, or a fan.
For this lamp was lit by that girl with such a great mental exertion.
Furthermore, Ānanda, when the lifespan of beings is one hundred years, that girl will become a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha named Śākyamuni.

Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana were his foremost pair, the auspicious pair; the monk Ānanda was his attendant; Śuddhodana was his father; Mahāmāyā was his mother; Kapilavastu was his city; and Prince Rāhulabhadra was his son.
Having performed the distribution of his relics, he too will enter final nirvāṇa.
A report spread throughout the vicinity:
"A certain female city-dweller offered a lamp with her head at the Blessed One’s walkway;
she has been prophesied by the Blessed One for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment."
Having heard this, the faithful brahmin householders, anticipating her future virtues, provided her with all necessary requisites.
When King Prasenajit of Kosala heard of this,
he was filled with wonder and, taking a thousand jars of oil, prepared a magnificent garland of lamps.
He placed a lamp made of the four jewels at the head of the walking path,
and then, having gone into the presence of the Blessed One, he said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, I have invited the Blessed One for a week of meals on behalf of the worship of the noble Mahākāśyapa."
Regarding that ball of unsalted boiled beans, the Blessed One explained my past course of karma to me.
Furthermore, I fed the Blessed One together with the community of disciples for three months;
each and every monk was clothed in a pair of garments worth a hundred thousand pieces of gold, and having prepared ten million jars of oil, I offered them as a garland of lamps.
"And yet, I have not been prophesied by the Blessed One for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
It would be well if the Blessed One were also to prophesy me for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, [saying]:
'When indeed shall I become the Eldest of the World, the Guide?'"
The Blessed One said:
"Great King, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is profound;
it appears profound, difficult to see, difficult to understand, beyond reasoning, outside the sphere of reasoning, subtle, precise, and to be realized by the wise and the learned."

"It is not easy for you alone to acquire her by means of a single gift, nor by a hundred gifts, nor by a thousand gifts, nor even by a hundred thousand gifts. Rather, O Great King, as one who aspires to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, you must indeed give gifts, you must indeed perform meritorious deeds, and you must cultivate [virtue]."
"You should cultivate and attend upon spiritual friends;
in this way, you will one day become a leader, the eldest in the world.
When he had spoken thus, King Prasenajit of Kosala wept, shedding tears like rain.
Then King Prasenajit of Kośala, wiping away his tears with the corner of his robe, said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, how many gifts were given or merits performed by the Blessed One while seeking unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment?
The Blessed One replied:
"Let alone, O Great King, those past eons.

Listen well and attend thoroughly to that which I have done—having aspired for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment in this very Bhadrakalpa—I have given gifts and performed various kinds of meritorious deeds; I shall speak of it."
In the past, O Great King, during the era of the people of Amitāyus, there was a king named Upoṣadha.
A tumor grew upon his head;
it was soft and very tender, just like a tuft of cotton or a tuft of silk-cotton.
Or, because it had reached full maturity, it burst open and a boy was born—
handsome, beautiful, pleasing, fair-skinned, with a golden complexion, a head shaped like a parasol, long arms, and a broad forehead.
With a loud voice, joined eyebrows, and a prominent nose, his body was adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
As soon as he was born, the prince was brought into the inner apartments;
upon seeing the prince, eighty thousand women of King Upoṣadha experienced the flow of milk from their breasts.
Each woman said, "Māndhāya, Māndhāya!
Thus, the name Māndhātṛ, "Māndhāya," became established for him.
Others say:
"Since he was born from the crown [of his father's head], let the prince's name be Mūrdhāta. In this regard, some know him as Māndhātṛ, while others know him as Mūrdhāta.
The *Māndhātṛ-sūtra* is found in detail in the *Rājasaṃyuktaka-nipāta* of the *Madhyama-āgama*.
While Prince Māndhātṛ was playing at the games of childhood, six Śakras passed away.

Likewise, while he was exercising the duties of crown prince, six [Śakras] passed away; while he was exercising great sovereignty, six [passed away]; and while he was governing the districts of Jambudvīpa, six [passed away].
And with the mere arising of his thought, a rain of jewels and a rain of garments fell.
A rain of gold fell within the inner apartments.
At that time, there was a seer named Durmukha in Vaiśālī who possessed the five superknowledges;
in his hermitage, birds were constantly warbling.
"Meditations have words as their thorns;
he does not attain one-pointedness of mind.
Thus did that [seer] pronounce a curse upon the birds.
"May their wings fall off!
Then King Māndhātṛ heard this;
having heard it, he thought, "This seer is merciless," and said:
"You must not dwell within my domain.
He reflected:
"This king is the lord of the four continents; where should I go?"
He went to and stayed upon the terrace of Mount Sumeru;
while he was thus governing Avaragodānīya, six Śakras passed away,
and six in Pūrvavideha.
There are six in Uttarakuru;
six for one situated on Mount Nimindhara;
likewise on Vinataka, Aśvakarṇa, Sudarśana, Khadiraka, Īṣādhāra, and Yugandhara.
The intermediate summary verse:
Nimiṃdhara, Vinataka, and likewise Aśvakarṇa-giri.
Sudarśana, Khadiraka, Īṣādhāra, and Yugandhara.
Then, as he was ascending the summit of Mount Sumeru, his army of sages and soldiers was paralyzed.
Seeing this, a yakṣa who dwells in heaven and runs ahead of him spoke this verse:
"Restrain your anger, O Brahmin; this does not succeed everywhere."
"King Māndhātṛ is indeed here; these are not the cranes of Vaiśālī.
Thus King Māndhātṛ asked:
"By whom has this vanguard of the army been paralyzed?"
The royal sage asked:
"What is dear to those seers?"
O Lord, let their matted locks fall away; let their matted locks be destroyed,
and let them be my precursors.
Then their matted locks fell away;
with bows and arrows in hand, they began to run forward. The jewel among women said:
"O King, these are seers practicing austerities;
what is the use of them?
Let them be released."
They were released by the king;
having again applied themselves with vigor, they realized the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*).

Likewise, when Nanda and Upananda, the dragon kings (*nāgarāja*), saw Māndhātṛ’s army, thinking "these are indeed asuras," they went out to meet him with a fourfold military force (*caturaṅga-balakāya*).
They were broken simply by the sight of the army.
Your Majesty, the Karoṭapāṇi yakṣas, the Māyādhara yakṣas, the Sadāmatta yakṣas,
and all those such as Nanda and Upananda, being defeated, retreated toward where the gods of the Four Great Kings reside.
Having approached, he said this to the gods of the Four Great Kings:
"O worthy ones, you should know that a great army has arrived;
let the fourfold military force be arrayed."
"We have all been defeated," they realized;
they said:
"Sirs, this King Māndhātā, a universal monarch, is going to see Śakra, the lord of the gods. He is one of great power and merit;
what ability do we have to engage in battle with him?"
"But one should go out to meet him, taking half [of the offerings] and the water for washing the feet.

Thereupon, the gods of the Four Great Kings took half [of the offerings] and the water for washing the feet, and went out to meet him with parasols, banners, flags, and various kinds of musical instruments.
Then King Māndhātṛ, having greeted the gods of the Four Great Kings in return, proceeded toward the Heaven of the Thirty-three, surrounded by the gods.
Śakra, the lord of the gods, invited him to share half his throne.
Then the asuras, having arrayed their fourfold army, advanced against Śakra, the lord of the gods;
this was reported to Śakra, the lord of the gods, by the yakṣas.
"Kauśika, you should know that the asuras have arrived, having broken through the five outposts;
therefore, do whatever must be done or should be performed.
Thereupon, Śakra, the lord of the gods, set forth.
King Māndhātṛ said, "Stay; I myself will go.
Śakra replied:
"Do so," he said.
Thereupon, King Māndhātṛ, having ascended into the sky above with eighteen koṭis of the foremost of his military forces, struck his arms in defiance.
When the asuras saw those eighteen koṭis of the foremost of his military forces and heard that most terrifying sound, they covered their ears and fled.
Then this thought occurred to King Māndhātṛ:
"I possess the continent of Jambudvīpa—prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people; and likewise Pūrvavideha, Avaragodānīya, and Uttarakuru.
What if I were to exercise sovereign power and lordship over both gods and men?"
As soon as that thought arose, King Māndhātṛ’s supernatural power vanished; having returned to Jambudvīpa, he declared himself afflicted by a severe illness and spoke this verse:
"No satisfaction is found in sensual pleasures, even with a rain of kārṣāpaṇa coins."
Having understood that sensual pleasures offer little enjoyment and bring much suffering, the wise person finds no delight even in divine pleasures.
The disciple of the Perfectly Awakened One delights in the destruction of craving;
even a mountain of gold equal to the Himalayas would not suffice for one person— knowing this, the wise person should so conduct himself.
How could one who perceives that suffering has its source in these sensual desires ever find delight in them?
Having recognized that worldly acquisitions are a thorn, the wise person trains for their very removal.

Then King Māndhātā, having performed a sacrifice without restriction, spoke this verse: "Knowing life to be short and the state beyond [this world] to be very difficult to attain, one should perform meritorious deeds; for there is suffering for one who has not performed merit."
"Therefore, indeed, one who desires merit should give gifts according to the rule;
for those who have performed meritorious deeds rejoice both in this world and in the next.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
"What do you think, Great King? That King Māndhātṛ was none other than I at that time, on that occasion.

Although I performed such benefit for sentient beings, I did not thereby attain unsurpassed knowledge. Rather, this gift was merely a cause and merely a provision for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."
Furthermore, Great King, listen to how I performed every benefit while seeking unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Long ago, Great King, there was a universal monarch named Mahāsudarśana, endowed with the seven treasures and the four human supernormal powers.
This is told in detail in the *Mahāsudarśanasūtra*, in the *Ṣaṭsūtrikanipāta* of the *Dīrghāgama*.
Then King Mahāsudarśana, having fed five hundred pratyekabuddhas in the Palace of Dharma and having clothed each one with a pair of fine garments, spoke this verse:
"Having obtained abundant wealth, a wise person should not be negligent;
he should give to those of perfected virtue, wherein offerings bear fruit."
"Having thus given here with a faithful and liberated mind,
the wise and learned man shall be reborn in a world of happiness free from dispute.
"It may be, Great King, that you think the king named Mahāsudarśana at that time and on that occasion was someone else."
"One should not view it thus that he was a universal monarch, a lord of the four continents, endowed with the seven jewels and the four human supernormal powers;

rather, it was I myself who at that time, on that occasion, was the universal monarch named Mahāsudarśana, the lord of the four continents, endowed with the seven jewels and the four [supernormal powers]."

"By means of human supernatural powers, O Great King, you might think: 'Surely it was through that gift or that sharing of a gift by me that unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening was attained. But you should certainly not view it in this way.
Rather, that gift was merely a cause, merely a condition, and merely a provision for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening."
Furthermore, Great King, listen to that which was done by me while seeking unexcelled, perfect enlightenment—namely, the gifts I gave and the merits I performed.
Long ago, Great King, there was a wealthy brahmin householder named Velāma.
He bestowed such gifts as these upon the brahmins.
Of eighty-four thousand elephants adorned with gold ornaments, bearing golden banners, and covered with nets of gold—
as described in detail in the *Velāma-sūtra*, in the *Brāhmaṇa-varga* of the *Madhyama-āgama*—
having thus given these gifts, he spoke this verse:
For by giving a gift one shall indeed be happy; by giving a gift one becomes confident. Through generosity, one is rightly honored among both gods and humans.
Therefore, those who desire prosperity, liberation, constant sovereignty, and the abode of the gods should fearlessly practice generosity.
"It may be, Great King, that you think the great brahmin householder named Velāma at that time and on that occasion was someone else.
But it should not be viewed in this way;
for I myself was the great brahmin householder named Velāma at that time and on that occasion."
"I gave such a gift as that to the brahmins.
Now, Great King, you might think that unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment was attained by me through that gift or through that distribution of the gift; however, it should not be viewed in this way.
Rather, that gift was merely a cause, merely a condition, and merely a provision for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."
Furthermore, Great King, listen to that which was done by me while seeking unexcelled, perfect enlightenment—namely, the gifts I gave and the merits I performed.

Long ago, Great King, there was a king named Śakuna, a universal monarch (cakravartin) who ruled over the four continents, endowed with the seven precious jewels and the four superhuman powers (ṛddhi).
He was a friend and companion of Śakra, the lord of the gods.
His queen had neither son nor daughter;
placing his cheek in his hand, he remained lost in thought:
"In such wealth and sovereignty as mine, I have neither son nor daughter."
"After my passing, the family will become heirless.
Śakra, the lord of the gods, saw him and said:
"Friend, why do you sit there lost in thought with your cheek resting on your hand?
He replied,
"Kauśika, despite such great wealth and sovereignty of mine, I have neither son nor daughter."
"After my passing, the family will become heirless.
He said,
"My friend, I shall send you a medicinal herb."
The goddesses will drink [the water],
and from that they will become his sons and daughters.
Śakra, having taken medicinal herbs from Mount Gandhamādana, sent them to that king.
The king handed her over to the harem, saying,
"You shall drink this medicinal herb.
Now, that king’s chief queen was pregnant.
They gave her that medicine without having her rise up;
they all became pregnant,
and only afterwards did the chief queen recover.
She saw that they were pregnant and said,
"What have you done that you have become pregnant?"
They said,
"The King gave us medicinal herbs for our drink;
for what reason were we not raised up by you?"
But rather, by which vessel were the medicinal herbs drunk? Having tied up a bundle of *kuśa* grass,
where are those *kuśa* blades?
"These are here.
She washed the kuśa grass and drank it;
she too became pregnant.
After the lapse of eight or nine months, they all gave birth;
sons were born to all of them,
and to that chief queen also a son was born who was endowed with eighteen unfavorable marks.
With a face having the form of a lion’s mouth and possessing the strength of a great wrestler,
a grand birth ceremony was performed for him upon his birth, and the name Kuśa was established.
Upon seeing him, the king felt resentment, whereas seeing those other sons, he manifested great affection.
The neighboring vassal kings said, "Sirs,
we have all been overwhelmed by this great king of birds;
let us go and depose him from his kingdom."
Having arrived, they surrounded his city with a fourfold army and remained there;
King Mahāśakuni was unable to wage war against them.
Having closed the gates and caused the walls to be measured out, he remained there.
Kuśa went to his mother's presence and said,
"Mother, for whose sake have the gates been closed?"
"This father of yours is unable to engage in battle with the provincial kings;
he remains here with the gates closed.
Mother, I shall wage war against them."
"Let the king grant me a chariot.
My son, you are disliked and detested by him;
how will he give you a chariot?"
"Mother, go;
having gone, say this:
'Prince Kuśa will do battle with these.'"
"Give me the chariot.
Having gone there with her, she said to the king:
"Your Majesty, the prince says this:"
"I shall do battle with them;
provide me with a chariot.
He was then provided with a chariot by him.
Having fastened two quivers and mounted his chariot, he began to depart.
Śakra, the lord of the gods, observed:
"These minor kings are powerful."
"Who is this prince Kuśa, a Bodhisattva of the Fortunate Aeon, who will fall into exhaustion?
Assistance must be rendered to him.
Thereupon, he was given a conch, a discus, and a mace.
“O Bodhisattva, you should maintain your livelihood by these means. Having opened the gates, he went out and blew his conch shell.
Then, by the sound of the conch, the army was put to flight;
some were deafened by that sound,
while others fled, covering their ears.
If they hurled a discus or a mace, it would sink into the subterranean realm (rasātala).
Having gone into the midst of the battle, he blew his conch shell;
the ears of all [the enemies] burst asunder.
Thinking, "This is a man-rākṣasa," they fled.
Having achieved victory over all his vassals, he came into the presence of his father and said,
"Your Majesty, the country has been brought under my control."
Hearing that all the kings had been defeated, King Mahāśakuni was pleased;
he reflected:
Prince Kuśa was powerful and endowed with heroism;
how could I manifest a lack of faith toward him?
He began to manifest faith toward him.
He settled those sons there and began to ask for a maiden for Kuśa as well;
they all said:
"We shall give the girl, with the exception of Kuśa.
A certain king requested the daughter of another king;
however, the marriage was not yet performed.
Then, by means of another pretext, at the command of the Great Bird King, that maiden was bestowed upon Kuśa for the sake of his son;
and having observed an auspicious constellation, day, and moment, Prince Kuśa was married.
The king said,
"Gentlemen, no mirror must be presented to Kuśa, nor must he be bathed with the consecration vessel;
furthermore, he must not be allowed entry into the inner apartments during the day."
The prince Kuśa was playing together with his mothers;
he was seen by that wife, who said:
"Who is this piśāca playing in the midst of the princes? "He shall become your husband.
Furthermore, she saw him again playing together with the princes in water-sports.
"As long as he is indeed your master.
"What kind of master will he be for me?
She reflected:
"I shall make it manifest.
She lit a lamp, covered it with a cloth, and set it down;
then he entered the inner apartments.
She then showed him a lamp;
when he saw that [the being] was possessed of eighteen inauspicious marks and had a face shaped like a lion's, she cried out, "A piśāca! A piśāca! and fled.
A certain frontier district of King Mahāśakuni had risen in rebellion;
he dispatched Prince Kuśa with the command:
"Go and subdue the frontier district."
He went there,
and Kuśa’s wife sent word to her parents:
"Are there no men on this earth that you have given me to a piśāca?"
"If you take me, it will be well;
if not, I shall kill myself.
She was then taken by them.
Prince Kuśa, having conquered that border-town chief, returned;
he asked his mother,
"Mother, where is my wife?"
She said,
"I was taken away by my parents.
For whose sake?"
"Thinking 'you are a piśāca,' [he said:
'Mother, I am going; I shall bring her back. 'Son, do so.'"
Taking up his conch, discus, and mace, he set out.
When he reached a certain mountain hamlet, a great multitude of people, out of fear of a lion, had closed their gates and were standing there looking about in all directions.
Prince Kuśa said:
"Why do you stand here?
"Out of fear of a lion.
"Why then do you not kill it?"
"We are not able [to do so].
If I were to have him executed, what would you give me?
Half of a fourfold army."
Prince Kuśa went to Siṃha’s side and blew his conch shell; Siṃha’s ears burst and he passed away.
Having seized him, he went to the market town and said, "Sirs, this is that lion;
seize half of a fourfold army."
He said,
"Let it remain in your very hands;
you shall give it back once you have returned."
He went to the small town where his wife was, and having approached a florist in that town, [the florist asked:
"Who are you, being such as this?"
He said,
"I am the son of a garland-maker.
What is your name?"
Regarding the term "Vṛjika":
Bodhisattvas are skilled in those various fields of arts and fields of crafts;
he weaves a beautiful garland.
The garland-maker gave that garland to the girl,
and she said:
"You have never before woven such a garland;
what is the reason for this?
"It was woven by my pupil."
"I see your pupil.
He led him there, and she saw him.
She reflected:
"Who is this *piśāca* that has come? she cried out; "A *piśāca*, a *piśāca*! she shouted, and he was driven out.
He went into the presence of the cook,
who asked, "Who are you?"
"I am the son of a cook. What is your name? "I am named Sthālīsugandha."
He prepared an excellent meal.
That cook presented that meal to the girl,
and the girl said:
"O man, what is the purpose of this excellent preparation of food?
It was prepared by my pupil;
let me see it."
Your pupil—
[this continued] until he too was expelled from there;
he went into the presence of the censors.
He said,
"Who are you?
"I am the son of a physician."
"What is your name? "My name is Ātreya.
A headache arose for that girl.
The physicians were unable to restore her to health;
that physician remained lost in thought and said:
"Preceptor, why are you lost in thought?
The princess has a headache; we are unable to cure her."
"I am going; I shall restore him to health.
He departed and was seen by her.
She reflected:
"Who is this piśāca that has come?
He reflected further:
"If I say anything, he will not restore me to health."
"When I have recovered, I will expel him.
She was restored to health by him, and then a cry was raised: "A piśāca! A piśāca!"
He was expelled by her and went into the presence of the minister. "Who are you? [the minister asked].
"I am a fighter of a thousand. They made an alliance with him. That king's daughter heard that he was the one by whom she had previously been won.
"The princess who was previously obtained by me has abandoned Prince Kuśa and returned to her own home.
Therefore, he sent a message to that king:
'If you will indeed give me your daughter, that would be well.'"
"If not, I shall depose you from the kingdom.
He replied,
"This daughter of mine has been given in marriage to Prince Kuśa, the son of King Mahāśakuni."
"What shall I give to another now?
Having arrived with his fourfold army, he remained surrounding that royal capital.
That king was unable to wage war against him.
Having closed the gates, he remained there.
Prince Kuśa addressed the ministers:
"Sirs, why are the gates closed?"
They reported this to him in detail.
Prince Kuśa said:
"If the king grants me his daughter in marriage, I shall engage in battle with him."
They informed the king,
and he said,
"I have given this daughter in marriage to the son of Mahāśakuni."
"How shall I give this to him?
Moreover, this agitation is for the sake of the girl.
The ministers said:
"Your Majesty, let him first engage in battle with this man;
it is not yet known who will be victorious. We shall wait for the opportune moment."
Prince Kuśa, having fastened two quivers containing five hundred arrows each and taken up a conch, a discus, and a mace, went forth. He blew the conch, and their ears were split asunder.
They fled.
That princess reflected:
"This Prince Kuśa possesses great heroism and prowess."
"How could I manifest a lack of faith in his presence?
She manifested faith toward him and said this to the king:
"Do as you have promised.
Daughter, you have been given away by me to Kuśa.
"Father, this is indeed that very Prince Kuśa."
"Daughter, if it is so, then go. He provided him with a fourfold army and sent him off with great honor.
He went to that mountain stronghold.
He said to them,
"Sirs, give us half of your fourfold army.
They replied:
Prince, the fourfold army has proceeded like a flood of water.
Not far from where the fourfold army is being carried across, some sheep are grazing.
Prince Kuśa spoke this verse:
Where sixty-year-old elephants are carried,
there it should be understood by comparison that even goats and sheep have already been carried.
"If you grant [it] to me, that would be well;
if you do not grant it, I shall establish a great boundary.
They granted it to him.
He arrived at the bank of a river;
with his body weary, he entered the river to bathe,
and there he beheld the reflection of his own face.
He reflected:
"He is endowed with eighteen unfavorable marks and has a face shaped like the mouth of a lion;
for this very reason, this princess displays a lack of confidence toward me."
"What use have I for such a life?
I shall go and kill myself.
Having entered a certain thicket, he began to hang himself.
Śakra, the lord of the gods, perceived:
"This Bodhisattva of the Fortunate Aeon, deprived of the beauty of his form, is seeking to take his own life;
his heart's desire must be fulfilled."
Śakra said:
"O Prince, do not fall into despair; do not kill yourself.
Place this crest-jewel upon your head, and your heart's desire will be fulfilled."
Having said this, he departed.
Prince Kuśa began to enter the inner apartments,
but he was stopped by the gatekeeper.
"Do not enter the inner apartments of Prince Kuśa.
He replied,
"I am that very Kuśa."
They did not believe it;
therefore, he removed his crest-jewel,
and it became as it was before.
They believed him. Prince Kuśa reflected:
"I shall remain right here."
He sent word to his father:
"Father, give me your permission;
I shall remain right here."
Śakra, the lord of the gods, showed him four types of precious minerals;
having fashioned that city out of those four jewels, he established it.
Because it was perfumed by Prince Kuśa, it came to be known as "Kuśāvatī," meaning "Perfumed by Kuśa."

He became a king named Kuśa, a powerful universal monarch; having established sacrificial enclosures in those sixty thousand cities, he gave gifts to the brahmins for many years, many hundreds of years, many thousands of years, and many hundreds of thousands of years.
Seeing the perfection of his own sacrifice, he spoke this verse:
"Seeing such prosperity for oneself among gods and humans,
who would not bestow gifts, by which prosperity is obtained?"
He who, casting aside hundreds of men and overcoming envy that acts as a rival,
gives a gift out of fear for the next world— he, in my view, is the bravest among the brave.
The sages do not call him a hero who wanders through the ranks with weapon in hand;
rather, they call those all-knowing ones heroes who bestow gifts with confidence.

It might occur to you, Great King, that at that time and on that occasion, the king named Kuśa who was a powerful universal monarch and who gave gifts and performed meritorious deeds in those sixty thousand cities was someone else;
however, it should not be viewed in this way.

Moreover, Mahārāja, at that time and on that occasion, I myself was the king named Kuśa, a powerful universal monarch (*balacakravartin*). It was by me alone that sacrificial enclosures were constructed in those sixty thousand cities, gifts were bestowed, and meritorious deeds were performed.
Could it be, Mahārāja, that [the result] was due to that gift of mine?
One should certainly not view it thus that "unexcelled, perfect enlightenment was fully realized through the distribution of gifts.
Rather, that gift of mine was merely a cause, merely a condition, or merely a provision for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
The monks asked the Buddha,
the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, what karma was performed by King Kuśa, the ripening of which resulted in his being endowed with eighteen secondary marks,
yet born into a family that is wealthy, possessing great riches and great enjoyments?"
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by Kuśa alone; their conditions have been gathered, their causes have matured, they have arrived like a flood, and they are inevitable.
Monks, since these actions were performed and accumulated by Kuśa alone, who else shall experience them?"
Monks, actions that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element, nor in the fire element, nor in the wind element.
Rather, it is within the very appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases that actions—whether wholesome or unwholesome—are ripened.
Actions do not perish, even after hundreds of eons.
Having obtained the necessary conditions and the right time, the actions of embodied beings indeed bear fruit.
Once upon a time, monks, a householder lived in a certain village.
Taking with him an abundance of solid and soft food, he went to a park.

At times when Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, do not appear in the world, Pratyekabuddhas arise; they are compassionate toward the lowly and the destitute, frequent remote lodgings, and are the sole objects of veneration for the world.
Then, a certain Pratyekabuddha, while wandering on a journey through the countryside, arrived at that park.
He was seen by the householder,
who gave an order to his servants.
"Sirs, expel this renunciant!
They did not dare to expel him;
therefore, the householder himself rose, took hold of him, expelled him, and said:
"Endowed with eighteen unfavorable marks, including a lion's face, where are you entering?
The Pratyekabuddha reflected:
"Lest he should suffer, being utterly wounded and harmed. Having understood this, he rose high into the air; such is the detailed account.
When he had been honored by him, he prostrated at his feet and began to make a formal vow:
"Since I have uttered harsh words toward such a truly worthy recipient of offerings, may I not be a partaker of the fruit of this action."
"However, because he performed acts of service, by this root of merit may I be born into a family that is wealthy, possessing great riches and great enjoyments.
What do you think, monks? That householder was none other than this Kuśa.
Because he uttered harsh words toward the Pratyekabuddha, as the ripening of that karma, he was endowed with eighteen secondary marks and had a face shaped like the mouth of a lion."
And because he performed acts of service, as the ripening of that karma, he became a powerful universal monarch (balacakravartin).
Thus, monks, for actions that are entirely black, the ripening is entirely black.
For those that are mixed, the result is mixed;
for those that are exclusively white, the result is exclusively white.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves in this way:
Having cast aside actions that are exclusively black as well as those that are mixed, one should apply oneself only to actions that are exclusively white.
Furthermore, Great King, listen to what gifts were given and what merits were performed by me while seeking unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

In the past, O Great King, there was a king of the *mataṅgas* named Triśaṅku among the Kaliṅgas. He had a retinue of many hundreds of *mataṅgas*, many thousands of *mataṅgas*, and many hundreds of thousands of *mataṅgas*. He was characterized by loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassionate, and sympathetic toward the welfare of all sentient beings.
Whenever there was a famine in his realm, the rain-god would send down rain through his invocation of truth (*satyopayācana*).
Famine never occurs there. He went forth among the rishis and realized the five supernormal powers.
At that time, a king named Brahmadatta was ruling in Vārāṇasī; the kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people.
Later, at another time, the fortune-tellers predicted a twelve-year drought.
Thereupon, King Brahmadatta had a proclamation made by the ringing of bells throughout the city of Vārāṇasī.
"Listen, O citizens residing in Vārāṇasī!
The astrologers have predicted a twelve-year drought.
Whoever among you has food for this duration, let him remain."
"Let him who has none go.
Then that multitude of people, terrified by the fear of death during the time of famine, began to converse among themselves:
"Sirs, this proclamation by ringing a bell has been made by the king regarding his conquered realm."
"How should we proceed? Where shall we go?
They heard that in the region of Mataṅga there was a seer of the Mataṅga caste, and that by his truthful prayer the rain-god would send down rain.
Then those who did not have provisions for twelve years went to the region of Mataṅga. There was a king of the Mataṅgas named Mataṅgarāja, the son of a seer;
he provided that body of people with food and drink for twelve years, sustaining them with sustenance.
Immediately following that, a famine appeared.
King Brahmadatta asked his ministers,
"Where has this body of people gone?"
The ministers said, "Your Majesty,
in the kingdom of Kaliṅga there is a king of the Mataṅgas named Triśaṅku, who is friendly by nature, compassionate, high-minded, and devoted to the welfare of all beings.
By his invocation of truth, Your Majesty, the rain falls."
A great multitude of people went there. The king said, "Sirs, this is a great famine, resembling an intermediate aeon of famine."
"How should one proceed in this matter?
They replied,
"Your Majesty, it is heard:"
"He who was the king in the realm of Mataṅga and has gone forth among the sages—he should be entreated.
Thereupon, King Brahmadatta went to the realm of Mataṅga and began to entreat that sage:
"Great Seer, in my kingdom there is a great famine, resembling the intermediate eon of famine."
"Therefore, you ought to make a vow of truth.
He began to make that vow of truth:
"Born in a family of outcaste dog-cookers, I was Mataṅga, a wicked and violent man."
He was renowned among both gods and men as Triśaṅku.
By this word of truth, that my mind of loving-kindness has been well-cultivated toward all sentient beings without exception— O Naga, satisfy these creatures with rain!
Since from birth I have cultivated a mind of loving-kindness,
by this word of truth, O Naga King, satisfy all living beings.
Then, through that truthful supplication, the rain god poured down in Vārāṇasī;
the famine ceased and a time of plenty appeared.
Thereupon, the multitude of people residing in Vārāṇasī came from the district of Mataṅga to Vārāṇasī.

It may be, O Great King, that you think the one who at that time, on that occasion, was the king of the Mātaṅgas named Triśaṅku— compassionate by nature, merciful, and sympathetic toward the welfare of all beings, through whose truthful prayer the rain fell from the sky,
the famine ceased, and abundance appeared— was someone else. [But he was not.]
Indeed, it should not be viewed in this way; rather,

it was I myself who at that time and on that occasion was the king of the Matanga hunters named Triśaṅku— compassionate by nature, merciful, and sympathetic toward the welfare of all beings— for whom the god sent rain through the power of a truthful prayer.
It might be, Great King, that you think: "I have attained unexcelled, perfect enlightenment through giving or through the distribution of gifts.
Indeed, it should not be viewed in this way.
Rather, that gift was merely a cause or merely a provision for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, Great King, listen to that which was done by me when, aspiring for unexcelled perfect enlightenment, I gave gifts and performed meritorious deeds.
Long ago, Great King, there was a universal monarch named Mahādeva in Mithilā;
this is told in detail in the *Mahādeva-sūtra*, in the *Rājasaṃyuktaka-nipāta* of the *Madhyamāgama*.
Having seen the perfection of his own sacrifice, he spoke this verse:
"By one who desires sovereignty among gods or men,
and who is terrified by the fear of poverty, a gift should be given according to one's ability."
"In this world the donor is honored; among the gods the donor is honored. He is a refuge for all beings, just as a fruit-bearing tree is for birds.

It may be, O Great King, that you think that at that time and on that occasion, the universal monarch named Mahādeva—who established that certain, auspicious Dharma—was someone else. [But he was not.]
Regarding the statement that eighty-four thousand great gods, having followed the path that leads certainly to what is auspicious, practiced the holy life as royal sages (*rājarṣi*),
it should not be viewed in this way.
For at that time, on that occasion, I myself was the universal monarch (*cakravartin*) named Mahādeva.

It was by me alone that this certain, auspicious Dharma was set in motion—that certain, auspicious path having been set in motion, eighty-four thousand great gods and royal sages practiced the holy life (*brahmacarya*). Now, Great King, you might think: "Was it through that gift or through that distribution of gifts by me that unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) was attained?"
Indeed, it should not be viewed in this way;
rather, that gift was merely a cause, merely a condition, and merely a provision for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, Great King, listen to those gifts which were given and merits which were performed by me while aspiring for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
In the past, O Great King, in this very city of Mithilā, there was a king named Nimi, the last of that line, who was a universal monarch (*cakravartin*).
This is told in detail in the *Nimisūtra* of the *Madhyamāgama*, in the section on kings (*rājasaṃyuktaka-nipāta*).
Having observed the perfection of his own sacrifice, he spoke as follows:

"Having seen those who have performed auspicious deeds as well as those who have performed inauspicious deeds, those men who remain heedless are to be pitied; they are the lowest of persons. Thus it is said.

Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to King Nimi: "Dwell here, Nimi; enjoy yourself, Nimi! Right here, endowed and possessed of the five strands of sensual pleasure, play, rejoice, and amuse yourself!
He then spoke this verse:
Just as a charioteer uses borrowed goods only for a limited time,
so too is this state which is subject to the control of others.
"Since I shall go to Mithilā and perform much merit, I will then go to heaven, having accomplished my religious duty and realized my potential.
Having thus spoken, he went to Mithilā, gave gifts, performed meritorious deeds, and recited this verse:
The virtuous praise that gift which is bestowed even in times of distress,
whether given to a Kṣatriya, a Brāhmaṇa, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, or even to a Caṇḍāla or a Pukkasa.
Having given gifts during a famine and having satisfied virtuous people,
one avoids the states of woe and is honored here in the heavenly world.
"Knowing this benefit, the wise should practice giving;
from giving, liberation, sovereignty, and the abode of heroes are attained.
Great King, you might think that at that time and on that occasion, the one who was the universal monarch named Nimi was someone else. [But it was not so.]

He who had gone to the thirty-three gods was invited by Śakra, the lord of the gods, to share half his throne; endowed and possessed of the five divine qualities of sensual pleasure, he sported there.
Indeed, it should not be viewed in this way;

for at that time, on that occasion, I myself was he. It was by me alone that, having come to Mithilā, sacrificial enclosures were constructed at the four city gates, and gifts were given and meritorious deeds performed.
It may be, Great King, that you think: "By that gift or by that distribution of gifts, I have attained unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
But it should not be viewed in this way.
Rather, that gift is merely a cause, merely a condition, and merely a provision for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
After that, there was a powerful king named Ānanda.
In detail, up until the point when one, two, and eventually five sons were born to him;
the one who was his last-born son had a face like a mirror.
He came to be known by the name Ādarśamukha.
He was raised and grew until he became a great man.
Prince Ādarśamukha was pleasant and well-disciplined.
Those others were fierce, impetuous, and harsh;
though they were all intent on accomplishing their father’s purpose, they could not penetrate anything through their wisdom.
But Prince Ādarśamukha analyzed even the most profound questions by means of his own wisdom.
King Ānanda became ill;
he reflected,
"Upon whom shall I establish in the kingship?"
"If I were to establish any one of my four elder brothers in the kingship, they would be fierce, impetuous, and cruel, bringing ruin to the provinces through unjust conduct.
On the other hand, if I were to establish Prince Ādarśamukha in the kingdom, I would be censured by my kinsmen, who would say:
'How is it that this king, setting aside his eldest sons, establishes a younger one in the kingdom?'"
Nevertheless, a strategic arrangement must be made.
He addressed his ministers:
"Come, village chiefs, after my passing, each one of you must examine a prince."
For him, the pair of jeweled sandals remains steady when he sits upon the lion throne, remaining motionless.

The crown bound upon his head becomes motionless, and the women of the inner apartments rise to greet him. Six things to be known through the penetration of wisdom should be understood: a treasure within, a treasure without, a treasure both within and without, a treasure at the top of a tree, a treasure at the peak of a mountain, and a treasure at the edge of water.

"Whosoever possesses all these qualities must be established by you in the kingdom after my passing," he said; then, having declared, "All accumulations end in exhaustion; all elevations end in a fall," he passed away.
Thereupon, those ministers presented a pair of jeweled sandals to the eldest prince.
He did not achieve equanimity;
as he sat, his lion throne shook and his bound crown trembled.
Even the women of the inner apartments did not rise to greet him;
he was informed of the six things to be experienced through wisdom,
yet he neither knew nor understood them.
In this manner, a pair of jeweled sandals was presented to Prince Ādarśamukha, the third of the three brothers.
It remained level;
and when he sat down, the lion throne became established without trembling.
A crown was bound upon his head and remained there, filling it completely.
The women of the inner apartments rose up to greet him.

The ministers said, "In his case too, six things to be understood through wisdom must be known: a treasure within, a treasure without, a treasure both within and without, a treasure at the top of a tree, a treasure at the peak of a mountain, and a treasure at the edge of the water."
Ādarśamukha reflected:
"What is meant by 'an inner treasure'? An inner treasure is a treasure located inside the threshold."
What is meant by "an external treasure"? An external treasure is one located outside the threshold. What is meant by "an internal-external treasure"?
"Treasure inside and outside" means treasure in the middle of the threshold.
"Treasure on the top of the tree": what does this mean? It means treasure at the top of the tree.
For that king, there is a *saṃsthāna* tree; where its shadow flickers and remains at midday, there is a treasure.
On the mountain peak there is a treasure.
For that king, there is a pleasure pond; beneath the bathing stone therein is a treasure.
"At the edge of the water is a treasure.
Wherever the water from the house flows out, at the edge of the village is the treasure.
Those ministers, having inspected everything, brought it forth.
He was consecrated in that kingdom and became a king;
he was a powerful monarch known by the name Ādarśamukha.
In a certain mountain hamlet there lived a brahmin named Daṇḍin.
Having requested oxen from a householder and driven them during the day, he took those oxen and went to that householder’s residence,
arriving just as the householder was eating.
The oxen were ushered in by Daṇḍin;
they departed through another gate.
That householder, having finished his meal, arose from his seat.
When he did not see the oxen,
he seized Daṇḍin and asked,
"Where are the oxen?"
He said,
"They were brought into the house;
you have caused me to lose my oxen."
"Give me the oxen.
He replied, "I will not let them go.
He said:
"This King Ādarśamukha is wise; let us go into his presence.
Having investigated this matter, he will tell us what is appropriate and what is inappropriate.
The two of them set out.
The mare of a certain man ran away.
He said to Daṇḍin, "Hold this mare for me.
[Daṇḍin asked,] "How shall I hold her?"
As he was able,
he took a stone and struck her on the head;
she passed away.
That man said,
"You have killed my mare;
give the mare back to me."
"For whose sake shall I give the mare?
He replied,
"Come, let us go into the presence of King Ādarśamukha."
"He will conceal our transaction.
They set out for that place;
Daṇḍin then began to flee.
He released himself from atop the wall;
he fell upon a weaver who was weaving cloth beneath it,
and the weaver was killed.
Daṇḍin was seized by the weaver’s wife:
"You have caused my husband to be killed;
give my husband back to me!"
"How can I give you my master?
Come, let us go into the presence of King Ādarśamukha;
he will cut through our doubt."
They set out;
on the way, there was a deep river.
There, a carpenter was coming from one bank to the other, carrying an axe in his mouth.
He was addressed by Daṇḍin:
"How much water is there?
Having set down his axe, he replied:
The water was deep;
an adze fell into the water,
and he seized it by means of his staff.
"You have lost my adze in the water;
I will not let it go.
Come, let us go to the presence of Ādarśamukha."
"He will cut through our doubt.
Exhausted in body, they took Daṇḍin and entered the market of Kalapālī.
A son was born to that Kallapālī;
she wrapped the infant in a cloth and laid him down to sleep,
while Daṇḍin sat there.
He said, "The boy! The boy!
and then he saw that he had been killed.
He seized Daṇḍin by her:
"You have killed my son!
Give me back my son!"
He said,
"How could I give you my son?
I will not kill him."
She said,
"Come, let us go into the presence of King Ādarśamukha.
They set out.
Meanwhile, in another place, a crow was perched on a śākhoṭaka tree;
he saw Daṇḍin and said to him,
"Where are you going?"
"I shall not go;
these people are leading me away. Where?"
"Take my message as well to Ādarśamukha;
you should say to King Ādarśamukha:"
"In that place there is a śākhoṭaka tree;
a crow dwells there. He said:
There are other trees with glossy green foliage;
there I find no contentment.
For me, well-being is found only when staying here.
"What is the practice? "We have set out for it. A deer saw a staff-bearer.
He said,
"Daṇḍin, where are you going?
"I am not going," he replied.
"These [messengers] are leading me to the presence of Ādarśamukha;
take also my message to him.
In other places there are green, verdant grasses."
They do not please me.
For what reason?
Because they have already set out.
When he was seen by the partridge, the latter said to him,
"Where will you go?
as before.
Carry my message as well:
in one place I utter the cry "tittiri," and in another, "utittiri."
"What is the reason for this?
"In another place he was bitten by a snake;
as before, convey my message to him as well."
"I emerge with ease from my intention, but I enter with difficulty.
What is the reason for this?
In another place, a snake and a mongoose, who are naturally opposed to one another, are quarreling."
As before, up until: "Carry our message as well;
we two, quarreling with one another by day, find no peace.
What is the reason for this?"
One of the young brides, as before, up until she said:
"Carry a message for me as well:
when I am staying at my father's house, I long for the house of my parents-in-law."
"When I stay at my father-in-law's house, I yearn for my father's house;
what is the reason for this?
They set out.
They approached King Adarśamukha by way of victory.
Having approached and greeted the king with wishes for victory and long life, Daṇḍin sat down to one side;
the others also bowed their heads at his feet and sat down to one side.
The king asks Daṇḍin:
"Have you come?
"I have been brought by the gods," he replies.
"For what reason? [The king asked.
"The dispute with the householder Daṇḍin—everything has been reported.
The king questioned the householder.
"Did you see the ox?
"I saw it.
"Did you have the oxen with the staffed man enter?"
"Your Majesty, they have been brought in.
The king said,
"Cut out the tongue of this staff-bearer, since he did not speak!"
"Then pluck out his eyes as well, so that the oxen will not be tied up. The householder said, "Once my oxen were stolen; now another eye is being plucked out!"
"Let victory go to Daṇḍin!
That man said,
"Your Majesty, this Daṇḍin has killed my mare."
When he had related it in detail,
the king said:
"Cut out this man's tongue, since he said, 'Restrain him as you are able.'"
"Cut off the hands of this staff-bearer, for it is not possible for anyone else to hold her except by striking with a stone.
That man replied,
"Once a mare was killed by me, and a second time my tongue was cut out."
"May victory belong to Daṇḍin!
Thus it was reported in detail by the weaver’s wife,
and the king said:
"Go! Let this very man be your husband.
