She replied, "Once my husband was killed by him; will this other man become my master?"
"May victory be Daṇḍin's!
The carpenter reported this in detail,
and the king said:
"Cut out the tongue of this carpenter who, having released his adze into the water, utters speech;
and pull out the eyes of this staff-bearer who, even though he sees the deep water, asks the carpenter.
The carpenter replied:
"Once my axe was stolen; this is my second severing of the tongue.
Let victory go to Daṇḍin!
Thus it was related in detail by the tavern-keeper.
The king said:
"Cut off the hands of this nursemaid, who has lain down with the boy completely covered by another;
and you guards, pluck out the eyes of whoever shall sit upon a seat belonging to another without having inspected it."
She said:
"Once my son was killed, and a second time my hand was cut off;
let Daṇḍin be victorious!"
Daṇḍin reported the crow’s message,
and the king said:
"Daṇḍin, that crow should be told this:"
"You were once a village chief. In this region there was a śākhoṭaka tree,
and beneath this śākhoṭaka tree a treasure remains."
"Give it to someone and go;
you will recover.
The message for the deer has been delivered."
He said, "You must tell the deer:
'Above this tree, as drops of honey were falling, they sweetened the grassy swards; those you have eaten.'"
And he has set out for the honey;
abandon your greed for its flavor,
lest you fall into calamity through this deception.
The message from the partridge was announced.
The king said,
"That region where the partridge utters its cry is devoid of gold."
Wherever a partridge cries out, there a treasure-trove stands.
Go elsewhere after making that treasure known to someone;
do not fall into calamity because of it.
The message from the snake and the mongoose was announced;
the king said,
"They should be told this:"
"You two were once two brothers born as human beings. There, one said, 'Let us divide our wealth,' but the second, overcome by stinginess, did not divide it."
There, one of them, having formed a firm attachment, was reborn among venomous snakes;
the second, having seized the property and formed a firm attachment, became a mongoose.
Therefore, give this property to the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas and depart from that place.
"You shall be restored to health. The snake's message was thus delivered.
The king said:
"You must say this to that snake:
'Overcome by hunger and weakness, you emerge from your lair;
having eaten a great deal of food with your mouth, you enter your lair with difficulty.'"
Therefore, you should know the proper measure in eating;
thus, moving as you please, you will dwell in happiness.
The message of the bride and the young maiden has been delivered.
The king said:
"You must tell the young bride:
'In your father's house, he remains full of affection for you.'"
When you stay in your father-in-law’s house, you cause anxiety for the sake of your beloved;
when you stay in your father’s house, you cause anxiety for the sake of your husband.
Therefore, abandon one place and secure the other well.
"You will fall into calamity through pride,

just as the bride, the young girl, and the venomous snake acted according to their instructions. He then bestowed the two snakes, the mongoose, and the staff-bearer as a gift for the master's household.
Even by the crow, they were instructed as they had been taught and acted accordingly.
The ministers said, "Oh, such is the king's inspired eloquence!"
With a joyful mind, the king had almshouses constructed at the four city gates and appointed men as overseers of the gifts. At that time, there was a famine there lasting twelve years.
While that twelve-year famine was occurring, he provided sustenance for many hundreds of thousands of living beings.
Seeing the success of his own sacrifice, he spoke this verse:
"A wise man, having acquired wealth through righteous means, should not engage in hoarding."
One should give a sacrificial gift to those worthy of offerings who are endowed with perfected virtue.
Having satisfied ascetics, brahmins, virtuous ones,
and beggars, that wise person, upon the dissolution of the body, is reborn among the gods.
Knowing this, the wise and faithful person with a liberated mind praises those who are heroic in giving to those worthy of offerings, being free from stinginess.
It may be, Great King, that you think the illustrious king named Ādarśamukha at that time and on that occasion was someone else;
by whom, while that twelve-year famine was occurring, the support of many hundreds of thousands of living beings with food was provided.
But it should not be viewed in this way.
Moreover, it was I myself who, at that time and on that occasion, was the powerful king named Ādarśamukha.
While a twelve-year famine was occurring, I personally provided sustenance for many hundreds of thousands of living beings.
Now, Great King, you might think that I attained unexcelled, perfect enlightenment because of that gift or that distribution of gifts. But it is not so.
Indeed, it should not be viewed in this way;
rather, that gift of mine was merely a cause, merely a condition,
and merely a provision.
Furthermore, Great King, listen to that which was done by me when, aspiring for unexcelled perfect enlightenment, I gave gifts and performed meritorious deeds.

Long ago, Great King, there was a universal monarch named Sudhana. He had sacrificial enclosures constructed in eighty-four thousand cities and [performed sacrifices] for many years, many hundreds of years, and many [thousands of years].
For many thousands of years and hundreds of thousands of years, he had given gifts and performed meritorious deeds.
Seeing the success of his own sacrifice and beholding his own prosperity among both gods and humans, he spoke this verse: "Beholding my own success among gods and men..."
For who indeed would not give a gift, by which prosperity is obtained?
He who, casting aside hundreds of men and overcoming envy that acts as an adversary,
gives a gift out of fear of the next world— he, in my view, is the braver among the brave.
The sages do not call him a hero who wanders on the battlefield with weapon in hand;
rather, they call those all-knowing ones heroes who bestow gifts with confidence.
It may be, O Great King, that you think the one who at that time and on that occasion was the universal monarch—

the one by whom sacrificial grounds were established in eighty-four thousand cities and gifts were given and merits performed for many years, many hundreds of years, and many hundreds of thousands of years— was someone else. [But he was not.]
Indeed, it should not be viewed in this way.
Rather, that gift was merely a cause for perfect enlightenment, merely a condition, and merely a provision.

Furthermore, Great King, although I gave gifts and performed meritorious deeds while aspiring for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and although I fulfilled the perfection of vigor, I did not [attain] unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Listen to that which has been understood:
Once upon a time, O Great King, there were two kings in the realm of Pañcāla—
Uttarapañcāla and Dakṣiṇapañcāla."

There, in the city of Hastināpura, Uttara-Pañcāla, known by the name Dhana, was exercising his sovereignty over a realm that was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people; it was free from strife,
quarrels, tumult, and civil unrest, devoid of thieves and disease, and abundant in rice, sugarcane, cattle, and buffalo.
The righteous King of Dharma ruled his kingdom according to the Dharma.
In that city there was a great lake, covered with blue, red, yellow, and white lotuses, adorned with swans, *kāraṇḍava* ducks, and ruddy geese, and delightful.
In that lake lived a young nāga named Janmacitra.
Because he bestows the proper showers of rain from time to time, there is an abundance of crops;
the earth is rich with grain, and the region has plenty of food and drink.
Furthermore, the people are characterized by generosity, respect, and hospitality, providing sustenance for ascetics, brahmins, the destitute, and beggars.
But King Dakṣiṇapañcāla was preponderantly unrighteous—fierce, impetuous, and harsh—and he governed the kingdom through injustice.
Constantly through punishments, beatings, executions, confiscations, imprisonments, shackles, fetters, and confinements, he terrified the inhabitants of the realm.
And because of his excessive unrighteousness, the god did not grant timely and proper showers of rain at the appropriate seasons.
Then that multitude of people, terrified and overcome with a sense of urgency, abandoned the kingdom out of regard for their own lives and went to dwell in the territory of King Uttara-pañcāla.

Later, on another occasion, King Dakṣiṇa-pañcāla set out under the pretext of a hunt to inspect the countryside; he saw that the villages and cities were empty, and the pleasure groves and temples were shattered and ruined.
Having seen this, he addressed his ministers:
"Sirs, why are these villages and cities empty, and why are the parks and temples broken and ruined?
Where has that body of people gone?"
The ministers said,
"Your Majesty, we have gone to the territory of King Dhana of Uttarapañcāla."
"For what purpose?
"O God, grant us fearlessness; we shall speak.
"Let it be granted."
Then they said to him, "Your Majesty, King Uttarapañcāla rules his kingdom with righteousness.

His territories are prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people; they are free from strife, quarrels, tumult, and disorder, and are devoid of thieves and disease."
The people were abundant in rice, sugarcane, cattle, and buffalo, and were characterized by generosity, honor, and hospitality;
they provided sustenance for ascetics, brahmins, the destitute, and beggars.
But the king was fierce, impetuous, and harsh, constantly employing punishment, beating, execution, fines, imprisonment, shackles, fetters, and confinement.
Since he terrified the kingdom, that body of people became frightened and filled with a sense of urgency, and they went to the territory of the King of Northern Pañcāla.
The King of Southern Pañcāla said:
"Sirs, what means might there be by which this body of people would return and dwell again in these villages and towns?

The ministers replied, "If Your Majesty, like the King of Northern Pañcāla, exercises the kingdom according to the Dharma— protecting your own realm with a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of benefit, and a mind of compassion— then before long, that body of people will [return]."
Having arrived, he should dwell in these villages and cities.
King Dakṣiṇapañcāla said:
"Sirs, if this is so, I too shall rule the kingdom righteously like Uttara-pañcāla—with a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of benefit, and a mind of compassion—toward the realm."
"I shall protect [them].
You must act in such a way that this body of people returns once more and dwells in these villages and towns.
Your Majesty, there is yet another benefit therein."

In that city there was a great lake, covered with blue, red, and white lotuses, and adorned with swans, *kāraṇḍava* ducks, and ruddy geese. There lived a young nāga named Janmacitra; from time to time, he would duly release showers of rain.
There is an exceedingly great abundance of crops; because of that, the earth there is rich with grain, and the region has plenty of food and drink.
What might be the means by which this [abundance] could be [secured]?
"Let a young nāga be brought here.
"Your Majesty, those who hold the spells and mantras will bring him;
let them be sought out."
Then the king, having fastened a golden casket to the top of his banner, caused a proclamation by bell to be made throughout the entire realm:
"To whoever shall bring the young nāga Janmacitra from the territory of Uttarapañcāla, I will give this golden casket and honor him with great ceremony.
Eventually, a certain snake-charmer went to the ministers and said:
"Give me this golden basket; I shall go and bring back the young nāga Janmacitra.
The ministers said, "Take it."
He said,
"Let it remain in the hands of whoever among you is trusted and reliable;
once the young nāga Janmacitra has been brought here, I shall take it."
"Do so," he said.
Then that snake-charmer, having placed the golden basket in the hand of a trusted man, went to the city of Hastināpura.
Thereupon, he surveyed that lake from all sides.
He had observed that the young naga Janmacitra was stationed in that place;
therefore, having returned from there for the purpose of offering a sacrifice,
he said to his ministers, "Give me the sacrificial offerings, for on the seventh day I shall seize and bring back that young naga."
And that snake-charmer was observed by him [the prince], who thought: "He has come to abduct me;
on the seventh day he will carry me away.
There will be great suffering born from separation from my mother and father."
"What shall I do? To whom shall I go for refuge?
Not far from that lake lived two hunters, Sāraka and Phalaka;
they made their living by depending upon that lake.
Those land-dwelling creatures such as deer, rabbits, śarabhas, and boars that approached that lake he would slaughter; likewise those water-dwellers such as fish, turtles, and frogs.
There, Sāraka had passed away, while Phalaka remained alive.
The young nāga Janmacitra reflected:
"I have no other refuge except for the hunter Phalaka.
Thereupon, assuming the guise of a human being, he went into the presence of Phalaka.

Having gone there, he said: "O man, do you know by whose power the territories of King Dhana are prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, crowded with many people and inhabitants— as before— up to being abundant in rice, sugarcane, cattle, and buffalo?"
He replied, "I know him.
That king is righteous; he governs the kingdom according to the Dharma, protecting the realm with a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of welfare, and a mind of compassion."
He said:
"Is this all there is? Or is there something else as well?"
The hunter said,
"There is yet another benefit:
there dwells in this lake a young nāga named Janmacitra, who from time to time provides a proper downpour of rain."
"There will be an abundance of crops; the earth will be rich with grain, and the land will have plenty of food and drink.

Janmacitra said, "If someone were to carry that young nāga away from this realm, what would happen? That young nāga would suffer the pain born of separation from his parents, and it would be a loss for the king and the kingdom."
"What would you do to him who steals it?
"I would deprive him of life. "Do you know which young nāga that is?"
I do not know;
I am being carried off by someone from the region of Dakṣiṇapañcāla.
He has gone to perform a ritual of offerings and oblations, and he will return on the seventh day.
Having arrived, he will drive stakes of acacia wood into the four directions of this lake, encircle them with threads of various colors, and recite mantras.
At that time, you must remain hidden in a nearby place. When he performs such a rite as this—
When the ritual application has been performed, then the boiling water from the middle of the lake will rise up,
and I too shall rise up.
At that time, you must strike that snake-charmer in a vital spot with an arrow.
Having approached him quickly, one should say: "Withdraw your spells!
Lest I cut off your head at its roots and cast it down upon the earth.
For if he does not withdraw his spells and is deprived of life, then once he is dead, I would remain bound by the fetters of his spells for as long as I live.
The hunter said:
"If even you alone possessed such a quality, I would still act in this way; how much more so for the sake of an entire kingdom?"
"I shall go to that place.
Then, that young nāga pointed out a secret location on one side of it to him.
Thereupon, on the seventh day, that hunter remained hidden in a secluded spot, concealing himself.
Then that snake-charmer arrived and began to perform an offering of oblations;
he drove four stakes of khadira wood into the ground in the four directions,
wound them with threads of various colors, and invoked them with mantras.
Then that water began to boil.
Struck in a vital spot by the hunter with an arrow, he drew his sword from its scabbard and said:
"You are stealing away by means of a mantra the young nāga who dwells in this domain!"
"Withdraw your spells!
Lest I cut off your head at its roots and cast it upon the earth!
Thereupon, the snake-charmer, overwhelmed by the sensation of pain, withdrew his spells.
Immediately thereafter, he was deprived of life by the hunter.
Then the young nāga, released from the bonds of the mantra-noose, emerged from the lake and embraced the hunter, saying:
"You are my mother, you are my father, for it is because of you that the suffering born of separation from my parents has not arisen for me."
"Come, let us go to my own realm.
He was led by him to his own realm, where he was gratified with various kinds of food and drink, shown precious jewels,
and [the matter] was reported to his parents.
"Mother, father, this is my friend and refuge, my kinsman; by his power, the separation from you has not occurred for me.
He was also invited by them to choose a boon, and various jewels were given to him.
Having taken those [fruits], he emerged from that lake.
Not far from that lake was a hermitage, abundant with flowers and fruits and resounding with the songs of various birds;
there dwelt a seer who was compassionate by nature, merciful, and affectionate toward living beings.
Thereupon, that hunter began to visit the seer three times a day;
and he related in detail everything that had occurred between him and the young nāga Janmacitra. Then the seer said:

"What use have you for jewels, or what use for gold? In that world of the nāgas there stands a noose named Amogha; ask for that. Then the hunter, having conceived a craving for the Amogha noose upon hearing the words of the ṛṣi, went once more to the nāga-world, where he saw that Amogha noose at the entrance of the nāga-city.
This thought occurred to him:

Realizing, "This is that very noose which I must request," he entered the realm of the nāgas. There, he was greeted with great excitement by the young nāga Janmacitra and other young nāgas, who offered him jewels; however, he said, "I have no need for jewels, but please grant me this unfailing noose."
Janmacitra said:
"What use have you for this? It belongs to us."
"But there is a great purpose:
when we are afflicted by the fear of Garuḍas, then we protect ourselves with this.
The hunter said:
"This [tail] is of use to you who are afflicted by the fear of Garuḍas, but for me, I have a constant need for it. If you have done or rendered any favor, then give it to me.
This thought occurred to the young nāga Janmacitra.
"Much has been done for me by this man; I shall give it after looking upon my mother and father.
Having looked upon his mother and father, he gave him the noose.
Then that hunter, his mind nourished by a happiness and gladness as vast as the earth itself, took the unfailing snare and, emerging from the realm of the nāgas, went to his own home.
Later, at another time, King Dhana was sporting, enjoying himself, and diverting himself with his queen;
yet, as he so sported, enjoyed himself, and diverted himself, he had neither son nor daughter.
Placing his cheek upon his hand, he remained lost in thought:
"My house is filled with manifold wealth, yet I have neither son nor daughter;
upon my passing, with the severance of my own family lineage, the kingdom will be lost."
"Thinking that all this wealth would, in the absence of an heir, become subject to the king's authority,
he was addressed by the ascetics, brahmins, friends, relatives, and kinsmen: 'Your Majesty, why are you so preoccupied with anxiety?'"
He related this matter to them in detail,
and they said,
"Perform propitiation of the deities; a son will be born to you."

Being childless and longing for a son, he made supplications to Śiva, Varuṇa, Kubera, Śakra, Brahmā, and other specific deities; that is to say, he supplicated the deities of gardens, the deities of groves, the deities of crossroads, the deities of junctions, the deities who receive offerings,
as well as those deities who are innate, those who share his dharma, and even those deities who are constantly attached to him.
There is a common saying in the world that sons and daughters are born as a result of prayers;
but that is not so.
If it were otherwise, every single person would have a thousand sons, just like a universal monarch (cakravartin).
Moreover, sons and daughters are born through the coming together of three conditions.
What are these three?
The mother and father must be filled with passion.
The three conditions have come together:
the mother is healthy and in her fertile period,
and the gandharva is present.
Through the presence of these three conditions, sons and daughters are born.
While he remained thus intent on his prayers,
a certain being belonging to the Fortunate Aeon (bhadrakalpika) [descended].
The Bodhisattva descended into the womb of that chief queen.
Five unique qualities are found together in a woman of wise nature.
What are these five?
She knows the man who has shed his seed;
she knows the time;
she knows the season.
She knows that she has conceived;
she knows from whom the embryo has descended;
and she knows whether it is a boy.
He knows whether it is a girl:
if it is a boy, he remains resting against the right side of the womb;
if it is a girl, she remains resting against the left side of the womb.
With a joyful heart, she announced it to her husband:
"By good fortune, noble son, you prosper;
I have become pregnant."
"And since he remains resting against my right side, it will certainly be a boy.
Delighted and overjoyed, he raised his upper body, extended his right arm, and uttered this exclamation:
"Perhaps I might behold the face of a son, long desired by me for so long;
may he be well-born and not ill-born;
may he perform my duties."
Having been supported, he should support [me] in return;
he should receive his inheritance;
and thus my family lineage may endure for a long time.
"Furthermore, when we have passed away, having given gifts and performed meritorious deeds, whether small or great, they will dedicate the merit in our names, saying:
'May this follow those two wherever they go, whatever state of rebirth they have attained.

And knowing that she was pregnant, he kept her in an upper chamber on the palace roof, unrestrained, providing her with cooling requisites in the cold and warming requisites prescribed by physicians in the heat."
With foods that were not too bitter, not too sour, not too salty, not too sweet, not too pungent,
and not too astringent— foods devoid of bitterness, sourness, saltiness, sweetness, pungency, and astringency— he saw her, her body adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces,
like an apsaras sporting in the Nandana grove, descending from couch to couch and from seat to seat until she reached the ground below.
And she did not hear any unpleasant sound whatsoever until the fetus reached full maturity;
after the lapse of eight or nine months, she gave birth,
and a boy was born.

He was handsome, beautiful to behold, pleasing, fair-skinned, with a golden complexion, a head shaped like a parasol, long arms, a broad forehead, a resonant voice, well-knit eyebrows, a prominent nose, and endowed with all major and minor limbs. At his birth, drums of joy were beaten;
hearing this, the king said:
"What is this? he asked.
The women of the inner apartments informed the king:
"Your Majesty, congratulations! A son has been born to you."
Then the king had that entire city cleared of stones, pebbles, and gravel;
it was sprinkled with sandalwood water, with banners and flags raised high, with incense burners filled with fragrant smoke set out, and strewn with various flowers, making it delightful.
And he issued this command:
"Bestow gifts upon the śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, the poor, and beggars;
effect the release of all prisoners!
Thus, after performing the birth festival for the newborn in detail for three times seven—that is, twenty-one days—the naming ceremony was established.
"What shall be the name of the boy? the ministers asked. They replied, "This boy is the son of King Dhana."
"Let the boy's name be Sudhana.
Thus the name Sudhana was established for him.
The boy Sudhana was entrusted to eight nurses.
He was raised by eight nurses: two to carry him on their shoulders, two to provide milk, two to clean him, and two to play with him.
Reared by these eight nurses with milk, curd, fresh butter, ghee, the cream of ghee, and other excellent, refined nourishments, he grew rapidly like a lotus in a pond.
When he had grown up, he was introduced to writing;
as before, he became an expert in the eight examinations, a master of recitation, a scholar, and one of quick wit.

Whatever those [qualities] are that belong to consecrated kings who have attained sovereignty, power, and heroism over their territories, and who dwell having conquered a vast circle of the earth—as previously described—until he became skilled in the five areas [of royal policy].
His father established for him three harems: the senior, the middle, and the junior.

Three dwelling-houses were constructed: one for the winter, one for the summer, and one for the rainy season. Three pleasure gardens were also laid out: one for the winter, one for the summer, and one for the rainy season.
Then Prince Sudhana, having gone up to the roof-terrace of the palace, played, enjoyed himself, and amused himself with musical instruments performed by women alone.
Then, at another time, a hunter named Phalaka, while searching for deer and wandering here and there, reached a certain mountain.
At the foot of that mountain, he saw the hermitage of a seer, abundant with flowers and fruits and frequented by flocks of various birds;
and he saw a great lake covered with blue, red, and white lotuses, and adorned with swans, kāraṇḍava ducks, and ruddy geese.

He began to wander through that hermitage until he saw the seer, whose hair, beard, nails, and body hair were long, whose body was withered by wind and sun, who wore robes of bark, and who resided at the foot of a certain tree, having made his dwelling in a grass hut; and having seen him, he prostrated at his feet and, with palms joined in reverence, asked:
“Blessed One, how long have you been residing in this region?
“For forty years.
“In all this time, have you seen or heard from anyone in this region of any marvelous or extraordinary phenomenon?”
That seer spoke very softly:
"O gentle-faced one, have you seen this lake?
"I have seen it, Blessed One."

This lotus pond named Brahmasabhā is covered with blue, red, white, and yellow lotuses, frequented by flocks of various birds, filled with water as white as snow, silver, and frost, and its waters are perfumed with fragrant flowers. On every fifteenth day, the daughter of Drumakinnara-rāja, named Manoharā, surrounded by five hundred kinnarīs, comes and bathes in this pond after performing various kinds of head-baths and anointing rituals.
"At the time of his bathing, the deer and birds are captivated by the sound of sweet dancing, singing, and instrumental music.
Hearing that sound, I too remain entranced for seven days with great joy and gladness.
This wonder, O gentle-faced one, was seen by me."
Then this thought occurred to the hunter Phalaka:
"I have obtained an excellent unfailing snare from the nāga;
I shall cast it upon the kinnarī Manoharā."

At another time, on the full moon of the fifteenth day, he took his net and stationed himself near the bank of a lake, taking refuge in a thicket of trees with branches laden with flowers and fruit, intent on remaining vigilant.

Just then, the Kinnarī Manoharā, surrounded by five hundred Kinnarīs and accompanied by great magnificence, descended into the Brahma-sabhā lotus pond to bathe; immediately thereafter, a hunter cast an infallible net from a boat, by which the Kinnarī Manoharā was caught.
Bound by that Amoghapāśa noose, she caused a great upheaval in the lake and let out a terrifying sound;
hearing which, the remaining host of kinnarīs became bewildered and began looking here and there for the kinnarī Manoharā.
He saw her bound;
having seen her, he became afraid and fled.

And Kiṭibhaka must be slain by an arrow released from my bow for my sake.
Wherever you see two rams butting heads with one another,
you shall regain the path by breaking off one of their horns.
Upon seeing two iron men, terrifying with weapons in their hands,
you will obtain the path by striking one of them.
When one sees the Rākṣasī contracting and extending her iron mouth,
then one should drive a stake into her forehead.
Likewise, you must cross a whirlpool of stones and a well sixty cubits deep;
there dwells a fierce yakṣa-rākṣasa with hair and eyes as tawny as a lion's.
Having drawn his bow into a circle, that unassailable one must be slain;
and the rivers, teeming with crocodiles and sharks, must be crossed by force.
The rivers are the Nangā, Pataṅgā, Tapanī, Citrā, Rudanī, Hasanī, Āśīviṣā, and Vetravatī.
In the Nangā there is the wrath of rākṣasīs; in the Pataṅgā, non-human beings; in the Tapanī, an abundance of crocodiles; and in the Citrā, those who can assume any form at will.
In Rudanī there are Kinnarī maidservants; in Hasanī, Kinnarī daughters-in-law;
in Āśīviṣā, various kinds of serpents; and in Vetranadī, the Śālmali tree.
In Naṅgā there is the cultivation of fortitude, and in Pataṅgā, valor.
In Tapanī there is the binding of the mouths of crocodiles; in Citrā, various songs.
In the Rudanī River, there is crossing by means of joy;
in the Hasanī, by means of silence;
in the Āśīviṣā, by the application of mantras against snake venom; and in the Vetravatī River, by the application of a sharp weapon.
Having crossed the river, there is a military outpost belonging to five hundred yakṣas; that must be overcome by summoning courage. Beyond that is the palace of Druma, the king of the kinnaras.
Then Prince Sudhana, having procured the medicinal herbs, mantras, and applications of elixirs as instructed, paid homage at the feet of that seer and departed.
Thereupon, he procured everything exactly as instructed, with the exception of the monkey;
taking these items, he returned once more to the presence of that seer.
And it was said:
"Enough, prince! What is the use of this resolve? What is the use of Manoharā?
You will fall into physical peril, alone and without assistance."
The prince said:

"Great Seer, I shall certainly go. Why? Because what need is there for a companion for the moon as it wanders through the sky, or for the powerful lord of beasts by virtue of the strength of his fangs?"
And what assistance could fire provide against a forest conflagration; and what would be the use of the strength of an ally for one such as I?
"O friend, is the water of the great ocean not to be plunged into? Is that which is infested with serpents not to be treated?
One should exert great vigor as witnessed by those of heroic character; if success is not achieved despite effort being made, what fault is there in that?

Then Prince Sudhana, setting out according to the method instructed by Manoharā, gradually overcame mountains, rivers, caves, precipices, and other obstacles through the application of medicines, mantras, and antidotes.
Having approached the vicinity of the palace of Druma, the king of the kinnaras,
the prince beheld that city nearby, adorned with magnificent gardens.
It was endowed with various flowers and fruits and frequented by various birds.
It was surrounded by *kiṃnaras* at its ponds, lakes, and reservoirs;
and there he beheld *kiṃnarīs* who had come for the sake of water.
Then they were addressed by Prince Sudhana:
"What is to be done with this much water?
They replied:
The daughter of Drum, the king of the kinnaras, named Manoharā,
has fallen into human hands;
her scent of humanity is now vanishing.
Prince Sudhana asked,
"Are all these jars to be poured over her simultaneously, or is it to be done in succession?
They replied:
In due order, he reflected:
"This is a good stratagem; I shall throw this finger-ring into one jar."
Thereupon, he secretly placed [the powder] into the jar of one kinnarī,
and that kinnarī was told:
"With this jar, you must bathe Manoharā before anyone else."
She reflected:
"Surely there must be some purpose here.
Then she was the first to drop that jar upon Manoharā's head, until the finger-ring fell into her lap.
She was recognized by Manoharā;
thereupon she asked the kinnarī,
"Has any human being arrived there?"
She said:
"A guest has arrived; go and lead him in secretly."
Having been ushered in by her, he was placed in a well-concealed location.
Then Manoharā, prostrating at her father’s feet, said:
"Father, if that Prince Sudhana, by whom I was abducted, were to come here, what would you do to him?"
He said:
"I would cut him into a hundred pieces and cast them in the four directions; what would that man have to do with him?"
Manoharā said,
"Father, how could one who has become a human being come here? I myself shall explain it."
Then the agitation of Druma, the king of the kinnaras, subsided. With his agitation gone, he said:
"If that prince should come, I would give you as a jewel of a wife—adorned with every ornament, surrounded by a thousand kinnarīs, and provided with abundant articles for your pleasure."
Then, with Manoharā thrilled, satisfied, and overjoyed, Prince Sudhana, adorned with divine ornaments, was presented to Druma, the king of the kinnaras.
Thereupon, Druma, the king of the kinnaras, beheld Prince Sudhana—handsome, beautiful to behold, gracious, and endowed with the most excellent excellence of auspicious complexion;
and having seen him, he was filled with supreme wonder.
Then, desiring to test his discernment, seven golden pillars were raised, along with seven palm trees, seven drums, and seven boars. And he said:
"By your beauty, these young *kiṃnaras* have already been surpassed."
Having displayed your power, you ought now to reveal your divine lineage.
Having made this vast thicket of reeds, pull up a single reed in an instant;
having gathered it back without omission from where it was sown, give me an *āḍhaka* measure of sesame seeds again.
Demonstrate your mastery in the science of archery, such as your skill with a firm target and other feats.
Therefore, this captivating banner of your fame is now at your disposal.
The prince Sudhana is a bodhisattva;
and bodhisattvas become skilled in various arts and crafts, and the deities will apply themselves with zeal so that there may be no obstacles for them.

Then the bodhisattva, by means of various kinds of [instruments] such as dance, song, the lute (*vīṇā*), the small drum (*paṇava*), the sweet-sounding drum (*sughoṣaka*), the harp (*vallarī*), and the kettle-drum (*mṛdaṅga*)...
They were surrounded by many thousands of *kiṃnaras*, while being filled on all sides with various musical instruments played by [beings] summoned by divine power; [as it is said]:
"By Yakṣas in the form of boars, commanded by Śatakratu... (KAvk 64.320–321).
When the thicket of reeds had been cleared away and leveled, a measure of sesame seeds was sown.
Having gathered them together into one mass by means of ants created by Śakra,
the prince presented them to the astonished king of the Kinnaras.

Taking up a sword that had the hue of a blue lotus petal, he went toward the golden pillars while the kinnara king Druma looked on, and began to cut those pillars into small pieces as if they were plantain stalks. Then, having scattered them like sesame seeds, he pierced seven palm trees, seven drums, and seven boars with a single arrow, and stood unshakable like Mount Sumeru.

Then, from the expanse of the sky, deities and hundreds of thousands of kinnaras let out a loud cry of "Hā! Hā! and a tumultuous roar of joy; seeing this, the king of the kinnaras was struck with supreme wonder. Then, having placed Manoharā in the midst of a thousand kinnarīs whose beauty equaled her own, he addressed Prince Sudhana.
"Come, prince, do you recognize Manoharā?
Then Prince Sudhana, having recognized her, spoke with a song in verse:
"Just as you are the daughter of Druma, so are you my Manoharā here."
By this truth, O Manoharā, go quickly to that place.
Then she advanced with quickened steps.
The Kinnaras said, "O King, this Prince Sudhana is endowed with strength, vigor, and prowess; he is a worthy match for Manoharā."
"Why have you deceived me?
Let Manoharā be given to him!
Then Druma, the king of the kinnaras, being praised by the host of kinnaras, [bestowed] Sudhana with great honor appropriate for a kinnara.
Having honored him with hospitality and taking by his left hand Manoharā, who was adorned with divine ornaments, while holding a golden water-pot in his right hand, Prince Sudhana said:
"Prince, here is Manoharā, surrounded by her kinnarī attendants, given to you as a wife; humans are strangers to you."

"So that you will not abandon her. "Very well, father," Sudhana the prince replied to Druma, the king of the *kiṃnaras*. Staying in the *kiṃnara* palace together with Manoharā, he played, enjoyed himself, and dallied with her to the sound of music performed by women alone.
At another time, remembering his own country and being deeply afflicted by the suffering born of separation from his parents, he informed Manoharā.
"The suffering born of separation from my parents oppresses me.
Then Manoharā related this account in detail to her father,
who said:

"Go with the prince; you must remain on your guard, for men are deceivers. Then Druma, the king of the *kiṃnaras*, gave him a great quantity of jewels, pearls, gold, and other riches, and sent him forth.
Accompanied by Manoharā, he set out through the sky above along the path of the *kiṃnara* birds, and in due course arrived at the city of Hastināpura.
Then the city of Hastināpura was made fragrant in every direction by various delightful and sweet-smelling perfumes.
Upon hearing this, King Dhana had the drums of joy beaten;
and he caused that entire city to be cleared of stones, pebbles, and gravel, sprinkled with sandalwood water, and adorned with bundles of hanging silk ribbons and uplifted banners and flags.
Adorned with incense burners emitting fragrant smoke and made beautiful by being strewn with various flowers,
the prince then entered the city of Hastināpura together with Manoharā, surrounded by many thousands of excellent men.
Then, having dispelled the fatigue of the journey and taking various jewels, he approached his father.
He was embraced by his father around the neck and sat down on a royal throne at his side.
He then related in detail the account of his departure for and return from the city of the Kinnaras.
Then, King Dhana, recognizing him as one of exceeding strength, heroism, and prowess, consecrated Prince Sudhana with the royal inauguration. Prince Sudhana reflected:

"Since my reunion with Manoharā has occurred and the royal inauguration has been attained, this must be due to a particular cause created in the past; therefore, I shall now give gifts and perform meritorious deeds."

Thus, in the city of Hastināpura, he performed an unobstructed sacrifice for twelve years. Great King, you might think that at that time, on that occasion, the prince Sudhana was someone else. But it was not so. It was you yourself who were the prince Sudhana at that time and on that occasion. Why is that? Because, Great King, it was through the ripening of that very root of merit that you have now become a universal monarch, a wheel-turning king, possessed of the seven jewels, a conqueror of the four quarters, a stabilizer of the land, and a possessor of the seven precious treasures. What are those seven? They are: the precious wheel, the precious elephant, the precious horse, the precious jewel, the precious woman, the precious householder, and the precious counselor. Furthermore, Great King, you possess a thousand sons who are brave, heroic, and victorious over enemy armies, by whom this entire earth, including its oceans, is conquered without violence or weapons, and ruled with righteousness. This, Great King, is the fruit of giving and the fruit of self-restraint. Therefore, Great King, you should train yourself thus: "I shall give gifts, I shall practice self-restraint, and I shall perform meritorious deeds. For this is the path to heaven.
