Indeed, it should not be viewed in this way;
rather, at that time and on that occasion, while engaged in the conduct of a Bodhisattva, I myself was the king named Sudhana.
It was for the sake of Manoharā that I displayed strength, vigor, and prowess, and performed an unobstructed sacrifice for twelve years.

It was not by that alone that I attained unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; rather, that gift and that vigor were merely the cause, merely the condition, and merely the equipment for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
(Caṃcā Māṇavikā was) beautiful and pleasing to behold. We shall encourage her. She was summoned by those messengers and addressed by them:

"Indeed, sister, formerly we had such gain and honor; now people go to the presence of the ascetic Gautama and pay him honor. Our gain and honor have been completely cut off, yet you remain indifferent."
The young woman Cañcā said,
"Noble lady, what must I do? [The other replied,] "Sister, for the sake of your kinsmen, you must engage in unchaste conduct with the ascetic Gautama,
and you must bring about his censure."
Thinking, "By this means, we shall obtain gain and honor as before," when this had been said, the female wanderer Cañcā Māṇavikā spoke thus to the many other sectarian wanderers:
"Noble sirs, I do not dare to utter a disparagement of the ascetic Gautama.
"Sister, as long as you do not dare to utter a disparagement of the ascetic Gautama, so long shall we remain with you."
We shall not speak with you, nor converse with you, nor look at you, nor gaze upon you; nor will you have seats prepared for you in any of our dwellings.
Then, filled with remorse, you shall fall into the realm of hell.
Women have little wisdom.
Terrified, she said, "Noble lady, whatever must be done by me, come, sister; go frequently to the Jeta Grove and, after some time has passed, cause slander to be spread against the ascetic Gautama."
Rising every day, she went to the Jeta Grove;
having fastened a single vessel, she approached the place where the Blessed One was.
At that time, the Blessed One was seated before many hundreds of people, teaching the Dharma.
The Blessed One saw the young woman Cañcā from afar;
having seen her, this thought occurred to him:
"Today my deeds that have been performed and accumulated [will bear fruit]."
"Since the necessary conditions have been gathered, the causal factors have ripened, and they have arrived like a flood—being inevitable, who else shall experience them?
Then the young woman Cañcā, a female wanderer, stood before the Blessed One and said:
"I am pregnant as a result of my indulgence in sensual pleasure with you."
"Delight has been attained, fame has been proclaimed, and now you speak of the Dharma.
The Blessed One said:
"One who speaks what is untrue goes to the hells," said the young woman Cañcā Māṇavikā; "and also he who,
having done something, says, 'I did not do it.'"
The Blessed One said:
"For a mortal who is deficient in virtuous qualities attains an equal state in both worlds."

Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, thinking, "Alas! This young girl Cañcā will surely harm the Blessed One and the community of monks," perceived this and by means of his supernatural power caused that vessel to fall to the ground.
Then the young girl Cañcā, feeling ashamed, withdrew to a distance.
Thereupon, the elder monks said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, the discourse concerning the legal affairs of King Prasenajit has been concluded; he has been given his prediction."
"And where the first thought was generated for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, up to the accounts of the gain and honor received from the perfectly enlightened ones—
let us, at the great lake Anavatapta, in the presence of the Blessed One, relate the unfolding of our respective karmas.
The Blessed One consented to the request of the elder monks by remaining silent.

It is indeed the natural law (*dharmatā*) of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, while they are living, remaining, enduring, and maintaining themselves—that there are ten things that must necessarily be accomplished.
The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, do not pass into final nirvana until a Buddha has been predicted;
until a being has generated the irreversible mind set upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; and until all those to be trained by the Buddhas have been trained.
A third part of his lifespan has been relinquished;
the boundary has been established;
and the pair of foremost disciples has been designated.
The Great Miracle was displayed at Śrāvastī; the Descent from Heaven was displayed at the city of Sāṃkāśya;
and both mother and father were established in the Truths.
At the great lake Anavatapta, the exposition of the past web of karma was declared together with the community of disciples.
Then the Buddha, the Blessed One, desiring to declare the past web of karma at the great lake Anavatapta together with the community of disciples, addressed the monks:
"Come, monks, let us go to the great lake Anavatapta so that we may each declare our own past web of karma."
"Venerable Sir, it is so," the monks replied to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One,

together with four hundred and ninety-nine arhats, vanished from Śrāvastī and appeared at the great lake Anavatapta, which was frequented by fierce yakṣas and rākṣasas and adorned with various flowering trees.
That delightful place, frequented by fierce yakṣas and beautifully adorned with trees bearing variegated flowers,
is where from here the four rivers flow toward the ocean, spreading out in the four directions.

The Gaṅgā, the Sindhu, as well as the Vakṣu and the Sītā— those which humans cannot cross except by those who possess the power of supernatural success (*ṛddhi*)— well then, I shall go here to the great ocean lake.

It is indeed the nature of things that at whatever time the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, give rise to a worldly thought, at that very moment even living beings such as ants and termites understand the mind of the Blessed One with their own minds.
Then, this thought occurred to the two Naga kings, Nanda and Upananda:

For what purpose did the Blessed One produce a worldly thought? Desiring to explain the web of karma while beholding the great lake Anavatapta, he was then surrounded by a thousand-petaled lotus in the midst of that great lake Anavatapta, its stalks and filaments made of all kinds of gold and inlaid with jewels, and its petals resembling the wheels of a chariot fashioned by karma.

The Blessed One sat upon the pericarp of a lotus together with the community of monks, while the elder monks also sat upon other lotus pericarps. At that time, Śāriputra was sewing his outer robe on Vulture Peak Mountain.
Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Go, Maudgalyāyana, and bring a companion for the going-forth. "So be it, Venerable Sir," replied the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
He vanished from Lake Anavatapta and, standing before the venerable Śāriputra on Vulture Peak Mountain, spoke thus:
"Venerable Śāriputra, together with five hundred Arhats, the Teacher [is about to recount] the former course of karma for each one individually."
Desiring to give a prophecy, he waited expectantly for you; [when you] arrived, he said, "Let us go," but the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana replied, "I am currently sewing this outer robe;
I shall come later."
He said, "So be it, friend.
Then, Mahāmaudgalyāyana began to sew with his five fingers by means of his supernatural power. The Venerable Śāriputra said, "Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, it is sewn."
"Very well," he replied. Śāriputra said, "Venerable one, if you do not go, I shall seize you by force.
Then the venerable Śāriputra pulled his girdle and said:
"Mahāmaudgalyāyana, have you not been designated by the Blessed One as the foremost of those possessed of supernatural power? Therefore, you take them there first; afterwards, you shall lead me.
Thereupon, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana led them there.
Then, the Venerable Śāriputra reflected:

"This one possesses great supernatural power; he might carry this entire place away. Thus, when the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana fixed his attention upon Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, that mountain Gṛdhrakūṭa began to tremble as it was being pulled by him.
Then the venerable Śāriputra reflected:

"This man has shaken Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain; what if I were to fix it upon Sumeru? He then fixed it upon Sumeru, the king of mountains. However, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana pulled it back, and Mount Sumeru as well as the two nāga kings Nanda and Upananda were shaken.

The great lake Anavatapta was entirely agitated. Then the elder monks, who were seated upon the pericarps of lotuses, began to tremble; they questioned the Blessed One: "For what reason, Blessed One, have the two naga kings Nanda and Upananda [acted thus]?"
They were shaken.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, having heard that there is no shaking for the two Naga kings, Nanda and Upananda, they [performed] a display of supernatural power."
"Do so," [said the Blessed One]. Then the Venerable Śāriputra reflected: "What if I were to fix myself upon the stalk of the Blessed One’s lotus?
He fixed himself upon the stalk of the Blessed One’s lotus and remained there motionless. When his supernatural power was thus surpassed by the Blessed One’s supernatural power, then— (MSV I 166)
He spoke thus to the Venerable Śāriputra:
"Go, Venerable Śāriputra; come with a display of supernatural power; let us go together. "Go, Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana;
here I have already arrived. Before the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had even returned, the noble Venerable Śāriputra had already departed.

Having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he sat down to one side upon the pericarp of a lotus flower. Thereafter, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana arrived; seeing the Venerable Śāriputra, he said, "Have you come, Venerable Śāriputra? We two have both arrived."
A doubt having arisen, the monks questioned the Blessed One, the cutter of all doubts:

"Venerable Sir, the Blessed One has designated the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana as the foremost among those possessed of supernatural power (ṛddhimat), yet he was defeated in supernatural power by the Venerable Śāriputra.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it is not only now; in the past as well, he was defeated by one skilled in the arts.

Long ago, in the Middle Country, there was a certain master painter who, for some business matter, traveled from the Middle Country to the realm of the Yavanas. He arrived at the residence of a master of mechanical devices, and by him..."
Having fashioned a mechanical puppet, she was made to enter;
she stood there after running to his feet. Then, at the time of her departure, he said to her:
She remained silent.
He reflected, "Surely she has been sent here as my attendant. Grasping her by the hand, he began to pull her, only to find that she was a heap of chain-links.
He was ashamed and reflected:
"I have been put to shame by him;

I too shall put him to shame, along with his royal retinue," he thought. Therefore, he drew a picture of himself as a hanged man facing the door, and remained hidden in the joint of the door-panel. The time for his [the king's] rising had passed.
Then the master of the mechanical device reflected:
"This man has come from afar;
why is this gate not barred?"

Having entered, he saw that [the man] was dead, having hanged himself. He reflected, "For what reason has this man deprived himself of life? He saw that wooden doll, its joints piled together, and he reflected, "This man has been put to shame."
Having performed the customary rites appropriate for the occasion, the guest passed away; however, he was not accorded the honors due him until it had been reported to the king.
Thereupon, he went into the presence of the king and informed him: "Your Majesty, there was once a master painter in the realm of the Yavanas."
He came into my presence;
for the sake of attending to him, I had a wooden doll brought in.

He took hold of her hands and pulled, whereupon a heap of chain-links remained. Overcome by passion, he hanged himself. Therefore, it behooves Your Majesty to investigate this matter, after which I shall pay him due honor.
Then the king dispatched royal officers with the command: "Sirs, you must conduct an inspection today.
Thereupon, they went there and performed the inspection.
The thought occurred to them:
"How are we to get ourselves down from this elephant-tusk?
Others said, "The snare must be cut. Taking an axe, they began to cut it.
When they saw the master painter,
the master of the art of painting emerged from behind the door and said,
"O man, I was alone when you challenged me, but you, moreover, did so in the midst of an assembly including the king."
It was split by me.

What do you think, monks? At that time, on that occasion, he who was the master of mechanical arts was none other than this monk Maudgalyāyana; at that time, on that occasion, he who was the master painter was none other than this [monk Śāriputra].
At that time, on that occasion, Śāriputra the monk was also defeated by him through his craft; even now, he has been defeated by him through his supernatural power.
Furthermore, listen to how he was defeated by him who is skilled in the arts.

Long ago, monks, a dispute arose between two masters of the art of painting. One said, "I know the beautiful craft," and the second also said, "I know it even more beautifully. Out of mutual rivalry, they went into the presence of the king and prostrated at his feet.
One said,
"I shall display a beautiful craft.
The second also said:
"I shall demonstrate a more excellent craft.
Then the king showed them the gate-chamber, saying, "Sirs, I do not know which of you two possesses the more excellent craft; however, let one paint one wall and the second the other."
[GBM_6.1066a] They both began to paint.
There, one performed the work of painting for six months, while the second prepared the wall surface for six months.
When his painting was completed, he approached the king; having approached him, he said, "Your Majesty, my painting is finished; you should deign to see it."
Then King Sahāya, having gone out and seen it, was delighted, saying, "The painting work is excellent.
The second one prostrated at his feet and said, "Now you ought to see my painting work. He removed the curtain, and the shadow fell there. [MSV]

When the king saw this, he was filled with wonder and said, "This painting is most excellent. Drawing back the curtain, he prostrated at his feet and said, "Your Majesty, this is not even a painting; it is merely the surface preparation of the wall.
Thereupon, the king was struck with even greater amazement and remarked, "This craftsman is truly most excellent."
"What do you think, monks? He who performed the plastering of the wall in six months was none other than this monk Śāriputra;
he who performed the painting work in six months was none other than this monk Maudgalyāyana.
At that time, on that occasion, even then he was defeated by him in this craft; now too, he has been defeated by him."
He was defeated by means of supernatural power.
Furthermore, listen to how he was defeated by means of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*).
Once upon a time, monks, there lived near the city of Vārāṇasī two sages named Śaṅkha and Likhita.
At another time, when it rained and a mire had formed, Śaṅkha slipped and fell into the mud; his water-pot (*kuṇḍikā*) broke, whereupon he uttered a curse: "Therefore, you of evil conduct..."
"It must not rain.
When King Brahmadatta and the multitude of people dwelling in Vārāṇasī heard this, they went to him and petitioned him: "Great Seer, do not do this!
He replied, "I cannot endure the wicked conduct of this man; for twelve years, it shall not rain because he has been defeated."

Then King Brahmadatta and that multitude of people petitioned and made a request to him, saying, "O Lord, let it rain. What do you think, monks? He who at that time, on that occasion, was the seer Śaṅkha, was none other than this Maudgalyāyana. And he who was Likhita at that time was none other than this monk Śāriputra.
At that time, even then, he was defeated by him through supernatural power.
Furthermore, hear how he was defeated by him through supernatural power:

Likhita fell at the feet of Śaṅkha on account of some business; having been kicked by Śaṅkha with his feet, his matted locks were pulled out, and he was told by Likhita: "At the time of the sun's rising, your head shall split apart."
Śaṅkha said,
"Therefore, the sun shall not rise. Consequently, darkness appeared in the world.
Then the king and the brahmins and householders entreated Śaṅkha, saying, "Great Seer, let this not be done!
He replied,
"The sun will surely rise, and my head will certainly burst apart."
He was told by Likhita: "If that is so, let a head made of clay be fashioned.
When the head made of clay had been fashioned, it shattered at the rising of the sun. What do you think, monks?
That Śaṅkha was none other than this monk Maudgalyāyana; that Likhita was this very person.
Such was that monk Śāriputra.
Furthermore, hear how he was defeated by this artisan:

A master ivory-worker from the Middle Country, taking a *prastha* of ivory-powder, went to the realm of the Yavanas; he arrived at the house of a master painter, which was empty, and spoke to his wife.
"Friend, prepare a prastha of rice for my wife and give it to her. Having set it aside, he departed; she then began to cook it.
The wood was consumed, yet it was not accomplished; then her husband arrived and asked, "Good lady, what is this? She explained it to him in detail.
He began to examine it and saw the rice-grains between the teeth. Deceiving her, he said, "Good lady, this water is alkaline; bring another jar, for with that these rice-grains will be prepared.
She then said to that master of dentistry, "Bring some pure water."
Having said that to her, he drew a pond in a certain place and within it, he drew a bloated dog.
Then the master Dantakara, taking a water-jar, arrived at that spot and saw the dead, bloated dog.
Covering his nose, he began to look, until that water vessel of his was broken and the master ivory-carver was revealed.
"What do you think, monks? That master ivory-carver was none other than this monk Maudgalyāyana; that master painter was none other than this monk Śāriputra.
Furthermore, those meditations, liberations, concentrations, and attainments which the Tathāgata has acquired, even the names of those the Pratyekabuddhas do not know."
Of those [attainments] for which the Pratyekabuddhas are recipients, the monk Śāriputra does not know even the names;
of those for which the monk Śāriputra is a recipient, the monk Maudgalyāyana does not know even the names;
and of those for which the monk Maudgalyāyana is a recipient, the other Śrāvakas do not know even the names.

Śāriputra possesses great supernatural power, yet it was with reference to his frequent dwelling therein that I declared Mahāmaudgalyāyana to be the foremost among those possessed of supernatural power.
The Chapter on Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana.
Then the Venerable Mahākāśyapa explained his own web of karma. Having gone there, he uttered these words in accordance with his former lives and conduct:
"He quickly remembers one small thing, having done which he experiences a great fruit. (1)
Just as a lion, dwelling upon mountain peaks, goes fearlessly to his range, so did that Kāśyapa... [who was] formerly dwelling...
[and who gave] a prastha of śyāmāka grain as a gift to the south.
When his mind was entirely liberated, free from outflows, dwelling in a state of passionlessness, and his mental disposition was irreproachable—
then he realized the supreme Dharma; having fixed his mind upon that Dharma,
he [attained] the convergence of [all] things.
...a thousand times I was born among the Kurus,
who are long-lived, free from possessiveness, [possessing] superior progress, and whose conduct is not inferior.
And by the fruit of that very same single deed, a thousand times I approached the Tridaśas.

Adorned with various garlands, ornaments, and ointments, with a most excellent body... [I was reborn]. And again among the auspicious gods in the Nandana grove, and again among the auspicious humans, I have attained rebirth once more due to the power of my mental vow.
By the fruit of that very same single deed, I was born as a twice-born man in a family of great *śāla* trees;
possessing abundant wealth, I was honored by men and women. [And yet] at no time did I ever behold those peerless disciples.
Having fashioned a patched robe from scraps of cloth, I prostrated before the Arhats in the world and went forth.
Having thus gone forth, I beheld the Jina seated in the Bahuputra Caitya;
bowing at the feet of the Sage, I said: "The Blessed One is my Teacher; I am your disciple."

“I am your teacher, and you, in turn, are my disciple. Listen to the sweet and sublime Dharma, if you wish to be liberated from all suffering—those very teachings which were taught by me, the Protector, the Supreme among Men, the Greatly Compassionate One. (11)
The four dhyānas, the powers, the faculties, and so forth—

having attained the stainless Dharma through these, I am one whose outflows are exhausted and who bears his final body. This is my meeting with those who bear their final bodies, who are upright and free from passion.

For the Conqueror, the Tathāgata, speaks what is true; he is indeed accomplished in the one who possesses virtue, if you so desire. Just as it was intended by my mind... [this is] my final existence. (14) Birth is exhausted for me, and likewise craving; the bond has been severed.

I am the legitimate son of the Dharma King, and I shall attain nirvāṇa through the destruction of the multitude of afflictions. I have been designated by the All-Seeing One as the foremost among those who dwell in the ascetic practices (dhūta). With outflows exhausted and faults vomited forth, I have reached the state beyond sorrow.
Thus, the Elder Kāśyapa, standing at the head of the community of monks,
proclaimed his own karma at the great lake Anavatapta.
The first section, on Kāśyapa.

Then the elder monks said this to the venerable Śāriputra: "What karma was performed by the venerable Śāriputra, as the ripening of which he has become so greatly wise and possessed of such great eloquence?
He replied:
At that time, in the forest, I saw a peaceful seer, a *śramaṇa*,
a Blessed One who was a *pratyekabuddha*, wearing coarse robes.
Having purified my mind toward him, I washed his robe.
Having sewn it and dyed it, and having likewise saluted him again and again,
he then rose up into the air out of compassion for me,
blazing with his own splendor, and [remained] in the sky.
Then, having joined my palms in reverence, I made this aspiration:
"May I become one such as this, with sharp faculties and great wisdom;
may I not be born into a wealthy family, nor among those of lowly conduct. (21)
"May I always be born into a noble family and be frequently intent upon the life of renunciation.
By that root of merit, for five hundred births, having obtained human birth, I went forth into the homeless state. (22–23)
This is my final birth; I have obtained this human existence.
I have propitiated the incomparable Buddha, the Caravan Leader.
And I have attained the going-forth in the teaching of the Lion of the Śākyas. (24)
"I have attained arhatship; I have become cooled and am extinguished.
In half a month, O Venerable One, I have reached the perfection of the destination.
And the Teacher himself was present before me and the community of monks."
The one of supreme wisdom prophesies the follower of the Wheel of Dharma;
Śāriputra, possessed of great insight, stands at the head of the community of monks and proclaims his own karma at the great lake Anavatapta. (26–27)
The second chapter: The Chapter on Śāriputra.
Then the elder monks said this to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the venerable Śāriputra has explained the course of his own karma; now you too should explain the course of your own karma."
When this had been said, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana spoke thus to the elder monks:
"Formerly, when I was a seer dwelling in a forest retreat, a man came there and requested ordination from me. (28)
Having shaved off his hair and washed his robe, he then dyed it and gave it to him; at that time, he became joyful.
Having approached a solitary place, he sat down cross-legged.
Having realized the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, he remained there for a long time;
then, filled with joy and joining my palms together, I made a vow there, praying for supreme supernatural power.
"May I possess such supernatural power as this great ṛṣi has.
(31) By that root of merit, wherever I was reborn—whether as a god or a human—I shone forth, having performed meritorious deeds. (32)
This is my final birth; I have attained this human existence.
I have propitiated the incomparable Guide, the Perfectly Awakened One.
And I have obtained the going forth in the teaching of the Lion of the Śākyas. (33)
I have attained arhatship; I have become cooled and am extinguished.
I have been designated by the All-Seeing One as the foremost among those possessed of supernatural powers.
Although my wholesome deed was small, the happiness experienced has been great.
And as for that unwholesome karma, listen as I explain it:
in the supreme city of Rājagṛha, I was once the son of a guild-president;
having played outside the house, I was entering for the sake of a meal. (36)
Seeing both my mother and father there in private, I was ashamed and felt reproachful;
I conceived a sense of mental aversion toward my father and mother.
When I shall become a man, I am thus struck by the reaper of the reeds;
having committed an offense with the mind, I have not acted against it with the body...
[enduring] supreme suffering. 38–39.
Then, by the remainder of that karma, in his final existence,
ascetics of other sects will kill him with reed-blades;
that very affliction shall be my own, ending in death.
Then the final remainder of karma will be exhausted.
Therefore, having inspired faith... [for] it is because of this that sentient beings go to a happy destination. 42
Thus did the Elder Kolita, standing at the head of the community of monks,
declare his own karma at the great lake Anavatapta.
This concludes the third section, the Kolita-varga.

Then the elder monks said to the venerable Śobhita, "Since Kolita has now explained his own web of karma, let the venerable Śobhita also explain his own web of karma. Thereupon, the venerable Śobhita explained his own web of karma in the presence of the community of monks.
Having gone to the monastery and seen that courtyard unclean, [I thought: "If only this courtyard were clean! Then, having purified my mind upon seeing that courtyard cleaned, I said:
"May I become free from defilements, just as this courtyard is now clean."
By that root of merit, wherever I was reborn, I became gracious, beautiful to behold, and handsome;
then, by the remainder of that karma... [46]
It was indeed a blessing for me.
For I was born radiant at the head of my circle of kinsmen;
beloved and pleasing to all my relatives, I was always held in high esteem.
I have propitiated this unsurpassed Perfectly Awakened One, the Caravan Leader;
I have attained Arhatship, become cooled, and am at peace. And as for the vow that I made... 49... [the rest of the verse follows].

One who has accomplished what was to be done and is free from outflows might sweep even the whole of Jambudvīpa with a Kāśi cloth; yet one who sweeps even a single walkway of a seer who is free from passion [is superior]. 50–51.
One might cleanse all the hermitages throughout the entire Jambudvīpa;
yet, whoever should cleanse even a space the size of a mat for the Saṅgha of the four quarters [is superior]. 52. [In] Jambudvīpa... [the former is not equal to the latter].
And whoever [should] even [anoint] a single span of a Jina’s [relic],
having understood this distinction which has been personally realized by me,
cleanse the stupa of the Sugata and gladden your mind. (54)
Therefore, those who truly understand the many virtues of the Perfectly Awakened One should pay honor to his stūpas;
this, O Venerable Ones, I remember as the wholesome deed I have performed.
... its fruit is lovely, desired, and delightful. 56 Therefore, one should perform beautiful worship at the stūpas of the Jina;
this, O Venerable Ones, is the supreme, unsurpassed field of merit. 57
For there is no small result for the clarity of mind directed toward the Perfectly Awakened One or toward the disciples of the Buddhas.
Śobhita, the Elder, stood at the head of the community of monks.
He explains his own karma at the great lake Anavatapta.
// 59 // The fourth chapter, "The Section on Śobhita," is concluded. //
Then the elder monks said this to the venerable Sumanas: "Venerable Sumanas, the venerable Śobhita has already explained his own karma; now may the venerable one also explain his own karma."
Having placed a flower behind my ear and having arranged a garland upon my head,
I went out to the park grounds surrounded by my companions;
there I beheld the stupa of the Great Sage Vipaśyin.
Being honored on all sides by a great multitude of people,
his companions, each taking their own garland,
placed it upon that stupa with minds full of serene faith.
Then, having seen them there as well as many other people, I took a flower from Karna and offered it upon the stupa. By that root of merit, wherever I was reborn, [I attained such excellence]. 63.
Having been both a god and a human, I shone forth through my performed merit.
I propitiated this unsurpassed Perfectly Awakened One, the Caravan Leader;
and having attained Arhatship, I have become cooled and extinguished.
Having offered a single flower, I served among the gods for hundreds of millions of years; by the remainder [of that merit], I have attained final nirvana.
If, O Venerable One, I had known the many virtues of the Perfectly Awakened One,
I would have performed even greater acts of honor with a mind of profound faith.
Therefore, for those who understand his many virtues—
Veneration toward the stūpas shall yield great fruit.
For the gift resulting from a serene state of mind toward a Tathāgata, a Perfectly Awakened One, or toward the disciples of the Buddhas, is never small. (68–69)
"Venerable sirs, I remember this wholesome deed that was performed by me;
I have experienced its fruit, which is lovely, desired, and delightful.
(70) By that karma... [there is] birth and renewed existence."
I am an Arhat, with defilements destroyed; I have become cooled and attained nirvāṇa.
I shall never again lie upon the bed of rebirth within saṃsāra. This will be my final birth, without further clinging.
"For that very reason, my name is Sumanas;
I am liberated from all sufferings and have crossed over the ocean of existence.
Thus spoke the Elder Sumanas, standing at the head of the community of monks.
He declares his own karma at the great lake Anavatapta.
// 74 // The fifth chapter, the Sumanas Section. // 74 //
Then the elder monks said this to the venerable Koṭīviṃśa: "Venerable Koṭīviṃśa, the venerable Sumanas has explained his own web of karma. Now may the venerable one also explain his own web of karma.
What deed was performed by the venerable Koṭīviṃśa, as the ripening of which deed he was declared by the Blessed One to be foremost among those who have initiated vigor?"
The field was pointed out; he said, "I have built a single dwelling for the Saṃgha of the four quarters at Bandhumatī, the royal capital of Vipaśyin’s dispensation. (75)
Having spread the ground of my dwelling with fine cloths, I cast it down with a joyful heart and a serene mind; at that time, I made this vow:
"May I propitiate the Perfectly Awakened One and may I receive full ordination. (76)
And supreme peace, nirvāṇa, the unaging state.
By this merit, having transmigrated for ninety eons, I have been born as a god and as a human, radiant and one who has performed meritorious deeds.
Then, by the remainder of that karma, in this final existence, I became the son of a preeminent merchant. Upon hearing that I had been born, my father’s desire was this: 79. [He thought: "This..."
Furthermore, on the soles of the Prince’s feet, twenty million hairs grew; they were four finger-breadths long,
extremely fine, soft to the touch, auspicious, and like tufts of cotton wool.

Ninety-one eons have passed; during one of those eons, when the ground was not yet covered [with grass], he placed his foot upon the earth. Thus was this unsurpassed Perfectly Awakened One, the Caravan Leader, propitiated.

I have attained arhatship; I have become cooled and am at peace. I have been declared by the All-Seeing One to be the foremost among those who have exerted vigor. With outflows exhausted and faults vomited forth, I have reached the unshakable state.
Standing before the assembly of monks at the great lake Anavatapta, he proclaims his own karma.
This concludes the sixth chapter, the "Twenty-Crore Group."

Then the elder monks said this to the venerable Vāgīśa: "Venerable Vāgīśa, the venerable [Śāriputra] has already explained his own web of karma; now may the venerable one also explain his own web of karma.
He replied:
Ninety eons have passed, yet I do not recall ever falling into an evil rebirth;
having performed meritorious deeds, I have shone forth as a god and as a human.
It was only through the mere sight of one another that I failed to recognize what was wholesome.
Then, having honored the stūpa of Vipaśyin with perfumes, garlands, and ointments, I did not fall into an evil rebirth. (87–88)
Having performed even a small amount of wholesome merit, I have experienced great happiness;
I have attained Arhatship, I am cooled, and I am at peace. (89) For if indeed, having known the Perfectly Awakened One...
... [it] would be so.
90 Therefore, for those who understand correctly, veneration should be performed toward the stūpas of the Perfectly Awakened One; it will bear great fruit. 91
I have been declared by the All-Seeing One to be the foremost among composers of verses; I am highly learned, a master of speech, and possessed of excellent eloquence. [In the great lake... 92–93.
The seventh chapter is the Vāgīśa-varga.
Then the elder monks said this to the venerable Piṇḍolabharadvāja:
"Venerable Bharadvāja, the venerable Vāgīśa has explained his own web of karma...
Piṇḍolabharadvāja replied:
I was the son of a guild-leader, a master in my father’s house;
out of devotion to my father, I behaved falsely toward my mother.
I gratified my mother with food and drink, yet I spoke harshly to her;
overcome by stinginess, I uttered these words: "Eat this stone for your meal! (95–96)
By the ripening of that karma, he was cast for a long time into hell;
in the Pratāpana and Kālasūtra hells, he experienced no small amount of suffering.
Then, having passed away from those hells and attained a human existence, 97. [he remained there].
By the ripening of that karma, [I fell] upon a stone... in those various rebirths;
and thus, through hunger and thirst, I met my death.
"This is my final birth; I have attained this human existence.
I have propitiated the caravan leader, this unsurpassed Perfectly Awakened One. And I have obtained the going forth in the teaching of the Lion of the Śākyas. (100)

I have attained arhatship and am extinguished; I am declared by the All-Seeing One to be the foremost of those who roar the lion’s roar. All my afflictions have been cast off; I am free from affliction and without outflows.
"Even now, Venerable Sirs, although I possess such supernatural power,
stones alone shall be my food within this cave;
Venerable Sirs, this [vow] was made by me."
The fruit of that has been experienced; indeed, karma does not perish.
(104) The Elder Piṇḍolabharadvāja, standing at the head of the community of monks, declares his own karma at the great lake Anavatapta. (105)
The eighth chapter: The Section on Piṇḍola-Bharadvāja.
Then the elder monks said this to the venerable Svāgata:
"Venerable Svāgata, the venerable Piṇḍola Bharadvāja has now explained his own web of karma; let the venerable Svāgata also now explain his own web of karma."
Then, at that time, the venerable Svāgata explained his own web of karma:
"In the royal capital of Bandhumatī, I was the son of a merchant; I possessed abundant wealth and grain, and I was esteemed by the populace. (106)
Then I was honored by the merchants and ministers;
[I was] handsome, and they were infatuated by the sight of my form. (107) [Infatuated by beauty and youth: J.W. de Jong; IIJ 7 (1964), pp. 232–235]
Then, having mounted my chariot and being preceded by a multitude of people,
I went forth to the park grounds, provided with every object of desire. There in the park, I saw a śramaṇa whose senses were fully restrained.
Seeing that ascetic, whose sensory conduct was tranquil and who wore coarse robes, I felt dejection; loathing him for his faultless speech and mind, I reviled him.
"Whose renunciant is this, so ill-favored and terrible to behold, leprous with sores on his limbs, emaciated and covered in a network of veins?
By the ripening of that karma and by his own misconduct of speech," (111) [he was born thus].
Then, having passed away from there and reached the end of my time, I was reborn in the hells.
I am ill-favored and miserable in the hells; with limbs covered in sores, emaciated, and with veins standing out, I am tormented.
With a skull in hand, clothed in a garment of hemp, sleeping on heaps of refuse, homeless and without refuge— whichever way I go for the sake of alms as my food, [I am thus]. (114)
"The staff-bearers ward me off, and I am loathed;
for five hundred births, wherever I was reborn, there I met my end suffering from hunger and thirst. (115–116)
My name was Durāgata, despised by all names; at that time, I was disliked by everyone and loathed.
Then I beheld the Perfectly Awakened One, preceded by the community of monks.
Seeing him teaching the supreme state to a great multitude of people, he ran toward that crowd with haste, thinking:
"Perhaps I might obtain as much food and drink as I require. 118–119.

And seeing that multitude of people seated for the sake of the Dharma, the Protector, the Sage of great compassion, spoke thus as he withdrew in disappointment: "There is no one to give even a portion of food. (120)
"Welcome! May it be well with you; please sit here on this seat.
(121) Then, having attained great joy and joining my palms in reverence, I bowed at the feet of the Teacher and sat down to one side. (122)
Then the compassionate Teacher Gautama, out of pity, [taught] the gradual sequence; thus I beheld the truths. Having seen the truths, I then requested the Great Sage for ordination.
The compassionate Gautama ordained me out of pity for me;
the Leader of the World gave me the name Svāgata and designated me as foremost in the attainment of the fire-element concentration.
Thus did the Elder Svāgata, standing at the head of the community of monks,
proclaim his own karma at the great lake Anavatapta.
This concludes the ninth chapter, the Chapter on Svāgata.
Then the elder monks said this to the venerable Nandika:
"Venerable Nandika, the venerable Svāgata has explained his own web of karma; now you too, Nandika, should explain your own web of karma.
Thereupon, at that moment, the venerable Nandika explained his own web of karma.
In the supreme city of Rājagṛha, I was a wealthy merchant.
While a famine was occurring, sages were fed there. [Then] a certain sage arrived.
The Blessed One, a Pratyekabuddha who has attained mastery and is free from outflows, [thought:
"Out of the fault of stinginess and thought, I have conceived an evil thought: 'Who now would feed this little ascetic for seven years? (128–129)
Having boiled [it] in horse urine, he then cooked rice;
he fed that rice to the ṛṣi... [he who was] cooked in hell for a long time.
In the hells of Saṃghāta, Raurava, Tapana, and Pratāpana,
having fallen from those states and attained a human birth,
I am sickly, dependent on others, and die in misery. (131–132)
For five hundred births in this very manner... [this verse continues] ...133 This is my final birth; I have obtained this human existence.
I have propitiated the Caravan Leader, this unsurpassed Perfectly Awakened One. 134
I have obtained the going-forth in the teaching of the Lion of the Śākyas, and I have attained arhatship; I have become cooled and am extinguished. [I was] a sick man, a turner-around. 135–136.
Thus did the Elder Nandika, standing at the head of the community of monks,
proclaim his own karma at the great lake Anavatapta.
This concludes the tenth chapter concerning Nandika and Aniruddha.
The summary verse:
Piṇḍola, Svāgata, and Nandika.

Then the elder monks said this to the venerable Yaśas: "Venerable Yaśas, the venerable Nandika has now declared his own web of karma; it is now the turn of the venerable one to declare his own web of karma. Thereupon, the venerable Yaśas proceeded to declare his own web of karma.
Formerly, while wandering through the forest for alms in a village,
O Sage, I saw the corpse of a woman, bloated and discolored;
having reflected upon it with proper attention, I sat down cross-legged.
There, with one-pointed mind and well-composed, I cultivated the meditation on the foul. Then, having arisen from that concentration, I beheld excrement and blood situated within her womb.
That foul-smelling, impure body, oozing from all sides—
its intestines, mesentery, kidneys, heart, and lungs—
was being devoured by hundreds of worms, and once again... 141–142.
Having seen this within my own body, I bound it [therein], just as this is, so is that; just as that is, so is this. Then, rising from that meditative absorption, I departed toward the hermitage.
At that time, I did not go for alms, nor did I eat any food. And when I entered the village again seeking food,
I cultivated [the mind] there.
All this that belongs to the realm of form is like a corpse;
it is filled within with impurities and is entirely loathsome.
By contemplating this repeatedly, I have attained freedom from passion.
The four immeasurable divine abodes have been well-cultivated. Having reached the Brahma-world as my final destination through these divine abodes,
I passed away from the Brahma-world and was born in the city of Vārāṇasī.
Born as the illustrious only son of a preeminent merchant there, I was beloved and pleasing to all, having reached the pinnacle of prosperity.
By day I attended to my duties, and by night I prepared my bed.
Rising quickly from there, I saw many women;
having placed mṛdaṅgas, bherīs, paṇavas, and vallarīs upon their heads,
they lay sleeping with arms outstretched, uttering incoherent cries.
Then my former cause, which was of great significance, arose within me:
the perception of the cemetery and the impurity [of the body] that had been present even in my inner apartments. Thereupon, overcome by spiritual urgency, I let out a cry.
"I am beset, O worthy ones, I am afflicted on all sides.
(153) Having risen from that bed upon the palace, the deities, out of compassion, opened my door for me. (154)
Having departed from the city, I approached the riverbank;
there on the opposite shore I saw a śramaṇa with his senses well-restrained.
Upon seeing that śramaṇa, I raised my voice loudly.
"I am beset, O Śramaṇa; I am afflicted, O Noble One! [he cried]. Then [the Buddha] addressed him with words that were like nectar:
"Come, young man, without fear; this place is free from affliction for you. 156–157.
Having crossed to the far shore of the river and cast off my jeweled sandals,
I approached the compassionate Buddha, the peerless one. Then, perceiving me to be thirsty, that teacher, the peerless one—
He taught the sweet Dharma, and I understood it.
Then, having seen the truth, I requested the Great Sage for the going forth;
out of compassion and pity for me, the merciful Gautama granted me ordination.
"By dwelling there overnight, when this sun had risen, all my outflows were exhausted; I have become cooled and attained nirvāṇa.
Thus spoke the Elder Yaśas, standing at the head of the community of monks.
He declares his own karma at the great lake Anavatapta.
This is the eleventh section concerning the Elder Yaśas.
Then the elder monks said this to the venerable Śaivala: "Venerable Śaivala, the venerable Yaśas has related his own web of karma;
now let the venerable Śaivala relate his own web of karma.
Thereupon, at that time, the venerable Śaivala related his own web of karma.

When the Jina Kāśyapa had passed into nirvāṇa in the city of Vārāṇasī, King Kṛkī had a great stūpa made consisting of jewels. I was the eldest son of the illustrious King Kṛkī. (163) *{a great stūpa}*
And first, I established a parasol upon a stūpa of the Jina. Having performed that wholesome deed, wherever I was reborn— whether as a god or a human— I shone forth, having accumulated merit.
In those various rebirths, I became wealthy and possessed of great enjoyments;
I was a great master of giving, endowed with riches and grain.
For five hundred births, I gave no small amount of gifts.

Beggars were fully satisfied, as were the various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas; all the pratyekabuddhas, who are entirely free from outflows, five hundred in number, were satisfied with a mind of supreme faith. 167–168.
Having performed that wholesome deed here in this final existence, he was born into the wealthy Śākya clan; as soon as he was born, he spoke these words:
"Is there perhaps wealth, grain, or [other riches]? (169)
"Since I shall give gifts, I will satisfy the supplicants;
I have not yet reached my own satisfaction, so I shall satisfy the supplicants.
It would be well for you to tell me quickly: do you have any wealth here? (170–171)
Having heard my speech, they became agitated in mind;
having established [the teaching], they fled in every direction,
yet at that time he spoke with deceitful words.
"Are you a god, a human, a yakṣa, or what are you? Tell me quickly!
173 'I am your son, mother; I am a human, not a rākṣasa.
Remembering my past lives, I am a lord of generosity and always strive to give gifts. 174"
Hearing those words of mine, my mother was delighted; she comforted me and,
together with her retinue, the mother nourished me.
I was pleasing to all, and I could never have enough of seeing him.
From the very moment I was born, that family constantly increased in wealth, grain, gold, as well as in servants and laborers. (176–177)
A boy named Śaivala was born; as soon as he was born, he spoke:
"Śaivala... [The rest of the verse is lost].
Then, having satisfied the beggars with gifts, I... [The rest of the verse is lost].
Having propitiated the Perfectly Awakened One and having gone forth into the homeless life—179 I did not go forth out of debt, nor out of fear for my livelihood;
rather, having gone forth with faith at that time, I attained the six supernormal powers. 180
... by kings and others... [of] the [Dharma]... 181. Thus spoke the elder Śaivala, standing before the community of monks.
He explains his own karma at the great lake Anavatapta.
The twelfth chapter, the Section on Śaivala.
Then the elder monks said this to the venerable Bakkula:
"Venerable Bakkula, the venerable Śaivala has now declared his own web of karma; let the venerable Bakkula also now declare his own web of karma."
Then, at that time, the venerable Bakkula declared his own web of karma:
"In the past, in the capital city of Bandhumatī, I was a perfumer. During the teaching of Vipaśyin, I invited the community of monks. (183)
"I give medicine for the sick... [184] ...The Saṅgha was invited, yet no one asked for anything;
however, a certain ascetic took only a single myrobalan fruit. [185]
For ninety-one eons, I did not fall into an evil rebirth;
behold this great benefit, the ripening of the gift of medicine. (186) [I have experienced...]
...delighted. 187. Then, by the remainder of that karma, I obtained this human birth;
for as one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), I did not know how to accept alms from the kingdom. 188.
Within just three nights, I have directly realized all three types of knowledge.
One should pass one's time wearing a rag-robe made of discarded refuse,
remaining unadulterated and pure.
"In this existence, my lifespan was one hundred years.
Venerable sirs, I do not recall having experienced even a moment of illness during that time; I remember this small amount of wholesome merit I performed."
"The fruit of that [action] has been experienced— lovely, desired, and resulting in happiness.
Thus did the Elder Bakkula, standing at the head of the community of monks,
declare his own karma at the great lake Anavatapta.
The Thirteenth Chapter: The Section on Bakkula.
Then the elder monks said this to the venerable elder named Sthavira:
"Venerable Sthavira, the venerable Bakkula has now explained his own web of karma; it is now the turn of the venerable Sthavira to explain his own web of karma."
Then, at that time, the Elder named Sthavira explained his own web of karma:
"In other previous births, I was a leather-worker. During a famine, I [took] pieces of hide from there... (193)
"Furthermore, for the sake of food alone,
another ascetic came seeking alms, desiring a meal.
Having purified my mind toward him, I gave him a mixture of leather."
Having partaken [of the offering], that ascetic then rose into the sky. 195.
Having attained great joy, I then joined my palms in reverence... 196. And having obtained vast delight, I made this vow:
"May my meeting with such elders as these come to pass!
May I touch that very stainless Dharma which has been touched by the body of this monk!"—such was the aspiration I then formed. (197–198)
At that time, I gave a gift that was lacking in color and fragrance, and had fallen away from its proper flavor;
yet, having performed that wholesome deed, I experienced much happiness. (199)
Having been both a god and a human, I have shone forth through my performed merit.
This is my final birth; I have attained this human existence.
I have propitiated the caravan leader, this unsurpassed, perfectly awakened one.
"And that supreme vow which [I made]... I have become cooled and attained nirvāṇa.
(202) Thus, there, the Great Elder named Sthavira...
He proclaims his own karma at the great lake Anavatapta.
This concludes the fourteenth chapter, the Section on the Elders, concerning those named Sthavira.
Then the elder monks said this to the venerable Uruvilvākāśyapa:

"Venerable Kāśyapa, the elder who bears the name of an elder has now explained his own web of karma; may the venerable ones also explain their own webs of karma. Thereupon, they began to explain them.
We were three caravan leaders, brothers who traveled together.
Having seen the stūpa of Kāśyapa broken and shattered into pieces, we restored it there, making it new again. (204) [GBM_6.1065b]
"Brothers, let us together raise three parasols;
having performed that meritorious deed, we shall rejoice for a long time in the heavens.
Having returned to the human state, we have been born into a wealthy and noble family. (205–206)
Not seeing the Perfectly Awakened One, we, who were followers of other sects, went forth [into homelessness];
[the Buddha] performed miracles near the Nairañjanā River.
We now entreat the Sage.
Therefore, O compassionate one, let us go forth out of compassion for us.
Having gone to Gayāśīrṣa, we then entered the teaching of Gautama;
through our exerted vigor, we attained supreme nirvāṇa.

Having performed an act of veneration for the Teacher here and having paid homage to that stūpa, we all went forth and became cooled and extinguished—these three elders: Uruvilvākāśyapa, Nadīkāśyapa, and Gayākāśyapa. 210.
They proclaim their own karma at the great lake Anavatapta.
This is the fifteenth section concerning Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, Nadī-Kāśyapa, and Gayā-Kāśyapa.

Then the elder monks said this to the venerable Yaśas: "Venerable one, the venerable Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, Nadī-Kāśyapa, and Gayā-Kāśyapa have each explained their own web of karma; now let the venerable Yaśas also explain his own web of karma."
In the past, I was a perfumer, skilled in the trade of fragrant goods;
at that time, young women came there for the sake of merchandise.
And having seen those beautiful women there... [212]
And having seen those women with hearts full of passion, I did not venture to bestow [myself] upon them; yet, acting without discernment, I made physical contact with the wives of others. 213–214
[His] hand withered and dried up.
216 Having propitiated [him], I went forth into the homeless life; I have attained Arhatship, become cooled, and am extinguished (nirvṛta). 217
"Venerable sirs, I remember this which was done by me as unwholesome;

its fruit has been experienced, for indeed karma does not perish. Just as the right hand is not like the left, so too [is the result]. 218–219. [The rest of the verse is omitted as per the source text.]
Furthermore, even a man experiences painful sensation.
(220) A wise and learned person should abandon another's wife as if she were a blazing fire; he should find contentment in his own wife. (221)
The man who, looking upon the wives of others,
[commits such an act]— whatever sin I have committed in previous births, I have experienced its no small fruit in hell for a long time. (222–223)
This is my final birth; the unsurpassed state has been attained.
I am liberated from all sufferings; I have become cooled and I am at peace. 224 Therefore, [from] liberation... [the remainder of the verse follows]. 225
Just as the Elder, standing at the head of the community of monks, proclaims his own karma by the great lake Anavatapta.
This is the sixteenth chapter: The Chapter on the Elder Yaśas.

Then the elder monks said this to the venerable Jyotiṣka: "Venerable Jyotiṣka, the venerable Yaśas has now declared his own web of karma; it is now the turn for the venerable Jyotiṣka to declare his own web of karma."
Then, at that time, the venerable Jyotiṣka explained his own web of karma:
"In the royal capital of Bandhumatī, [I was] the protector of the earth; at that time, I [served] the Bull among Men."
With ever-increasing devotion, we satisfy [the Buddha] together with his retinue. (228) For three months, the Buddha was fed... [and so forth].
(229) ...[He provided] a thousand [meals] as well as clothing.
At that time, a no small gift was given to each individual monk.
(230) There were elephants well-adorned and covered with nets of gold... [and so forth] ...the final [act of merit] was performed. (233)
Having been fully gratified by the great king, the preeminent seer Vināyaka then fell into reflection upon seeing the excellence of the seats:
"May I have food to chew and food to eat, but not a seat such as this... [and so on].
Śakra said to me, "I shall be your companion.
By him was created a beautiful, divine, and enchanting garden;
a divine seat was prepared, as were divine coverings.
Then, from Vipaśyin...
[the gods], beautifully adorned, held a parasol over each of the monks' heads. 238–239.

Then that Vināyaka, having been gratified with divine food and clothed in divine garments, [said]: "O Sage, together with your disciples, may I, having performed meritorious deeds, shine resplendent among gods and humans. (240–241)
Having paid honor to the glorious Great Seer Vipaśyin, [I said:
"This is my final birth; we have been born in Rājagṛha, [the city] of King Bimbisāra... [and so forth].
I was constantly satisfied with divine desires by all the ministers and the merchants;
though born as a human, I experienced those delightful, divine pleasures. (244–245)
Then the unsurpassed caravan leader, the Buddha, the Great Sage, the Guide, [proceeded]... 246 ...
he set out toward where that Blessed One, the Sage, was located. 247
[He] descended from his chariot on foot and approached the Sage, who was a radiant lamp, a bearer of the torch, and a maker of light.
Having bowed my head at the feet of the Great Sage, I was filled with joy... [he spoke] words of praise. 249... [he continued] with further verses of eulogy.
The caravan leader, the sun among men, who has severed Māra’s bonds—this unsurpassed teacher of the world taught the Noble Truths out of compassion for me; at that time, I penetrated them. (250–251)
Then I approached the Compassionate One, the Perfectly Awakened One, the peerless person among men. He said to me, "Come, monk," and that was my full ordination. 252–253.
With an undistracted mind and through firm energy and concentration, he touched the auspicious, deathless state of unsurpassed Nirvana. He had propitiated [the Teacher]... [254–255]
“... by birth and by death, and by sorrows... I am liberated from everything.
Thus spoke the Elder Jyotiṣka, standing at the head of the community of monks.
He proclaims his own karma at the great lake Anavatapta.
(257) This he said. "Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla, the venerable Jyotiṣka has now proclaimed the web of his own karma; let the venerable Rāṣṭrapāla also now proclaim the web of his own karma.
Then, at that time, the venerable Rāṣṭrapāla proclaimed the web of his own karma.
I was then the youngest son of King Kṛki, named Vardhana; at that time, I indeed caused a great stūpa for the illustrious Kāśyapa to be constructed. 258.
He protected a small parasol for that very father’s great stūpa.
Having performed that wholesome deed, wherever he was reborn, [he enjoyed its fruit].
Having performed meritorious deeds, I shone as both a god and a human.
This is my final birth; I am born in Sthūlakoṣṭhaka as the son of a guild-leader... [262] ...[the rest of the verse].
And likewise in the countryside, I shall be one who is pleasing, handsome, well-formed, and well-proportioned;
endowed with human supernatural powers, I shall be provided with all objects of desire. (263–264)
The Teacher was beloved and pleasing; he was... [265] ...skilled in all dispositions. My Teacher is a peerless person.
Having understood my disposition, he rejected my request for ordination. [266]
The Buddhas do not [ordain] one who has not been permitted by mother and father...
[267] ...Then I said to my mother and father:
"Father and Mother, grant me permission; I shall go forth into the homeless life. [268]
When my mother and father heard that I had become a monk, they were overcome with grief at the thought of my death; if you do not grant me your permission, [I shall depart]. 269–270.
Desiring liberation for six nights, he remained without food. [He thought: "If this son of yours delights in this life of renunciation, you shall perform the funeral rites with my dead body. 272.
If this son of yours indeed finds joy in this renunciation...

Thus you shall see life... (273) ... [omitted] ... otherwise than [through] mother and father, what other refuge could there be for him? (274) My mother and father said: "O dear friends... (275) ... [omitted] ...
My mother and father said to me: "If you have gone forth, come back again and show yourself; go, my son, and enter the religious life.
(277) "I replied, 'Very well,' and [I went]... (278)

Then, having gone forth here under the teaching of the Teacher, all my fetters have been exhausted and my taints have indeed been destroyed. [The fruit] has been experienced... [the remainder of the verse].

I have attained [the goal]; I have become cooled and am at peace. Therefore, having pacified your minds toward the Conqueror of great compassion, pay honor at his stūpa; you shall be liberated from great fear.
The eighteenth chapter: The Section on Rāṣṭrapāla.
Then the elder monks said this to the venerable Svāti:

"Venerable one, the venerable Rāṣṭrapāla has explained his own web of karma; now may the venerable Svāti also explain his own web of karma. Then, at that time, the venerable Svāti explained his own web of karma:
"I was in Rājagṛha, the chief merchant, possessing great wealth... [and so on].
They fed all the sages, one by one in every household;
whatever food was always cooked for their own sake, that very same kind was to be given to each of them. (286–287)
Just as five hundred portions of food were prepared for me in a basket, I gave exactly that same amount of food to that monk. 288–289.
Then, a most cruel stinginess arose within me there:
"How much more so for this monk who has stayed for three months? This expenditure will be excessive; it amounts to five hundred [pieces] of mine."
"What if I were to exert myself for the sake of this ascetic’s death?
[I] gave him food together with poison..."

And as soon as he had eaten that, a terrible disease arose within him; his intestines, mesentery, and kidneys came out through the lower part of his body. (295) [The rest of the verse is omitted]. (296)
The merchant killed this sage, a Pratyekabuddha who had become cooled and was free from outflows. Consequently, his kinsmen on all sides became enraged and reproached me. 297.
Great demerit has been produced by you because this [being] was killed;
therefore, having confessed your transgression, you must then ask for forgiveness for everything and subsequently renounce that fault.
With half a thousand meals, I satisfy them with devotion.
(300) Having confessed that sin and asked those sages for forgiveness, [I pray: (301) ... so that all these may be liberated, may I likewise be released from bondage. (302)
May I never be born in the homes of the poor; may never at any time arise in my mind the thought of stinginess.
[I have killed a Pratyekabuddha... 303–304.
I experience painful sensations; having returned once more to human birth, I soon meet my death. Yet, I become one of great wealth, affluent, honored, and worshipped by the world. (305)
With entrails falling out...
[and so forth]... 306 ... [and so forth]... 307 When my nirvāṇa shall come about through non-clinging, passion will have been entirely eradicated.
The intestines, the mesentery, and the kidneys will fall out as one; 308. [and] whatever else...
309. ...in Śrāvastī, there was a monk named Svāti, possessed of great supernatural power.
He declares his own karma at the great lake Anavatapta.
[End of] the nineteenth section, the Svāti-varga.

"Jaṅghākāśyapa, since the monk Svāti has now declared his own web of karma, may the Venerable Jaṅghākāśyapa also declare his own web of karma. Then, at that time, the Venerable Jaṅghākāśyapa declared his own web of karma: "In the past, O monks, in this very city of Śrāvastī, I was a master potter. At that time, there was a festival of the four-month rains-retreat (*cāturmāsya*). During that festival, people would go to the riverbank to bathe. While they were bathing, I would take their earthenware vessels and, having filled them with water, carry them back to my home. I would then sell them for a profit. In this way, I accumulated great wealth through that trade. Later, when the festival had ended, people would come to me and say: 'Master, we have returned from the riverbank after bathing; please give us back our vessels. I would reply: 'I do not have them; they were lost while you were bathing. They would say: 'Master, do not deceive us; give us back our vessels. I would reply: 'I do not have them; they were lost while you were bathing. Then, O monks, those people, being angry and displeased, seized me by the neck and dragged me along the road. As I was being dragged, I thought: 'If I were to die right now, what would become of me? I then reflected: 'I have committed no evil deed that would lead to such a state. It must be that I have failed to perform some wholesome deed that would lead to such a state. I then reflected further: 'In this very city of Śrāvastī, there is a certain householder who is virtuous and of good character. I should go to him and serve him as a servant. Having thought thus, O monks, I went to that householder and said: 'Householder, I am a servant; employ me. He replied: 'What work will you do? I replied: 'Whatever work there is, I shall do it. He said: 'Very well, sir; stay here. Thus, O monks, I lived there as a servant for twelve years. After twelve years had passed, O monks, that householder fell ill. Knowing he was near death, he called me and said: 'Come, sir; whatever wealth I possess, all that is yours. Take it and do as you wish. I replied: 'Householder, I have no need for wealth. I wish to enter the religious life under the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One. He said: 'Very well, sir; do as you wish. Then, O monks, having received permission from that householder, I went to the Blessed One. Having approached the Blessed One, I prostrated at his feet and sat down to one side. As I was sitting there, the Blessed One taught me the Dharma, which is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end, with its meaning and its phrasing, and he revealed the holy life that is perfectly complete and pure. When the Blessed One had taught me the Dharma, I attained the stainless, immaculate eye of Dharma regarding phenomena: 'Whatever is subject to origination is subject to cessation. Then, O monks, having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, known the Dharma, penetrated the Dharma, crossed beyond doubt, dispelled uncertainty, attained fearlessness, and become independent of others in the Teacher's dispensation, I rose from my seat, prostrated at the Blessed One's feet, and said: 'Blessed One, I go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has taken refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts. Then, O monks, the Blessed One addressed the monks: 'Monks, this is the first person who has entered the stream (*srotāpanna*) in this world.'"
While a famine was prevailing throughout the entire village,
one Śītala, who had become cool and free from outflows— the Blessed One— arrived there by my lot. 311–312.
Having reflected thus, I conceived an evil thought: "What shall I give as alms-food to this monk who performs no work? [314] ... [omitted] ... [315] ... [omitted] ...
In the Saṃghāta and Tapana hells, I experience painful sensations. [316]
Having fallen from hell, wherever I was reborn, [I performed] such [deeds];
having gone forth with faith, in this way the outflows have been destroyed by me.

The six higher knowledges have been realized by me; I have attained arhatship... [I] am one who dwells in the final existence. 321. Jaṅgha, of the Kāśyapa gotra, is named Karman, possessed of great supernatural power.
He explained his own karma at the great lake Anavatapta.

(322) The monks said this to the venerable Cūḍapanthaka: "Venerable Cūḍapanthaka, the venerable Jaṅghākāśyapa has explained the web of his own karma; now let the venerable Cūḍapanthaka also explain the web of his own karma."
Then, at that time, the venerable Cūḍapanthaka explained his own web of karma:
"In former births, I was a butcher of pigs; having bound the pigs by the mouth, I ferried them across the river. (323)
I reached the middle of the river...
[the sages], out of compassion for me who had arrived,
liberated me there and then ordained me.
In the state of non-perception (āsaṃjñika), indeed... [and] ... 326.
I propitiated the Perfectly Awakened One and went forth into the homeless life; yet, being deluded and slow-witted, I did not master the oral instruction (uddeśa). 328.
"Venerable Sir, for three months I [practiced]... [omitted] ...
wandering through this long and not insignificant cycle of existence for many eons. Having wandered thus, Cūḍapanthaka received his prediction in the presence of the Lord of the World."
"Black and white karmas [ripen] in the Anavatapta [Lake]...
(331) This he said. "Venerable Sarpadāsa, you have been questioned by the venerable Cūḍapanthaka regarding your own web of karma; now let the venerable one also explain his own web of karma.
Then, at that time, the venerable Cūḍapanthaka explained his own web of karma.
...I was a young ascetic;
I was learned and a master of the Tripiṭaka. ... I would recite [the scriptures] to the monks, but I did not teach the Dharma.
"Let the monks know me; let it not be otherwise... [333] ...[334] "...you do not proclaim the Dharma; this is certainly not fitting for you.
Having taught [the Dharma] and having dispelled that stinginess,
I then taught the Dharma to the assemblies for seven nights.
For seven nights at that time, I [taught].

Having rejoiced in the world of the gods, endowed with all objects of desire, 340 Then, having passed away from the world of the gods, I obtained this human existence; born into the family of the Śākya king, [I have attained]... 341 ... [and so forth]. 342-343
Beloved and pleasing to all, having reached the pinnacle of prosperity,
this man has gone forth from family to family; yet,
being fully endowed with the enjoyment of sensual pleasures, I have no desire for the life of renunciation.

Out of compassion for me alone, the Perfectly Awakened One, the peerless person, [will grant this]. For seven years, I shall give no small amount of gifts; having given these gifts for seven days, at the passing of those years, [I shall do so].
"And therefore, O one of excellent wisdom, I shall go forth into homelessness...
[346] ...Out of reverence for the Buddha, I would not reject his word:
'O Venerable One, out of compassion, I shall go forth within seven days. [348]
Having given gifts for seven days, and having [performed] the supreme [rites], without regard for the people, he went forth into homelessness. 349–350.
Having gone forth with faith, I am devoted to the teaching of the Jina; for many years... [I have practiced]. ... I shall go to the state of immortality.
Then a sense of shame and dread of blame arose within me, possessing great power:
"I shall become an object of reproach for the assembly of my kinsmen...
[Having taken hold of it, I sat down cross-legged.]
When the weapon was placed against my neck, then my mind was liberated.
(355) [The remainder of the verse is lost. ... (356) ... (357) In that very instant, supreme peace was attained by me. (357)
Because in the past I was a eunuch, stingy with the true Dharma,
the fruit of that [is this]...
[Sarpadāsa, possessed of great supernatural power].
He explains his own karma at the great lake Anavatapta. [End of] the Section on the Snake-Servant, 360.
At that time, I made this vow: "May I be born among elders such as these.
(403) Wherever I was reborn, my wealth was well-established through me.
(406) Having performed that wholesome deed, I was born in the city of Vārāṇasī. (211r3)
Through bathing in a steam-heated bathhouse, by anointing with *tāla* paste, and by the raising of a parasol, much happiness was experienced.
(411) Thirty short years passed; then, I attained the going forth into homelessness. (413)
with a friendly physical action, as well as with speech and mind,
you yourself should prepare a bed and seat, displaying a miracle for me.
That which was my vow has been fulfilled; that which was contemplated has been accomplished. This is the twenty-seventh [chapter].
Then the elder monks said this to the venerable Upasena: "Venerable Upasena, the venerable Dravyamallaputra has already explained his own web of karma;
