Thereupon, the venerable Upasena—
I wandered through various difficult terrains; at that time, I struck an arrow into the body of a harmless sage. Then, having passed away from the hells, I entered the womb of an animal.
Pray! O Coccaku!
Having performed meritorious deeds, I have shone forth; I have experienced sovereignty both divine and human, as well as human existence.
This peerless, perfectly awakened Śākyasiṃha has been propitiated; I am now at peace. Bhadrika, a kinsman of the Buddha, has gone forth from the family of kings.
O Venerable Lavaṇabhadrika, [this was said] by the Venerable Bhadrika, the Śākya king.
I was a laborer, a hired servant for the Protector at that time. Through the ripening of my karma and due to my verbal misconduct,
I passed away and departed from there.

Dwelling in a forest grove on the road, there I [encountered] the Light of the World; having passed away from there, I have touched the state of immortality. Thus spoke Madhuvāsiṣṭha before the assembly of monks.
I saw the Buddha Vipaśyin entering the supreme city. Having seen that one of great compassion, I neither heard the Dharma nor went to him for refuge;
yet I simply purified my mind.
By exerting himself, striving, and struggling, he realized arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions.
"Venerable sir, what karma was performed by the Blessed One?
And by Bharadvāja, who was reciting and devoted to study, were the three Piṭakas mastered?"
He became a master of the Tripitaka, a preacher of the Dharma, and possessed of appropriate speech and eloquence.
Eventually, he converted a certain householder,
who, for his sake, had a monastery constructed, fully equipped with all necessary requisites.
Then he sent a message to his brother Vasiṣṭha:
"Come; let us dwell together.
Having heard this, he arrived.
Then that householder saw his peaceful deportment—both his body inspiring confidence and his mind inspiring confidence.
Upon seeing him, he was filled with faith;
then, having been moved by that faith, he satisfied him with exquisite food and clothed him in a pair of costly garments.
Then jealousy arose in Bharadvāja:
"I have been his leader in all matters, yet I have never been covered by him with a garment;
but this man, having arrived only recently, has been covered with a garment. Thus, he became one who sought out the vulnerabilities of his brother Vasiṣṭha.
He perceived this and thought:
"This woman is jealous by nature;
if I do not give her this pair of garments, she will become even more deeply displeased."
He gave it to him;
nevertheless, that man remained intent on searching for a vulnerability.
Now, whenever the householder’s maidservant came to that monastery to perform her work, she was addressed by Bharadvāja:
"Girl, I give this pair of garments to you;
you must do as I say.
She replied:
"Noble one, what should I do?
You should put on this pair of garments and perform the household chores.
If the householder asks, 'Where did you get this pair of garments? [you should say:]"
He should say, "It was given to me by the noble Vasiṣṭha.
If he should ask, "For what purpose?
he should say, "Noble sir, this too must be asked."
"For what purpose do men give [gifts] to women?
Then she carried out everything exactly as she had been instructed.
Thereupon, that householder expressed his lack of confidence toward Vasiṣṭha.
Those great beings are fearful of disrespect.
He rose and departed.
What do you think, monks?

He who was that Bharadvāja was none other than myself at that time, on that occasion. Because I treated an Arhat with disrespect and slandered him with false accusations, through the ripening of that karma, I was cooked in the hells for many years, as previously described, until even now, at my final awakening, I have been [afflicted] by Sundarikā.
He was falsely accused by a female wanderer.
"Venerable One, what karma did the Blessed One perform,
the ripening of which resulted in his being falsely accused by the young girl Cañcā?"
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by the Tathāgata himself in other previous births—both common and uncommon—and the necessary conditions for them have been gathered.
As before, up until: 'Indeed, they bear fruit for embodied beings.'"
What are the common [circumstances]?

Once upon a time, monks, in Vārāṇasī there was a certain brahmin who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas; he was teaching the mantras to five hundred young brahmin students and was exceedingly honored, revered, and esteemed by the populace living in Vārāṇasī.
He was honored and esteemed as an Arhat.
Now, a certain seer possessing the five superknowledges (pañcābhijña), while wandering on a tour through the countryside, arrived at Vārāṇasī.
He was seen by the multitude of people residing in Vārāṇasī and was found to be inspiring.
Upon seeing this, the entire multitude of people became filled with faith;
whatever was to be given or whatever funeral rites were to be performed for the sake of the next world, each person bestowed upon him.
Consequently, his gain and honor vanished.
With a mind obsessed by envy toward that seer,
he addressed the young brahmins:
"Young brahmins, moreover, this man is a consumer of sensual pleasures."
They also said, "It is even so, Preceptor; he is merely a seeker of sensual pleasures, not a seer.
Thereupon, they proclaimed this in the streets, lanes, crossroads, and junctions, as well as among the families of brahmins and householders.
Rather,
upon hearing that he was a seeker of sensual pleasures, a great multitude of people expressed their lack of confidence;
fearing disrespect, he departed from Vārāṇasī.
"What do you think, monks? That brahmin at that time and on that occasion was I myself.
Those five hundred young students were these very five hundred monks.
Because I slandered him, as a result of that karma—as previously described—he was cooked in the hells."

By the very remainder of that same karma, even now, although he has attained the enlightenment of a Perfectly Awakened One, he has been falsely accused by the young woman Cañcamāṇavikā along with five hundred monks.
This is common karma. What, then, is uncommon karma?
Once upon a time, monks, a king named Brahmadatta reigned in Vārāṇasī; it was prosperous and so forth [in detail].
At that time, there lived a courtesan named Bhadrā, and there was also a rogue named Mṛṇāla.
He sent her garments and ornaments for her enjoyment;
she put on those garments and ornaments.
Then a certain man arrived, bringing five hundred kārṣāpaṇas.
He said, "Noble lady, come; let us enjoy ourselves together.
She reflected:
"If I go, I shall not receive five hundred kārṣāpaṇas;
moreover, it would be improper to depart elsewhere after having rejected one who has come to my house.
Having thought this, she spoke to her maidservant.
"Go and tell Mṛṇāla: 'The noble lady says that she is not yet ready; I shall come later.
Having gone, she reported this to him.
That man, who had many duties, attended upon her and departed during the very first watch of the night.
She reflected:
"A long time has passed;
will I be able to win over his heart as well?"
Then she spoke again to that girl:
"Go and inform Mṛṇāla:
'The noble lady has become ready.'"
"Tell me, which garden shall he come to?
She went and informed him; he said:
"In one moment your noble lady is ready, and in another moment she is not ready"—
this was the secret between that girl and her.
It was explained by her [to the king].
"Noble son, she is not ready.
Rather,
she has been enjoying herself with another man using your clothes and ornaments."
His obsession with sensual desire vanished,
and an obsession with ill will arose;
filled with resentment, he said:
"Daughter, go and tell Bhadrā: 'Go to such-and-such a garden.
She went and informed Bhadrā, and she went to that garden.
The rogue Mṛṇāla said,
"Is it right for you to enjoy yourself with another man while wearing my clothes and ornaments?
She replied:
"Noble son, there is indeed my transgression;
however, women are constantly prone to offense, so please forgive me.
Then, filled with resentment, he drew his sword from its scabbard and deprived her of life.
Then that maidservant raised a great outcry:

"The noble lady has been killed! The noble lady has been killed! Hearing this, a great multitude of people ran forth until they reached that grove where the Pratyekabuddha named Suruci was meditating.
Then that Mṛṇāla—
The rogue man, terrified, cast the blood-stained sword before the Pratyekabuddha Suruci and entered the midst of that very great crowd of people.
And the great crowd of people, seeing the blood-stained sword, [thought], "This renunciant has deprived Bhadrā of her life."
Then those who had attained noble realization said to that Pratyekabuddha:
"O renunciant, you bear the banner of a seer;
why do you act in such a manner?"
He asked, "What was done?
They replied:
"She enjoyed herself with Bhadrā;
she has been deprived of life.
He said:
"I am not the doer of this deed; it is peaceful," he said.

Although he spoke thus peacefully, that great multitude bound him firmly with his arms tied behind his back and presented him to the king, saying, "Your Majesty, this renunciant has been consorting with Bhadrā."
"She has been deprived of life," for kings are indeed lacking in discernment;
thus he says.
"If it is so, go and have him executed!
This renunciant has been abandoned by me.

Then, with a garland of *karavīra* flowers fastened around his neck and surrounded on all sides by men dressed in blue garments with weapons raised, he was paraded through the streets, lanes, crossroads, and junctions, being proclaimed [of his crime].
He was being led out from the city toward the park.
Then, the thought occurred to the rogue Mṛṇāla: "This poor ascetic has been falsely accused of a crime he did not commit;
he is now about to be executed."
"It would not be fitting for me to remain indifferent as well," he thought;
having understood this, he turned back, approached the king, prostrated at his feet, and said:
"Your Majesty, this renunciant is not the doer of this deed; it was I who committed this evil act.
Let this renunciant be released.
What do you think, monks?
I was that rogue named Mṛṇāla at that time and on that occasion.

Because I falsely slandered a pratyekabuddha, through the ripening of that karma, I was cooked in the hells for many years, as previously described, until now; and by the remainder of that karma, I have been falsely accused by the young woman Cañcā.

This is unique. Venerable Sir, what karma was performed by the Blessed One, the maturation of which caused him, together with four hundred and ninety-eight bhikṣus— excluding the venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana— to consume barley at Vairaṃbhya?
"It was divine nectar that was consumed.
The Blessed One said,
"Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by the Tathāgata himself in other previous births."
As before, up until: "Indeed, the deeds of embodied beings bear fruit.
When the lifespan of humanity was eighty thousand years, a teacher named Vipaśyin appeared in the world;
as before, up until: "the Buddha, the Blessed One."

While wandering on a tour of the countryside, he arrived at the capital city of Bandhumatī. In that city of Bandhumatī, there was a certain brahmin who was teaching the mantras of the brahmins to five hundred young students.
He saw the Perfectly Awakened One Vipaśyin accompanied by a retinue of five hundred.
He addressed the young brahmins:
"Gentlemen, these shaven-headed little ascetics do not deserve divine ambrosia; they deserve only to consume the hollowed-out barley.
They gave their approval.

"It is even so, Preceptor; these shaveling ascetics do not deserve to enjoy divine ambrosia; they deserve only to consume groats from hollowed-out husks. At that point, two young brahmins who were dressed in white spoke: "Preceptor, it is not as you say. These shaveling ascetics are indeed worthy of enjoying divine ambrosia, and they are not at all worthy of consuming groats from hollowed-out husks. The Preceptor asked them, "Who are you? They replied, "We are the two sons of Brahmā. He asked again, "What business do you have here? They said, "We have come to see the Tathāgata. He asked, "And what is the reason for your coming? They replied, "We heard, Preceptor, that the Tathāgata has arrived in Śrāvastī, and we thought: 'The Tathāgata is a field of merit for the world, including its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, for the assembly of ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans; he is the Teacher of gods and men, the Buddha, the Blessed One. We thought: 'It would be well if we could see the Tathāgata. Therefore, Preceptor, we have come to see the Tathāgata. Then the Preceptor said to those two young brahmins, "Go, sirs, and pay homage in my name with your heads at the feet of the Blessed One, and ask after his health, saying: 'Is the Blessed One free from illness, affliction, and discomfort? Is he strong, vigorous, and living in ease? And say this: 'Preceptor Kautsa pays homage with his head at the Blessed One's feet and asks after his health, saying: "Is the Blessed One free from illness, affliction, and discomfort? Is he strong, vigorous, and living in ease? "Furthermore, Preceptor, say this: 'The Blessed One should consent to accept tomorrow’s meal together with the community of monks from Preceptor Kautsa. "Very well, Preceptor," those two young brahmins replied to the Preceptor. Having paid homage to the Preceptor, they departed keeping their right sides toward him. Then, having approached the Blessed One, they paid homage with their heads at the Blessed One's feet and sat down to one side. Sitting there, they delivered the message exactly as the Preceptor had instructed. Then the Blessed One consented by remaining silent. Knowing that the Blessed One had consented, those two young brahmins rose from their seats, paid homage with their heads at the Blessed One's feet, and departed keeping their right sides toward him. Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada heard: "The two sons of the Preceptor Kautsa have gone to see the Blessed One. Hearing this, he went to the Preceptor Kautsa and said, "Preceptor, the two sons of yours have gone to see the Blessed One. He replied, "Householder, I sent them to see the Blessed One. The householder said, "Preceptor, may the Blessed One consent to accept tomorrow’s meal together with the community of monks from me. The Preceptor said, "Householder, I have already sent word to the Blessed One through the two sons of Kautsa. The householder said, "Preceptor, please go yourself and inform the Blessed One. The Preceptor said, "Householder, I am an old man; I cannot go myself. The householder said, "Preceptor, let the Blessed One wait; I shall go myself. Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, having approached the Blessed One, paid homage with his head at the Blessed One's feet and sat down to one side. Sitting there, he said to the Blessed One, "May the Blessed One consent to accept tomorrow’s meal together with the community of monks from me. The Blessed One consented by remaining silent. Knowing that the Blessed One had consented, the householder rose from his seat, paid homage with his head at the Blessed One's feet, and departed keeping his right side toward him. Then the Preceptor Kautsa, having passed the night, had various kinds of excellent food prepared in his own residence. Then, when the time had come, he informed the Blessed One: "It is time, Blessed One; the meal is ready. Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, entered Śrāvastī together with a great community of monks to eat his meal. The Preceptor Kautsa saw the Blessed One approaching from afar. Seeing him, he said to the Blessed One, "Blessed One, please enter; Blessed One, please sit down on this couch spread with a rug and a woolen coverlet, with a canopy above and red cushions at both ends. But the Blessed One did not sit on that couch. A second time and a third time, the Preceptor Kautsa said to the Blessed One, "Blessed One, please enter; Blessed One, please sit down on this couch spread with a rug and a woolen coverlet, with a canopy above and red cushions at both ends. A third time, the Blessed One did not sit on that couch. Then the Preceptor Kautsa thought: "Why does the Blessed One not sit on this couch? He thought further: "I have committed some fault against the Blessed One, for the Blessed One does not sit on this couch. Then the Preceptor Kautsa approached the Blessed One, paid homage with his head at the Blessed One's feet, and stood to one side. Standing there, he said to the Blessed One, "Blessed One, I have committed some fault against the Blessed One, for the Blessed One does not sit on this couch. The Blessed One said, "Preceptor, you have committed no fault against me. However, Preceptor, you addressed me with the words: 'Blessed One, please enter; Blessed One, please sit down on this couch spread with a rug and a woolen coverlet, with a canopy above and red cushions at both ends. "Preceptor, what you have said is not right;
these great-souled ones are indeed worthy of partaking of divine ambrosia.
What do you think, monks?
I myself was that brahmin with a retinue of five hundred at that time and on that occasion.

Because of the harsh verbal karma I uttered in the presence of the Perfectly Awakened One Vipaśyin and his community of disciples, as the ripening of that karma, for many years, many hundreds of years, many thousands of years, and many hundreds of thousands of years, I [ate] *koṭarayava* grains.
They were consumed.

"What do you think, monks?
That young brahmin named Uttara at that time and on that occasion was none other than myself."
