Venerable Sir, what karma was performed by the Blessed One, the maturation of which has caused even the Blessed One— who has fully awakened to enlightenment— to be touched by the illness of weak digestion?"

The Blessed One said: "Monks, those actions were performed and accumulated by the Tathāgata himself in other previous births... [as before] ...for indeed, embodied beings must experience the fruits [of their deeds].
Monks, in the past, in a certain mountain village, there was a physician.
Then, the son of a certain householder fell ill."
He summoned that physician and questioned him; the physician gave him medicine,
and he became healthy.
That householder did not provide him with any reward.
Even though that son of the householder fell ill three times and was restored to health by him three times,
he still did not give him any reward.
Then that physician, provoked by intense indignation, reflected:
"I have provided medical treatment for this householder's son even as many as three times, yet he has not rendered me even the slightest service."
"Now, if he should fall ill again, I will give him such medicine that his intestines will shatter into pieces.
Eventually, by the turn of fate, that householder’s son fell ill once more. The physician, having become resentful, gave him such medicine that his intestines were shattered into pieces...
"Let him give instructions out of compassion and without grasping.
The Blessed One said:
"I shall assign the gift in your names on this occasion,
provided that you approach at the time for the assignment of the gift within this very year.
They replied:
"How can we come without shame?
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke this verse:
"Those who feel shame where there is no cause for shame, and those who feel no shame where there is cause for shame."
Seeing fear where there is no fear, and seeing no fear where there is fear,
beings go to an evil rebirth due to their adherence to false views.
"Those who are shameless where there is no cause for shame, and shameful where there is cause for shame;
those who see no fear where there is no fear, and see fear where there is fear—by the adoption of right view, such beings go to a happy destination. Thus it is said.
They said, "Blessed One, we shall come this very day.

Then, during that same night, the brahmins and householders of Nāgarabindava prepared pure and excellent food, both hard and soft, as previously described, until they took lower seats and [approached] the Blessed One.
He sat down in front to listen to the Dharma,
and those five hundred hungry ghosts approached him.
Then, seeing the hungry ghosts, the brahmins and householders of Nāgarabindu began to flee.
The Blessed One addressed them:
"Sirs, for what reason are you fleeing?
They replied:
“Blessed One, these hungry ghosts are coming.
The Blessed One said, “Let them come; they are indeed your own kinsmen.”
"If you grant permission, I shall designate the sacrificial fee in their names.
They said,
"Blessed One, we grant permission."
Then the Blessed One began to assign the dedication of merit by means of their names with a voice possessing five qualities:
"Whatever merit arises from this gift, may it reach those hungry ghosts;
may they quickly emerge from this most dreadful world of hungry ghosts. Thus he spoke.
From that, there arose for them robes, food and drink,
and various kinds of bedding— all inexhaustible and available at all times.
Then, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the brahmins and householders of Nāgarabindava with a discourse on the Dharma, he rose from his seat and departed.
Thereupon, as the brahmins and householders of Nāgarabindava were seated and assembled in their hall of curiosity, this kind of conversation arose among them:
"O sirs, the ascetic Gautama has great desires, and his disciples likewise have great desires."
Others said, "Sirs,
the ascetic Gautama has few desires, and his disciples have few desires, unlike those of the heretics.
Now at that time, a brahmin named Vairaṭṭasiṃha was seated and present in that very assembly.

Then the brahmin Vairaṭṭasiṃha said this to the brahmins and householders of Nāgarabindava: "I shall demonstrate for you whether the ascetic Gautama is one of few desires or of great desires, and whether his disciples are of few desires or of great desires."
Then the brahmin Vairaṭṭasiṃha approached the Blessed One;
having approached, he said this to the Blessed One:
"May the Blessed One Gautama, together with the community of monks, accept my offering of molasses."
The Blessed One consented to Vairaṭṭasiṃha by remaining silent.
Then, the brahmin Vairaṭṭasiṃha, understanding the Blessed One’s consent through his silence, departed from the presence of the Blessed One.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"Monks, the brahmin Vairaṭṭasiṃha, seeking an opportunity [to find fault], invited the community of monks headed by the Buddha to a meal of molasses.
He said: 'Therefore, each of you should take as much as you can consume.'"
The brahmin Vairaṭṭasiṃha had five hundred jars of molasses.
Taking one jar of molasses from each of his sugar-houses, he took those five hundred jars of molasses and approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he said this to the Blessed One:
"May the Blessed One Gautama sit down together with his community of disciples; the molasses is ready;
please partake."
Then the Blessed One, having finished his meal from the bowl in his hand, sat down on the seat prepared for him in front of the community of monks.
Thereupon, the brahmin Vairaṭṭasiṃha took a single pot of molasses and began to distribute it;
however, the Blessed One exercised such supernatural power that it was distributed to the entire community of monks.
The remainder remained full.
Then the brahmin Vairaṭṭasiṃha became inspired with faith;
having thus conceived that faith, he raised a cry throughout the surrounding area.
"The ascetic Gautama has few desires, and his disciples have few desires as well. Thereupon, he invited the heretics.
They consumed molasses. They took the molasses in immoderate quantities;
some filled their bowls and, having taken it from there, set out.
Then the brahmin Vairaṭṭasiṃha said to them:
"You yourselves are deluded men of great desires;
but the ascetic Gautama is one of few desires."
"Or his disciples have few desires.
Having said this, he became even more deeply devoted to the Blessed One and approached where the Blessed One was.
Having approached and exchanged various greetings and pleasantries with the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Then the brahmin Vairaṭṭasiṃha, having extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One, said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, may I receive the going-forth and the full ordination into the state of a monk within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya; may I lead the holy life under the Blessed One."
Then the Blessed One addressed him with the "Come, monk" formula: "Come, monk; lead the holy life.
As before, [he followed] until he was established in accordance with the Buddha's intention.
{MS: nopacchito; read nepa-; cf. nepacchitā -} Pravr-v III, fol. 47r6}
Thereupon the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"Therefore, I authorize that molasses may be consumed at the proper time or at an improper time, when one is ill or when one is not ill. No remorse should be felt in this matter."
The venerable Vairaṭṭasiṃha could not achieve one-pointedness of mind due to the foul odor of a corpse.
The Blessed One reflected:
"The monk Vairaṭṭasiṃha is in his final existence; for what reason does he not perceive the Truths?"
He reflects:
"This is an abode of the foul odor of a corpse," and so on,
as before, up until...
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda:
"Go, Ānanda, and prepare the monastery of the monk Vairaṭṭasiṃha with perfumes, garlands, incense, and powders;
and fumigate the beds and seats."
"And spread a canopy of flowers gathered from fragrant blossoms.

"So be it, Venerable Sir," the venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. Then, having gone to his monastery while the Blessed One had gone for alms, he performed everything according to the procedure instructed by the Blessed One.
Then the venerable Vairaṭṭasiṃha, having wandered for alms, returned to the monastery.
He beheld a divine splendor;
thereupon, with a joyful mind, he consumed his alms-food. Having finished his meal and washed his feet outside the monastery, he entered the monastery.

Having entered, he sat down, having crossed his legs in the paryaṅka posture, set his body erect, and established mindfulness before him. Upon smelling that fragrance, a concentration of mind arose in him.
Then, through the abandonment of all defilements, he realized arhatship.
As before, up until he became one to be saluted.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"Monks, this is the foremost among my monks, my disciples who are devoted to the beautiful, namely, the monk Vairaṭṭasiṃha."
The monks, having become doubtful, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, behold! While other monks are resolved upon the beautiful, the Venerable Vairaṭṭasiṃha is also resolved upon the beautiful."
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, for five hundred births in succession, this man passed away from among the gods of the Thirty-three and was reborn in those very same realms;
now, in his final existence, he has been reborn among human beings."
Having smelled the stench of a corpse, he did not attain one-pointedness of mind;

but having smelled a sweet fragrance, he attained concentration of mind and became resolved upon the beautiful. [The Teacher said: "If this preparatory practice had not been performed for him, he would not have even produced the stage of heat (*ūṣmagata*)."
Therefore, I authorize that for anyone else who is likewise resolved upon what is wholesome, such a sequence of actions should also be performed;
no remorse should be felt in this matter.
Then the Blessed One, while wandering on a tour through the Vṛji countries, arrived at Vaiśālī and stayed there in the Gabled Hall on the bank of the Markaṭahrada lake.

The brahmins and householders of Vaiśālī heard that the Blessed One, while wandering on a tour through the Vṛji countries, had arrived at Vaiśālī and was staying in the Gabled Hall on the bank of the Markaṭahrada lake. Having heard this, they gathered together in one place and spoke.
"Gentlemen, it is heard that the Blessed One, while wandering on tour through the Vṛji republics, has arrived at Vaiśālī and is staying at the Gabled Hall on the bank of the Markaṭahrada lake.
If each one of us were to invite the Blessed One and feed him, the Blessed One would have to depart; otherwise, the others would find no opportunity."

(MSV I 225) "Therefore, let us establish this formal agreement (*kriyākāra*) that the community (*gaṇa*) alone, acting together, shall feed the Blessed One, and not a single individual. Having made this agreement, they established it.
Now at that time, four men of great merit were residing in Vaiśālī.
The master, the master’s wife, the master’s son, and the master’s daughter-in-law—
divine and human splendor appeared in their home;
they had not heard that agreement.

The householder Dhanika heard that the Blessed One, while wandering on a tour through the Vṛji countries, had arrived at Vaiśālī and was staying at the Gabled Hall on the bank of the Markaṭahrada lake. Having heard this, he departed from Vaiśālī and approached the Blessed One.
As before, up until [the point where] having been greatly gladdened, he remained silent.
Then the householder Dhanika rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and extending his joined palms toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"May the Blessed One, together with the community of monks, accept my invitation for a meal at my home tomorrow.
The Blessed One accepted the householder Dhanika’s invitation by remaining silent.
Then the householder Dhanika, understanding through his silence that the Blessed One had consented, bowed his head at the Blessed One’s feet and departed from the Blessed One’s presence.

Then the brahmins and householders of Vaiśālī approached the Blessed One; as before, they requested: "May the Blessed One, together with the community of monks, accept our invitation for a meal tomorrow at our home."
The Blessed One said,
"O Vāsiṣṭhas, I have already been invited first by the householder Dhanika.
They replied:
"Gentlemen, the householder Dhanika has violated the formal agreement of the community," some said.
"How could he have violated it?
He did not even hear of that agreement."
"Let the man feed us tomorrow; we shall feed him the day after tomorrow.
Then the Venerable Ānanda, rising early in the morning, took his bowl and outer robe and went to the residence of the householder Dhanika.
Having approached, he entered through the eastern city gate; when he saw that neither the seats had been arranged nor the food prepared,
he then said this to the householder Dhanika:
“Householder, you have invited the community of monks headed by the Buddha and yet remain with little concern.
He replied, “What are you saying, Noble Ānanda? Householder, I see no arrangement of seats, nor do I see any food prepared.”
"Noble sir, through which gate did you enter?
"Householder, through the eastern city gate. "Noble sir, please enter through the southern one."
He entered by the southern gate and saw that a divine arrangement of seats had been prepared and divine food brought forth.
Upon seeing this, he was overcome with great wonder.
Then the householder Dhanika announced the time to the Blessed One by means of a messenger.
"It is time, Venerable Sir; the meal is ready.

Then, having understood that the Blessed One had finished eating as before, that his hands were washed and his bowl put away, she took a very low seat and sat down before the Blessed One to hear the Dharma.
Then the wife of the wealthy man rose from her seat, extended her joined palms toward the Blessed One, and addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"May the Blessed One, together with the community of monks, consent to accept my invitation for a meal tomorrow at my home.
The Blessed One consented to the wife of Dhanika by remaining silent.
Having consented and having given a teaching on the Dharma to the householder Dhanika, he rose from his seat and departed.
The merchant’s wife had also prepared a meal.
Then, the Venerable Ānanda rose early in the morning, took his bowl and robe, and went to the residence of the householder Dhanika.
Having approached, he entered through the southern gate;
he saw neither the arrangement of seats nor food prepared.
Having seen this, he spoke thus to the wife of the moneylender:
The householder’s wife, having invited the community of monks headed by the Buddha, was asked, "For what reason do you remain so unconcerned, neither arranging the seats nor preparing the food?
She replied, "Noble sir, through which gate did you enter?
"Through the southern one."
"Noble sir, enter through the eastern gate. He entered by the eastern gate and saw that a beautiful arrangement of seats had been prepared and exquisite food had been served.
Having seen this, he was again struck with great wonder.
Then the householder’s wife announced the time to the Blessed One through a messenger:
"It is time, Venerable Sir; the meal is ready; may the Blessed One now do as he deems fit."
As before, until the Blessed One had washed his hands and set aside his bowl, the son of Dhanika took a lower seat and sat down before him to hear the Dharma.
Then the son of Dhanika rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and extending his joined palms toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"May the Blessed One, together with the community of monks, consent to take a meal at my house tomorrow."
The Blessed One consented to the son of the householder by remaining silent.
Then, after the Blessed One had given a teaching on the Dharma to the wife of the householder, he departed.
The son of the householder also prepared pure and excellent food, both solid and soft.

Then the venerable Ānanda, having risen early in the morning, took his bowl and robe and went to the residence of the householder Dhanika. Having arrived, he entered through the southern gate; however, he saw neither a prepared seat nor food set out.
Having seen him, he then said this to the son of Dhanika:
"Householder’s son, having invited the community of monks headed by the Buddha, why do you remain so unconcerned?
He replied:
"Noble one, why do you say this? I do not see any arrangement of seats, nor have food been prepared. Noble one, through which gate did you enter?"
"By the south;
Noble One, enter by the west. When he had entered...

When he saw that a beautiful arrangement of seats had been prepared and excellent food had been brought forth, he was filled with great wonder. Then the son of the householder announced the time to the Blessed One by means of a messenger.
"It is time, Venerable Sir; the meal is ready. Now, Blessed One, please do as you deem fit," [he said], as before, until:
having washed his hands and set aside his bowl, he took a lower seat and sat down before the Blessed One to hear the Dharma.
Then the daughter-in-law of the wealthy man rose from her seat, extended her joined palms toward where the Blessed One was, and addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"May the Blessed One, together with the community of monks, accept my invitation for a meal at my home tomorrow.
The Blessed One consented.
Having given a teaching on the Dharma to the son of the wealthy man, he departed.
Then the brahmins and householders of Vaiśālī approached the Blessed One;
having approached, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
As the brahmins and householders of Vaiśālī were seated to one side, [the Blessed One] instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them with a discourse on the Dharma, and then remained silent.
Then the brahmins and householders of Vaiśālī rose from their seats, draped their upper robes over one shoulder, and extending their joined palms toward the Blessed One, addressed him thus:
"May the Blessed One, together with the community of monks, accept our invitation for a meal at our home tomorrow.
The Blessed One said:
"O Vāsiṣṭhas, I have been invited by the daughter-in-law of the moneylender even before that.
Thereupon, the brahmins and householders of Vaiśālī were agitated and said:

"Sirs, does a single wealthy man possess such wealth that he feeds the community of monks headed by the Buddha every day, while we do not even find an opportunity? How should we proceed in this matter?
Others said:
"When the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, has finished eating and departs, we shall then lift one stone each from his house.
Then the Venerable Ānanda, rising early in the morning, took his bowl and robe and went to the householder's residence;
having arrived, he entered through the back door.
He saw neither the preparation of seats nor food being served.
Having seen this, he spoke thus to the merchant’s daughter-in-law:
"Daughter-in-law of the merchant, having invited the community of monks headed by the Buddha, why do you remain so unconcerned?"
She said,
"Do not say such a thing; I do not see any arrangement of seats, nor have any food been prepared."
"Noble one, through which gate did you enter?
"Through the western one.
"Noble one, please enter through the northern one."
He entered through the northern gate;
as he looked about, he saw a celestial arrangement of seats prepared and divine food brought forth.
Upon seeing this, he was again struck with supreme wonder.
Then the merchant’s daughter-in-law announced the time to the Blessed One by messenger:
"It is time, Venerable Sir; the meal is prepared.
Now, as before, he sat down on the seat prepared for him in front of the community of monks."
Then all the brahmins and householders of Vaiśālī gathered together and stood at the door of Dhanika’s house.
They said this to the householder Dhanika:
"Householder, the assembly of Vaiśālī is distressed and stands at your door."
"Go and ask his forgiveness;
do not let him cause you harm. Having gone out, he began to ask for forgiveness.
They said,
"Householder, do you alone possess wealth such that you feed the community of monks headed by the Buddha every day, while we find no opportunity?
He replied:
"Sirs, I have not heard of any formal agreement made by the community;
therefore, the community ought to forgive me.
Others said:
"Sirs, let this chief man be forgiven.
They forgave him,
and he said:
"If that is so, enter. They entered the house and saw that a beautiful arrangement of seats had been made and excellent food had been prepared.

Having seen this, they were again struck with great wonder and said, "Householder, you alone are worthy to feed the community of monks headed by the Buddha; we are not. He then gave those jewels to them.
They did not accept them. The Blessed One said to them, "Accept them; these jewels are difficult to obtain."
They took [the food],
and for each person, the appearance of its color became exactly as it had been taken by them.
Then, seeing that the community of monks headed by the Buddha was seated comfortably, the daughter-in-law of the wealthy man served them with pure and excellent [food].
With various kinds of solid and soft food— as previously described— until their hands were washed and their bowls removed, they took lower seats and sat before the Blessed One to hear the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One, having understood the disposition, latent tendencies, elements, and nature of the merchant, the merchant’s wife, the merchant’s son, and the merchant’s daughter-in-law, [taught] that which penetrates the four noble truths...
A teaching of the Dharma was given;

having heard it, the merchant, the merchant’s wife, the merchant’s son, and the merchant’s daughter-in-law shattered with the thunderbolt of knowledge the mountain of the view of a self-identity, which rises with its twenty peaks, and realized the fruit of stream-entry.
Having seen the truths, they uttered this inspired exclamation three times, as before, up until:
"We have transcended; we go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha of monks.
May you accept us as lay followers who, for as long as life lasts, have gone for refuge with our very lives and are full of faith."

Then the Blessed One, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened Dhanika, his wife, his son, and his daughter-in-law with a discourse on the Dharma, rose from his seat and departed. The monks, overcome by doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts.
"Venerable Sir, what karma was performed by the merchant, the merchant’s wife, the merchant’s son, and the merchant’s daughter-in-law,
as the ripening of which karma they were born into a family that is wealthy, possessing great riches and great enjoyments, where they experience both divine and human splendor,
and have also realized the Truth in the presence of the Blessed One?"
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, these very actions were performed and accumulated by them; their conditions have been gathered, their causes have matured, they have arrived like a rushing torrent, and they are inevitable.
As before, [the verse continues]: 'Indeed, for embodied beings, actions bear fruit.'"
Long ago, monks, there lived in Vārāṇasī a certain florist. He took a wife from a family of equal status, and he played, dallied, and enjoyed himself with her.
While he was playing, dallying, and enjoying himself, a son was born to him; he too married a wife from a family of equal status.

Then, at a later time, he became poor—extremely poor—and together with his son, wife, and daughter-in-law, they managed with great effort to produce a single garment. Wearing that very garment, the gardener would present flowers to the king;
wearing that same garment, the gardener’s wife would bring offerings to the inner apartments; and wearing that same garment, the gardener’s son would present gifts to the princes.
The daughter-in-law of the garland-maker, having put that very garment on, brought flowers for the king’s daughters-in-law.

When Buddhas do not appear in the world, Pratyekabuddhas arise; they are compassionate toward the lowly and the wretched, frequent remote lodgings, and are the sole objects of veneration in the world.
Eventually, a certain Pratyekabuddha, while wandering through the countryside, arrived at Vārāṇasī at the time of sunset.

And as that gardener was entering the city, he arrived at his house and stayed the night in its garden; having entered the fire-element concentration (*tejodhātu-samādhi*), he appeared to the gardener like a blazing mass of fire, whereupon faith arose in him.

It was told to his wife, and she was filled with faith; it was told by her to their son, and he too was filled with faith; it was also told by him to his daughter-in-law, and she was filled with faith. Then they began to converse among themselves: "Enough for us of tomorrow's meal;
this renunciant is one whose soul is peaceful; let us all join together and feed him."

Then, when the night had turned to dawn, he was presented with that alms-food by them. The florist said, "Noble lady, I give my share of the cloth to this renunciant. She replied, "Noble son, it has been given by me. Her son said, "It has been given by me. Her daughter-in-law said, "It has been given by me as well."
Then, having gathered together, they covered him with a cloth; for the teaching of the Dharma by those great-souled ones was through the body, not through speech.
Thereupon, out of compassion for them, that Great Being rose into the sky above and began to perform the miraculous displays of blazing, heating, raining, and flashing lightning.
For the supernatural power of an ordinary person quickly wins over others; thus, though they had been cut down by weapons—as if their very roots were severed—[they were restored].

Like trees, they fell at his feet and began to make this aspiration: "By the root of merit from having performed such service for one who is a truly worthy recipient of offerings, may we be born into a family that is wealthy, possessing great riches and great enjoyments; may divine and human prosperity manifest in our home, and may we become recipients of such qualities as these."
"May we please a Teacher even more distinguished than this one, and may we not displease him.
Then, out of compassion for them, that Pratyekabuddha performed a feat of supernatural power and set out above the royal palace.
As he was traveling, his shadow—[MSV]...
It fell upon the king; he began to look upward and saw that Great Being. He reflected: "This Great Being has destroyed the very roots of poverty for someone;
the time for that gardener to present flowers to the king has already passed."
The king also remained waiting for the flowers.

Then the garland-maker was summoned by the king’s men, and the king asked him, "For what reason have you exceeded the time for the flowers today? He related the matter in detail exactly as it had happened.

Then the king clothed him with his own garments; likewise, the florist’s wife was clothed by the women of the harem with their own garments, the florist’s son by the princes with their own, and the florist’s daughter-in-law by the royal ladies with their own.
In that very life, Dhana was provided with flowers and became free from poverty. What do you think, monks, as to who he was?
At that time, on that occasion, the florist was Dhanika; the florist’s wife was Dhanika’s wife;

the florist’s son was Dhanika’s son; and the florist’s daughter-in-law was Dhanika’s daughter-in-law. Because they performed services for the Pratyekabuddha and made a formal aspiration, through the ripening of that karma, they were born into a wealthy family of great riches and great enjoyments, possessing divine and human splendor.
"Having appeared in my house, they have seen the truths in my presence.

And by them, I—the Teacher who am more distinguished than hundreds of thousands of millions of Pratyekabuddhas—have been pleased and not displeased. Therefore, monks, as before, one must apply oneself to the fact that actions which are entirely black [yield black results], and so on."
"Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.

Then the brahmins and householders of Vaiśālī, with even greater faith, rose from their seats, extended their joined palms toward the Blessed One, and said this to the Blessed One: "May the Blessed One accept our invitation for the three-month rainy season retreat."
"Along with robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, together with the community of monks"—
the Blessed One consented to the request of the brahmins and householders of Vaiśālī by remaining silent.
Then the brahmins and householders of Vaiśālī, understanding that the Blessed One had consented by his silence, bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, rose from their seats, and departed.
Then the brahmins and householders of Vaiśālī, having prepared pure and excellent food, both hard and soft, during that very night—
as previously described— until their hands were washed and their bowls removed, took lower seats and sat before the Blessed One to hear the Dharma.
Then the Blessed One, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the brahmins and householders of Vaiśālī with a discourse on the Dharma, rose from his seat and departed.
In this manner, two or three days passed; the brahmins and householders of Vaiśālī, who possessed large retinues, were beset by a time of hardship.
Their kinsmen, thinking it was for the sake of a meal, approached them every day, and [the monks] were troubled by them.

The noble ones said, "A time of great difficulty has come upon us; our kinsmen approach us with expectations, and we provide for them every day. Yet we are unable to satisfy both you and them. Oh, if only the noble ones would attend to this! We shall provide the necessary requisites. Thus spoke the monks.
"Let us look upon the Blessed One.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One,
and the Blessed One said:
"Therefore, I authorize that the monks should look after the meal.
When the Blessed One had said that the monks should look after the meal,
they began to look after it.
While they were keeping watch in the open air, the gruel was being prepared and rain fell from the sky; however, it was ruined.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One said:
"It should not be prepared in the open air; they were preparing it in a gateway chamber and on a palace roof.
The Blessed One said, "Neither in a gateway chamber nor on a palace roof."
Therefore, monks, there are these ten improper sites for a refectory where one should not prepare a meal. Which ten?
An open space, a gateway tower, a palace, a fire-hall, a mechanical device, a royal courtyard, a temple, a householder’s hut, and a nunnery.
These are the monastic sites where food should not be prepared;
if one prepares it there, one incurs an offense of wrongdoing (*sātiśara*).
The summary verse (*uddāna*) is as follows: ...
The setting was Śrāvastī.
Now, a certain monk fell ill;
he approached a physician and said:
"Good sir, prescribe a medicine.
Having asked about the cause of the illness, he said, "Noble sir, drink rice-gruel; you will recover."
He said,
"Worthy sir, it has not been permitted by the Blessed One.
The physician said:
"Noble one, your compassionate Teacher might well grant permission; this is possible.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One said:
If a physician says, "Drink gruel," one should not feel remorse in this matter. The Blessed One said:
"According to the physician's instruction, lukewarm gruel is to be drunk. His attendant gave him cold gruel.
He went to the physician and said:
"O gentle-faced one, am I not well because of that gruel?
The physician said,
"Noble sir, why have you not drunk the gruel?"
He said, "Father,
is it hot?"
"It is indeed cold, Noble One. It was not well done;
it should be drunk after being warmed."
The monks did not know where they should heat it.
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, monks, a hall for allowable items (kalpika-śālā) should be designated."
The monks did not know what kind [of house] it was.
The Blessed One said:
"There are five types of permissible houses."

[The five types of building sites are: that which ends with the commencement, that which ends with the raising [of the structure], the "cow-pen" site, the site where the matter has been cleared away, and the site approved by consensus.
Among these, what is "that which ends with the commencement"?
It is as follows: a monk who is a supervisor of new construction stands at the very beginning and, having determined it to be a suitable place for the Saṅgha, declares: "This is a suitable place."
This is called the offense related to the commencement [of construction]. In that regard, what is the offense related to the raising [of the structure]?

It is as follows: when a monk who is a supervisor of new works (navakarmika) is having a stone raised, and at the very first moment the stone is being set down, he addresses the monks in the vicinity.
Venerable ones, please take note: this is the proper place for the Saṃgha; this alone is called "that which ends when it is raised. In that regard, what is the *goniṣādikā*?

Where there is an end to the gateway, that is called "the cow-pen" (goniṣādika). In that regard, what is meant by "having a manifest object" (*udbhūtavastukā*)? This refers to that which has its object already abandoned (*prahīṇavastukā*).
What is "consensus"?
It is that which is agreed upon by two; this is what is called "consensus. The monks did not know how it should be agreed upon.
The Blessed One said:

"That place which is established within the boundary, with a surrounding area of one vyāma outside, and which is agreeable to the Saṃgha, should be authorized. And it should be authorized in this manner."

Having prepared the seats and bedding, struck the ghaṇṭā, and questioned the monks by means of a formal inquiry, when the entire Saṃgha is seated and assembled, one monk should make a motion and perform the formal act (*karma*).
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen!..."
"May the Saṃgha authorize this hall for the Saṃgha, which is finished in every respect, within the boundary and surrounded by a fathom on the outside, as a proper storehouse.
If it seems the right time to the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha grant its permission that the Saṃgha authorizes this place as a proper storehouse. This is the motion (*jñapti*).
And the formal act (*karman*) should be performed in this way:

"May the venerable Saṃgha listen. This site, which is completed in every respect, within the boundary and surrounded by a fathom on the outside, the Saṃgha authorizes as a proper place (kalpikasthāna). Those venerable ones who consent to authorize this site as a proper place, let them remain silent."
Those who do not approve, let them speak.
Since there is silence, the Saṃgha has approved and authorized this; thus I hold it so.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Vaiśālī on the bank of the Markaṭahrada.
In Vaiśālī there lived a general named Siṃha.
He used to consume meat brought by his kinsmen;
however, once he had seen the truths in the presence of the Blessed One, he no longer consumed it.
He gives to the monks what has been brought for them,
and the monks consume it;
the non-Buddhist ascetics (tīrthikas) then reproach, revile, and speak against this.
"Venerable ones, meat was prepared specifically for General Siṃha and brought here;
he is now offering it to the Śākya-son ascetics.
Thus, meat prepared specifically for the Śākya-son ascetics has been consumed by them."
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"I declare that there are three kinds of meat that are improper and should not be consumed."
Which three?
I say that meat which is seen before one’s eyes to have been prepared specifically for oneself is unfit and should not be consumed.
I say that meat which is heard to have been prepared specifically for oneself is unfit and should not be consumed.
Such a reflection arises within oneself:
"Thinking, 'This was done for my sake,' one should not consume meat that is unfit. Thus I say.
Monks, I say that three kinds of meat are fit to be consumed.
What are the three?

I say that meat which is not seen before one's eyes, but is known to have been prepared specifically for oneself, may be consumed as permissible meat. I say that meat which is not heard to have been prepared specifically for oneself may be consumed as permissible meat.
"I do not say that one should eat meat that is permissible by oneself alone, as previously stated.
The setting was Śrāvastī;
it was a time of great hardship.

The monks stood leaning against their sides. Those brahmins and householders said, "Noble ones, in a teaching that requires exclusive application, for what reason do you stand leaning against your sides? Why do you not attend to the side of virtue?"
They said, "A time of hardship is prevailing; we do not obtain sufficient alms-food. We have become weak, afflicted by hunger."
Therefore, they stood with their sides turned toward him and said,
"Why do you not keep watch?"
"It has not been permitted by the Blessed One.
Your compassionate Teacher will find a way to permit it.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, monks, I authorize you:
in such a time of famine, hardship, and wilderness, the monks must remain vigilant."
One should not feel remorse in this matter.
The setting was Śrāvastī;
it was a time of great hardship.

The monks were addressed by faithful brahmins and householders: "Noble ones, please take your meal right here. Having finished their meal and taking what they had previously received, they went to the monastery, thinking, "We shall eat this during the time of famine. However, due to remorse, they did not consume it.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, I authorize that in such a time of famine, hardship, and wilderness, one who desires may consume what was previously received, considering it as 'previously received'."
One should not feel remorse in this matter.
The setting was Śrāvastī;
it was a time of great hardship.
Faithful brahmin householders, having invited monks to their homes, fed them;
however, some foodstuffs remained from those meals.
The brahmin householders said:
"Noble ladies, there remains food that was set aside for you;
please take this.
Having taken it, they departed.
Having gone there, they desired to consume it as well,
but due to remorse, they did not consume it.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, I authorize that in such a famine, in such hardship, and in such a wilderness, one may consume [food] considering it to be a gift of this kind.
No remorse should be felt in this matter."
The setting was Śrāvastī.
A time of hardship prevailed;
faithful brahmins and householders invited monks and provided them with a meal.
When they had finished eating, some foodstuffs remained;
the monks departed,
and the brahmins and householders said:
The noble ones have departed immediately;
only the delicacies remain,
and these are difficult to obtain.
"Take it and go. They took it away.
The monks also desired to consume that.
Out of remorse, they did not eat.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One,
and the Blessed One said:
Therefore, I authorize that in such a famine, hardship, or wilderness, one may consume [food] on the grounds that it was previously given;
no remorse should be felt in this matter.
The setting was Śrāvastī.
To the faithful brahmin householders, forest fruits from the northern regions became available;
they reflected,
"These are difficult to obtain and should be given to the noble ones."
These were given for the sake of being accepted by the monks;
thinking, "The monks should accept them," they do not consume them out of remorse.
Faithful brahmins and householders say:

"Noble one, when the Blessed One had not yet appeared in the world, the heretics were the ones worthy of offerings. But now that the Blessed One has appeared in the world, you are the ones worthy of offerings.
Therefore, please accept [this] out of compassion."
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, I authorize it."
Thinking that these things are difficult to obtain, they should be consumed;
one should not feel remorse in this regard.
In this context, these are the forest-dwellers.
[The section on] grapes, pomegranates, *tinduka* fruits, etc.
/ The setting was at Śrāvastī.
Faithful brahmins and householders, showing respect to the monks and inviting them [to eat], presented them with lotus-seed mats (*puṣkarāstika*).
The monks desired [to eat], but they did not consume it due to remorse.
The monks informed the Blessed One,
and the Blessed One said:
Thinking that these things are difficult to obtain, they should be consumed;
one should not feel remorse in this regard.
In this context, these are the *puṣkarāstika* [medicinal plants].
The ingredients were palm sugar, lotus stalk, water-lily seed, and lotus seed.
The setting was Śrāvastī.
A physical ailment arose in the Venerable Śāriputra due to an imbalance of the bodily elements.
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana reflected:
"Many times have I attended upon the Venerable Śāriputra according to my own judgment, yet I have never once consulted a physician; what if I were to ask him now?"
He asked the physician,
"Good sir, the bodily elements of the venerable Śāriputra are disturbed;
prescribe a medicine."
He said, "Noble sir, give me a lotus seed; he will recover.
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana reflected:

"It would not be fitting for me that I should not provide service with poison-milk for the sake of the Venerable Śāriputra. As soon as he had this thought, he vanished from Śrāvastī and stood upon the bank of the Mandākinī lotus pond, near the abode of the Naga king.
Then, the Naga king Supratiṣṭhita saw him and spoke.
"What is the reason for your coming, Noble One?
He replied,
"The bodily humor of the Venerable Śāriputra has become disturbed."
"The physician has prescribed poisoned milk for him," [the king said].
Supratiṣṭhita, the Nāga king, replied, "Noble sir, if that is so, please wait a moment."
Having descended into the Mandākinī lotus pond, he repeatedly plucked lotus-stalks as thick as a man and filled the bowl of the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana with those lotus-stalks.
As the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana began to look at the lotus-stalks being crushed,
the Naga king Supratiṣṭhita said:
"Noble one, do you wish to consume the lotus stalks?
He remained silent. Then he said:
"Noble one, go;
may it be well with you.

Then the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having filled his bowl with milk from the Visakṣīra cow, vanished from the bank of the Mandākinī lotus pond and reappeared in Śrāvastī, at Anāthapiṇḍada’s park in Jeta’s Grove.

Then the Venerable Śāriputra, following the physician’s instruction, consumed the poisoned milk. He recovered... [he said: "Go, cast it into the pond in the pavilion at the Jeta Grove in Śrāvastī, and then return."
Having arrived at Śrāvastī with a speed that carried him like the forceful impetus of the wind, he reached Jetavana.
A young elephant was born, and immediately thereafter a lion’s roar was let out. Then that female elephant, terrified, voiding urine and dung, abandoned the young elephant and fled.
Because he was raised with wealth and protected, the name "Dhanapālaka" (Wealth-Protector) became established for him.
Others recite: "By King Prasenajit [to King Bimbisāra]..."
Some poisons were consumed, some by the Venerable Śāriputra, and others were distributed among the Saṅgha;
thus, from that [remainder], there was left over...
The monks informed the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Gentlemen, divine lotuses are difficult for humans to obtain; therefore, I authorize [the use of] divine lotuses as they are difficult to obtain."

In the city of Bhadraṃkara, six kinsmen of great merit resided: the householder Miṇḍhaka, the wife of Miṇḍhaka, the son of Miṇḍhaka, the daughter-in-law of Miṇḍhaka, the male servant of Miṇḍhaka, and the female servant of Miṇḍhaka.
At the mere sight of them, [people’s] desires were fulfilled.

In this way, the householder Miṇḍhaka was renowned and possessed of great merit; how is it that Miṇḍhaka’s wife prepares a single pot for the sake of one person, yet hundreds and thousands partake from it? Thus, whenever Miṇḍhaka’s wife gives away [food], it remains full and is never exhausted. Likewise, Miṇḍhaka’s son and Miṇḍhaka’s daughter-in-law go and prepare [food] for the sake of one person, and it becomes sufficient for a hundred or a thousand.
In this way, Miṇḍhaka’s slave was of great merit; how so? When Miṇḍhaka’s female slave would watch over one measure [of grain], it would become seven measures.
Thus, Miṇḍhaka’s female slave was of great merit.
The Blessed One reflected:
"This householder Miṇḍhaka, together with his retinue, resides in the city of Bhadramkara;
the time has come for him to be disciplined."
There, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda:
"Go, Ānanda, and announce to the monks: 'Monks, the Tathāgata is traveling on a journey through the countryside toward Bhadraṅkara. Does anyone among you wish to go with the Tathāgata?'"
“Let him accept the robes so that we may go on a journey through the countryside to the city of Bhadraṅkara.
“So be it, Venerable Sir,” the venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One and informed the monks:

“Venerable sirs, the Blessed One intends to go on a journey through the countryside to the city of Bhadraṅkara. Whoever among you is willing to go on a journey through the countryside with the Blessed One to the city of Bhadraṅkara...”
"Let him receive the robes so that we may go. "Very well, venerable sir," those monks replied to the venerable Ānanda and followed closely behind him as they went.

Then the Blessed One— tamed with a tamed retinue, peaceful with a peaceful retinue, an Arhat with an Arhat retinue— set out for the city of Bhadraṅkara while wandering on a tour through the countryside.
When the Blessed One had displayed the Great Miracle at Śrāvastī, the non-Buddhist teachers were then humiliated.
Then some went to the city of Bhadraṃkara and stayed there.
They heard that the śramaṇa Gautama was coming; having heard this, they were again distressed, thinking, "Previously, we were [harassed] by the śramaṇa Gautama."
"Since we have been exiled from the Middle Country, if he should come here, he will certainly exile us from this place as well; therefore, a plan must be devised.
Having approached the storehouse for household goods, they said:
“A gain of Dharma! A gain of Dharma! Noble one, what is this? Have you been observed by us?
“We shall go; for whose sake?
“We have seen your prosperity; as long as we do not see your misfortune, we shall depart. “Noble ones, misfortune will befall us.”
"Sirs, the ascetic Gautama is coming, raining down the thunderbolt of his razor and making many women childless and husbandless.
"Noble one, if that is so, at the very moment we ought to remain here, we are being abandoned by you."
"Stay! You must not go.
They replied, "Why should we not stay?"
"You will not listen to us.
"Noble ones, speak; we shall listen.
They said:
"O Sāmanataka of the city of Bhadraṅkara, having caused the entire body of people to depart, cause them to enter the city of Bhadraṅkara;
plow the grassy meadows and level the open grounds."
"Cut down the trees bearing flowers and fruit; pollute the waters with poison!
They replied, "Noble ones, stay! We shall do everything."
They remained there.

Then, by them [the ministers], the entire population from the vicinity of Bhadraṅkara was driven out and made to enter the city of Bhadraṅkara; the grassy meadows were plowed, the sacrificial altars were leveled, the flowering trees were cut down, and the water sources—
[The food] was defiled with poison.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, reflected:
"It is not fitting for me that I should cause disrespect toward the Blessed One."

"How could I possibly remain indifferent when the Blessed One— who, over three incalculable eons and through many hundreds of thousands of difficult deeds, has fulfilled the six perfections and attained unsurpassed knowledge— will wander as a mendicant in an empty land, though he is the most distinguished in all the world and the victor over all disputants? Therefore, I shall exert myself for the sake of the Blessed One and his community of disciples so that they may dwell in comfort."
"May it happen so! he thought. He then gave a command to the sons of the gods known as the Vātabalāhakas:
"Go, dry up the poisonous waters!"
An order was given to the sons of the gods who are the clouds of the rainy season:
"Fill [the vessel] with water possessing the eight qualities."

The Cāturmahārājika gods were addressed: "Dwell all around the city of Bhadraṃkara. Thereupon, the water corrupted by poison was dried up by the Vātabalāhaka sons of the gods, and the wells, cisterns, ponds, lakes, and reservoirs were filled with the eightfold-endowed [water] by the Varṣabalāhaka gods themselves.
Filled with drinking water,
the entire vicinity of the city of Bhadraṅkara was occupied by the gods of the Four Great Kings.
The provinces became prosperous and flourishing.
Then, the non-Buddhist teachers, together with the body of city-dwellers, dispatched scouts, saying:
"Go and see what the provinces are like."
Having gone there, they see that the countryside is exceedingly prosperous and flourishing;
then, returning, they say:
"Sirs, never before have we seen such districts so prosperous and flourishing," they said.
The heretics replied,
"Sirs, even that which can cause insentient things to follow its lead will not cause you to follow it."
How can this be?
In every way, may you look upon us;
this is our final sight of you—we are departing.
They said,
"Noble ones, stay!
What does the ascetic Gautama do for you?"
"He too has gone forth, and you have also gone forth;
since he subsists on alms, how could he possibly forbid you from begging?
Thus spoke the heretics.
"Let us abide by an agreement:
if you all make a formal covenant that no one shall approach the ascetic Gautama for an audience,
and that whoever does approach him shall be fined sixty kārṣāpaṇas."
They gave their word and made a formal agreement.
Then the Blessed One, traveling by stages, arrived at the city of Bhadraṅkara and stayed in Bhadraṅkara at the Southern Monastery (*dakṣiṇāyatana*).
At that time, a brahmin girl from Kapilavastu had been married into the city of Bhadraṅkara.
Standing upon the wall, she saw the Blessed One situated in the darkness;
she reflected:
"This Blessed One, the joy of the Śākya clan, has gone forth into homelessness after renouncing his kingdom from the Śākya family."
"If there were a staircase here, I would descend taking a lamp.
Then the Blessed One, knowing her thought with his own mind, manifested a staircase.
Thereupon, joyful, satisfied, and delighted, she took a lamp and, having descended by the staircase, approached the place where the Blessed One was.
Having approached and placed a lamp before the Blessed One, she bowed her head at his feet and sat down to hear the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One, knowing her disposition, latent tendencies, elements, and nature, taught her a discourse that penetrates the Four Noble Truths as before, until she had gone for refuge and was exceedingly full of faith.
Thereupon, the Blessed One said this to the girl:
"Come, girl, go to where the householder Miṇḍhaka is; having approached him,
inquire after his health in my name and speak thus."

"Householder, I have come here for your sake, yet you remain with the door closed; is it not indeed fitting for a host to behave toward a guest as you have behaved? If he says, "A formal agreement has been made by the community," he should be told:
"A five-hundred-piece bag of nakula-berries tied at your son's waist remains there;
even if he spends a hundred or a thousand, it is always replenished and never exhausted.
You cannot come here by paying sixty kārṣāpaṇas."

"So be it, Venerable Sir," that girl replied to the Blessed One and set out. As if she were already fully acquainted with the way, she went to the presence of the householder Miṇḍhaka. Having arrived, she said:
“Householder, the Blessed One greets you with his blessing. He replied, “Girl, I pay homage to the Buddha, the Blessed One.
“Householder, the Blessed One says this to you:”
"I have come specifically for you, yet you remain with the door closed;
it is only right that a guest should be treated by you exactly as you have treated me."
He said,
"Girl, a formal agreement has been made by the community that no one should approach the ascetic Gautama for a visit;
whoever does so shall be fined sixty kārṣāpaṇas by the community."
"Householder, the Blessed One says:
'A purse containing five hundred [pieces] is tied at your son's waist.
Even if he spends a hundred or a thousand, it is always replenished and never runs out.'"
"You cannot come after giving sixty kārṣāpaṇas.
He reflected:
"No one understands this; surely that Blessed One is omniscient."
"I am going.
Having placed sixty kārṣāpaṇas at the gate, he descended by the staircase pointed out by the brahmin girl and approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down before him.
Then the Blessed One, having understood the underlying tendencies, the elements, and the disposition of the householder Miṇḍhaka,
gave such a teaching of the Dharma that penetrates the four noble truths; upon hearing it, Miṇḍhaka— as previously described—
realized the fruit of stream-entry.
Having seen the truths, he said,
"Blessed One, has even this body of people residing in Bhadraṃkara attained such dharmas as these?
The Blessed One replied:
“Householder, because you have come, the entire body of people has obtained much.
Then the householder Miṇḍhaka, having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, departed from the presence of the Blessed One.
Having gone home, he arranged a heap of kārṣāpaṇa coins and spoke this verse:

"Whoever wishes to see the Victor—who has conquered passion and hatred, who is free from dualities, peerless, and radiant as gold—should do so with an unwavering and well-resolved heart; I shall quickly bestow upon him the wealth that is to be given by me.
Thus the multitude of people spoke.
"Householder, it is better to see the ascetic Gautama.
He replied,
"It is better."
They said:
"If that is so, since the formal agreement was made by the community itself, let the community itself remove it;
what contradiction is there in this?"
Having torn up their agreement, they began to depart;
however, because of their mutual crowding, they were unable to get out.
Then, out of compassion for those to be trained, the yakṣa Vajrapāṇi hurled his vajra.
A section of the wall collapsed;
many hundreds of thousands of living beings emerged—some out of curiosity, others impelled by their previous roots of merit.
Then, due to that gathering of a great multitude of people, a vast assembly convened within a radius of one yojana around the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, having entered that assembly and sat down upon the seat prepared before the community of monks, delivered a Dharma teaching that establishes roots of merit within the mental continuums of many beings;
hearing which, some realized the fruit of stream-entry, while others, as previously mentioned, took up the refuges and the precepts.
After the Blessed One had taught the Dharma for a very long time, the time for the meal passed.
The householder Miṇḍhaka said,
"Blessed One, please perform the act of eating."
The Blessed One said,
"Householder, the time for the meal has passed.
He replied:
“Blessed One, what is permitted out of season?
The Blessed One said,
“Ghee and molasses.”
"There are also sugar-candies and drinks.
Then the householder Miṇḍhaka summoned the craftsmen and said,
"Sirs, quickly prepare out-of-season delicacies!"
They also said,
"The out-of-season snacks have been prepared."
The householder satisfied the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, with food and drink appropriate for that time.

Then the Blessed One, having established the householder Miṇḍhaka and his retinue in the truths, and having disciplined the body of people living in that small town according to their respective capacities, set out on his journey.
The householder Miṇḍhaka said:
“Blessed One, please accept this kārṣāpaṇa for the purpose of buying pathyā and other such items.
The Blessed One said,
“It may be accepted.”
The Blessed One said, "A kārṣāpaṇa coin may be accepted.
The monks did not know by whom it should be accepted or how.
The Blessed One said:
By a barber;
[if] he is not a barber,
the Blessed One said:
Regarding the novice monk:
the Venerable Upāli questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, as for that which was said by the Blessed One—that for a novice monk, the acceptance of gold and silver is the tenth training rule—"
The Blessed One said that it should be received by a novice monk (*śrāmaṇeraka*).
How so?
The Blessed One replied:

"Upāli, I spoke with reference to formal acceptance (*pratigraha*); do not, however, take what is not to be accepted. Therefore, a novice (*śrāmaṇeraka*) should receive it, but he must not make it his own through formal acceptance."
The householder Miṇḍhaka said,
"Blessed One, please accept some jaggery-rice.
The Blessed One replied:
"It should be accepted.
The monks did not know by whom it should be accepted or how;
the Blessed One said:
If there is no lay attendant or novice, the seven-day [period] should be consecrated by the monks themselves and carried [by them].
The monks did not know how it should be consecrated.
The Blessed One said:

"Having washed his hands and having caused [the object] to be received, placing it in the left hand and covering it with the right hand, standing before the monk, he should say: 'Venerable sirs, please attend to me.'"
"I, [name], will empower this seven-day medicine for their sake and for the sake of my fellow celibates.
Thus, a second and a third time.
The Venerable Upāli asked the Buddha, the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, regarding what was said by the Blessed One— that molasses may be consecrated for seven days— who is permitted to consume it? Upāli, it may be consumed by five types of persons."

[The following are exempt from the rule]: one who has set out on a journey, one whose meal has been interrupted, one who is ill, the attendant of the monastery, and the superintendent of building works.
Now, monks set out on a tour of the countryside;
they placed molasses in the midst of the rice and the flour.
Travelers desired to eat,
yet they ate with a sense of remorse.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it is not permissible to use that non-material thing for a material purpose.
That which was mixed among the rice grains should be winnowed out and then consumed."
As for the roasted barley flour (*saktu*), it should be consumed after being moistened with water;
another [type] also, when moistened, does not become entirely liquid.
The Blessed One said:
It should be scraped with a bamboo scraper and washed with water;
yet even so, it cannot be made free of meat.
The Blessed One said:
Having been well-boiled and made into a liquid with water, it was to be drunk.
The monks, overcome with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:

"Venerable Sir, what karma was performed by Miṇḍhaka, Miṇḍhaka’s wife, Miṇḍhaka’s son, Miṇḍhaka’s daughter-in-law, Miṇḍhaka’s male slave, and Miṇḍhaka’s female slave, by which they became possessors of the six superknowledges? (MSV I)
They have become possessed of great merit;
they have seen the truths in the presence of the Blessed One,
and they have pleased the Blessed One, not displeased him.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, these very actions were performed and accumulated by them; their provisions have been gathered, their conditions have ripened, and as before, they bear fruit for embodied beings.
Long ago, monks, in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a king named Brahmadatta, who—as before—ruled his kingdom according to the Dharma."
Now at that time, in the city of Vārāṇasī, the fortune-tellers had predicted: "There will be a twelve-year drought and a great famine characterized by the practice of living by counting sticks."

There will be three kinds of famine: the "beak" (cañcu), the "white bones" (śvetāsthi), and the "subsistence by sticks" (śalākāvṛtti). Among these, the "beak" is so called because people, having placed seeds in a casket, store them there with a view toward future beings.
"By means of this seed, humans will perform their work.
Because of its connection to a casket (*samudgaka*), it is called *cañcu*.
What is the "white bone" [period]?
At that time, humans collect bones and boil them until those bones have become white;
they then drink that liquid.
This is called "white bone" because of its connection to white bones.
What is the "subsistence by means of a probe"?
At that time, humans extract grains from the hollows of the ground with a probe, boil them in a pot filled with much water, and drink [the broth].
Because of its connection with the tally-sticks (*śalākā*), this is called the *Śalākāvṛtti*.
King Brahmadatta caused a proclamation by bell to be made in Vārāṇasī:
"Listen, you citizens residing in Vārāṇasī! According to the prognosticators, there will be a twelve-year [famine]."
"A drought has been predicted; there will be a famine of sticks for sustenance, of beaks, and of white bones.
Those who have food for twelve years should remain;
those who do not, may go wherever they please."
"When the famine has passed and there is abundance once more, you shall return.
At that time, in Vārāṇasī, there was a certain householder who was wealthy, possessing great riches and vast enjoyments, with an extensive and large retinue. He summoned his steward and said to him:
"O man, will there be food for me and my retinue for twelve years?
He replied,
"Noble sir, there will be."
He remained right there; however,
immediately thereafter, that famine occurred and his storehouse was completely exhausted.
All his attendants had passed away,
and he remained as the sixth person;
then that householder, having cleared out the treasuries and storehouses, gathered a single *prastha* of grain.
His wife placed it in a pot and cooked it.
When Buddhas do not appear in the world, Pratyekabuddhas arise in the world.

Compassionate toward the lowly and the wretched, devoted to remote lodgings and seats, they were the sole objects of veneration for the world. At that time, a certain Pratyekabuddha, while wandering on a journey through the countryside, arrived at Vārāṇasī.
Having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robes, he entered Vārāṇasī for alms.
And that householder was standing ready to eat.
That Pratyekabuddha, wandering for alms in due course, arrived at his house.
He was seen by that householder as pleasing in appearance and pleasing in mind.
Having seen this, he reflected again:
"Even by consuming this, I shall certainly be parted from my life;
what if I were to give my own portion to this renunciant?"
He said to his wife,
"My dear, give this portion that belongs to me to this renunciant.
She reflected:
"My master does not eat;
how can I eat?
she said, "Noble son... (MSV I 252)
"I too shall give my own share to him.
In this way, the son, the daughter-in-law, the male slave, and the female slave each relinquished their respective shares.
Then, having come together, they all offered alms-food to the Pratyekabuddha.
The teaching of the Dharma by those great-souled ones was physical, not verbal.
Like a king of swans with outstretched wings, he rose high into the air and began to perform the miracles of blazing, heating, raining, and flashing lightning.
The miraculous power of an ordinary person quickly inspires attraction.
Like trees cut at their roots, they fell at his feet and began to make aspirations as they desired.
The householder also began to make an aspiration:
"By this root of merit from having performed such service for one who is a truly worthy recipient of offerings, may my empty treasuries and storehouses become full the very moment I see them."
"May I be a recipient of such qualities as these;
therefore, may I please a teacher even more distinguished than this one, and never displease him.
Thus she began to make a formal vow.

"By this root of merit from having performed such service toward a truly worthy recipient of offerings, if I were to cook a single vessel of food for the sake of one person, it would not be exhausted even if a hundred or a thousand were to consume it, because my application has never ceased."
"May I become a recipient of such qualities as these; and may I please a Teacher even more distinguished than this one, and never displease him. Thus the son began to make his vow.

Monks, in a certain forest retreat there lived two sages,
