those who were exhorted by Śāriputra had dull faculties.
Had they not been exhorted by Śāriputra, they would have fallen away even from the stage of "heat" (uṣmagata).
All of you, being assembled together, listen with a serene mind as Kaineya the matted-hair ascetic likewise proclaims the praises of the Buddha.
At one time, the Teacher, the Great Hero, together with his disciples, was invited to a meal at the residence of Kaineya.
The brahmin Śaila saw food being prepared in the residence of Kaineya; having seen it, he said to Kaineya:
"Has a marriage been arranged, or has the king, or perhaps the kingdom, been invited? Or what else, O one of great wisdom, is it that you have asked? Tell me that."
Neither my marriage nor the king or the kingdom was invited by me;
rather, the Buddha, the Supreme Being, was invited by me for a meal.
Having heard that "this one is the Buddha," Śaila was moved to a sense of spiritual urgency.
He asked, "Kauneya, who is this Buddha? Tell me about him."
There is one born in the Śākya clan, that Teacher, the peerless person; because he possesses wisdom regarding all phenomena, he is therefore called "Buddha."
For the past has been seen by the Buddha, and likewise the future is seen;
the present too is seen—conditioned phenomena are subject to decay.
Whatever is to be known, the knower of reality knows it all;
because he is all-knowing and all-seeing, he is therefore called a Buddha.
That which is to be directly known has been directly known, that which is to be cultivated has been cultivated, and that which is to be abandoned has been abandoned; therefore, he is called a Buddha.
And when this earth, together with its oceans and mountains, trembled at his birth, I pay homage to him with palms joined in reverence.
I bow with palms joined in reverence to him who has attained the powers of a Tathāgata, by whom Māra, the kinsman of darkness, was defeated along with his mount.
Having gone to the city of Vārāṇasī, where he set in motion that twelvefold Wheel of Dharma, I shall pay homage to him with palms joined in reverence.
I bow with palms joined in reverence to him who liberates many beings who are bound by the fetters of passion and oppressed by desire and hatred.
Where is that Blessed Buddha, the Guide? How far away is he?
This very day I go for refuge to the Son of the Śākyas, the Light-Maker.
Go, brahmin; by this way you will see this delightful grove, resembling the realm of the Gandharva king, where you shall behold the unsurpassed Buddha.
Clad in saffron robes, radiant, golden-hued, and green-skinned,
he was like a heated brass vessel or like a golden image.
It was like a flowering *sāla* tree, or like a blossoming *karṇikāra*;
it was covered with various jewels, resembling a sacrificial pillar made of precious gems.
He illuminates all around and pervades everything with his splendor;
in height and circumference, he is symmetrical like a banyan tree.
Having abandoned all delight in sensual pleasures, along with his flourishing kingdom and kinsmen,
the Sage has gone forth into homelessness and delights in solitude.
Like a lion, the fearless one roars like a maned beast on Mount Gandhamādana;
you shall see the Buddha, O Brahmin, unafraid amidst the depths of the forest.
O Brahmin, you shall behold the Buddha, who possesses the voice of Brahmā, whose speech is charming and smooth, who is radiant with a smile, and whose resonance is like the sound of a drum.
O Brahmin, you shall behold the Buddha, who resembles the lunar disc, pure like the moon in the sky surrounded by the constellations.
O Brahmin, you shall behold the Buddha, resplendent like Vairocana, radiant with blazing rays in the expanse of the sky, shining brilliantly as all darkness has vanished.
O Brahmin, you shall behold the Buddha, the bull among men, the possessor of the ten powers, standing immovable like the hump of a leader of a herd of bulls.
You shall behold the unsurpassed Buddha, who is as deep as the ocean, immeasurable like the great sea, inconceivable, and the foremost among those who meditate.
You shall see the Buddha Gautama emerging from the dark fortnight like the sun in the sky, or like a mass of blazing fire.
Just as a universal monarch shines when surrounded by his ministers,
so does the Perfectly Awakened One shine when honored and attended by the Arhats.
Just as the Great Brahmā is a sovereign lord over the realms of desire,
so the Sage exercises mastery over the three-thousandfold world system.
He fully reveals the truths, flowing like honey from a hive;
having heard them, people find peace and cross over the great ocean.
The manifold kinds of suffering, the origin of suffering,
the cessation of suffering, and the path with its two and four factors.
He gives wealth to the destitute, he treats the sick,
and he provides refuge for those who are oppressed, liberating all beings from suffering.
For beings who have become blind, deluded, and wandering on wrong paths,
he reveals the straight path— secure and leading to Nirvana.
The Great Sage extinguishes the people who are ablaze with passion and hatred and set on fire by delusion, just as a great cloud does with its rain.
Endowed with beauty of form, complexion, and strength, his like is not to be found; he possesses the firm constitution of Nārāyaṇa, like a mountain well-established.
Unstained by gain or loss, by pleasures or pains, by blame or praise, and by fame or infamy— just as a lotus is unstained by water.
He abstains from taking life and does not delight in what is not given;
he speaks the truth, lives a life of celibacy, and has desisted from slander.
He does not utter harsh words, but speaks gently at the proper time;
he has no covetousness for sensual pleasures and maintains a mind of loving-kindness toward all beings.
Endowed with the vision of truth, having the power of meditative concentration as his domain,
possessing the six supernormal knowledges and great dhyāna, he traverses the path through the sky.
He hears various sounds, both those that are divine and those that are human;
he knows the minds of others, whether they are afflicted or unwholesome.
Skilled in former abodes, wherever he previously dwelt,
he knows the passing away and rebirth— the coming and going— of sentient beings.
With outflows exhausted, liberated, stilled, and well-nirvanized,
with senses calmed and mind at peace, he meditates upon the Full One within his heart.
O Brahmin, beholding an elephant or a sixty-year-old tusker in the midst of a lotus pond, you shall obtain joy and be fully satisfied.
"O Śaila, such is the Blessed One in his splendor, like a mass of fire;
upon his body are the thirty-two marks of a Great Man."
Even one who were to speak the praises of the Protector for a full hundred years would not reach the end; the Tathāgata is immeasurable.
O Brahmin, those who see this have the unsurpassed gain;
for those who, having seen it, go for refuge, their burden of gain is even greater than that.
Having heard the description of the great sage, the brahmin Śaila was filled with faith; with his mind and intentions set on solitude, he spoke thus to Kaineya:
"While I was a human being, I never heard of such a complexion as this;
he is the most excellent in all the world, just as you describe him, O son of Kaineya."
Having cast aside the banner of pride, like a merchant seeking wealth, serve him with a desire to learn; in this way, O Brahmin, you will attain joy.
Accompanied by five hundred young brahmin disciples,
the brahmin Śaila set out for the auspicious hermitage of the Buddha.
Secluded and of little noise, frequented by flocks of birds,
and endowed with flowering trees, it was like the Nandana grove of the gods.
Then the brahmin entered the abode of the King of Dharma, which was frequented by the son of the Śākyas and filled with the enchanting presence of kinnarīs and vyālas.
Seeing the Supreme Person, the charioteer who tames the untamed, Śaila addressed these words: "Are you free from ailment?"
With a voice full like that of a lute and with the melodic warbling of a kalaviṅka bird, the Buddha replied to Śaila: "Indeed, I am free from ailment."
I am without possessions, without grasping, and thus without debt; my doubts are severed, I am utterly liberated and detached, for I am entirely free from outflows.
I wander through the world free from dust, pure, stainless, and free from affliction.
O pure Brahmin, by that I have transcended all enmity and fear.
"Welcome to you as well, O Mountain; please sit upon this seat.
Are you not weary of body? I hope, O Brahmin, that you are at ease?"
"I am happy, O Great Hero, having seen you today, the Great Sage; with a tranquil mind, I am as satisfied as if I were adorned with ornaments."
Having delivered his discourse there in proper sequence,
the brahmin then sat down with a humble mind, feeling abashed.
The teacher, a master of mantras, learned in the three Vedas, and one who had reached the further shore of the Vedas—
the Brahmin Śaila— sat down and examined the marks of the Sage.
Śaila beheld thirty of the marks upon the body of the Lord of the World; he remained in doubt regarding two: the tongue being retracted within the mouth and the [mark of the] sheath.
Full of doubt and uncertainty regarding the marks of the Great Sage,
he questioned the Sambuddha, the descendant of Aṅgiras, whose name is Truth.
"O Great Sage Gautama, among those thirty-two marks that have been heard of, I do not see two of them upon your limbs."
Is your private organ concealed by a sheath here? And is your tongue, which is unsurpassed in its taste, not too short?
Are you indeed possessed of a broad tongue? O Great Sage, may I know this; quickly extend your slender tongue and dispel my longing.
Only once in a great while do leaders appear in the world; indeed, as rare as a flower on an udumbara tree is the Great Sage.
Just as one scorched by summer heat approaches water, or one hungry approaches food,
or one who is ill approaches medicine, so do we attend upon the Teacher.
With a voice full like a lute and with the melodic warbling of a kalaviṅka bird, the Buddha replied to Śaila: "O Brāhmaṇa, dispel your doubt."
He covers both eyes and ears with his tongue;
with his long tongue, he covers the entire circle of his face.
Skilled in the bases of psychic power, he also displayed his supernatural powers;
the Brahmin Śaila saw that the Sage was hidden, covered by a chest.
With his doubts dispelled and his mind’s intentions filled with joy at the marks of the Great Sage, Śaila, whose arrow of uncertainty had been extracted, uttered these words:
Those thirty-two marks which I have received through the mantras—
all of them are present upon your limbs, complete and without deficiency.
With virtuous speech, good conduct, and noble birth, you shine like the sun in the midst of the community of monks, O one of pleasing appearance.
What need have you for the state of a śramaṇa, you who possess the highest complexion?
O bull among men, you are worthy to be a Cakravartin king.
Endowed with the fourfold army and the seven precious jewels, turn the wheel upon the earth; become a king, a lord of the world!
"I am the king upon this mountain; for I am the unsurpassed Dharmarāja.
By means of the Dharma, I turn the wheel here upon the circle of the earth."
I am well-born in a noble family, a Kṣatriya by lineage;
having terrified Māra along with his army, I have attained supreme enlightenment.
"O Brahmin, mindfulness is my wheel; wisdom is my charioteer.
Diligence is my swift horse, which, when urged on, bears the yoke.
Concentration is my most excellent jewel, for it brings light to the darkness."
Equanimity is like a noble elephant that bears the burden when urged.
For those possessed by passion, women are indeed delight; O Brahmin, my delight is in the Veda.
O best of Brahmins, I have bestowed upon you the most excellent wealth that was within my house.
I awaken for you these seven jewels of the factors of enlightenment, which transcend all worlds, by means of which I shall rouse this sleeping and blinded populace.
All directions have been conquered by me; no rival enemy exists. My fourfold assemblies and my fourfold army are mine.
I dwell in the city frequented by former Buddhas,
which is endowed with pleasure groves of supernatural power and has crossroads fashioned by the Path.
It is interspersed with sūtras and jātaka tales, frequented by great beings,
and protected by the three doors of liberation and the guardianship of mindfulness.
Endowed with a sense of shame and dread of blame, I am the King, the Tathāgata;
I have waged a battle of Dharma and struck the drum of Dharma.
I have been consecrated for enlightenment, having overcome Māra along with his hosts;
the immeasurables are well-cultivated within me, and they are my ornaments.
The four divine abodes are the enclosures against the afflictions;
the doctrines of others have been struck down, shattered, and rendered powerless.
My rightness of view bestows light upon the living beings in this world;
my vision is severed by the weapon of knowledge, and discernment is my armament.
The bases of psychic power are my chariot, tranquility is its standing ground, and the grasp of the fist is its steadiness;
the chariot of ethical conduct has the sound of Nandi,
and insight is my charioteer.
Armor is patience and gentleness; the battle is the cultivation of the path;
the bundle consists of the five faculties by which the hindrances are destroyed.
The four right efforts, by which the afflictions have been destroyed;
the heroic battle has been given by me, and the drum of Dharma has been struck by me.
Having terrified Māra along with his army, I have been consecrated for enlightenment.
Having destroyed ignorance with knowledge and [seen] the arising and passing away of the aggregates, I have emerged from the forefront of battle; I am a Buddha for the sake of awakening the people.
There are three great thieves in the world by whom these living beings are oppressed:
passion, hatred, and delusion; all of them have been destroyed by me.
I am worthy and deserving of offerings, possessing the six super-knowledges and exerting the powers; I am the recipient of oblations for those who have entered the excellent field of merit.
Having exerted supreme vigor, the outflows have been destroyed by me;
having crossed the great flood, I stand firm while others are bewildered.
Just as a lion with powerful tusks, having encountered living beings in the forest,
strikes them equally— whether they be young, middle-aged, or old.
In the same way, the perfectly awakened one, the lion among men, the leader,
proclaims the Dharma equally to the foolish, the mediocre, and the great-souled.
O Gautama, dispel this longing of mine who am thus afflicted;
for you are the foremost among those who extract the thorns of existence and among those who know the world.
"O Brahmin, restrain yourself and pacify your doubt; have faith!
For the sight of illustrious, perfectly awakened Buddhas is difficult to obtain."
O Brahmin, I am that perfectly awakened one, the unsurpassed King of Dharma, whose appearance in this world occurs only rarely at any time.
"You say, 'I am the Fully Awakened One,'" Śaila said to the Tathāgata,
"just as you, Gautama, speak of turning the wheel that is unique."
Who is your general, your disciple, the son of the Teacher,
that wise one who turns the wheel set in motion by you?
"O Brahmin, I have a disciple who is my own son, equal to me in wisdom;
he is known as Upatiṣya, Śāriputra, who is possessed of great learning."
Free from all fetters, tranquil, and without outflows,
the wise one follows the wheel that has been turned by me.
Oh, what a marvel is the Perfectly Awakened One! Oh, what a perfection of disciples! A marvel has arisen in the worlds; oh, how supreme is the Triple Gem!
I say this to you: may it be well with you; having attained the state of a disciple, oh, having drunk the essence of the Dharma, I shall become perfectly at peace.
Then that brahmin, his mind and intentions filled with joy yet agitated,
spoke these words to the assembly, his thoughts directed toward solitude.
Listen to this, sirs, as the one with vision speaks:
the great meditator, the remover of the thorn, roars like a lion in the forest.
Let those who wish to follow come; let those who do not wish to go depart.
This very day I shall go forth into homelessness in the teaching of the one of supreme wisdom.
When this holy life has been well-practiced and this path well-cultivated,
the going forth becomes fruitful for one who dwells in heedfulness.
"If this pleases you, go forth into the teaching of the Jina;
having cut off your matted hair here, O Brahmin, we too shall go forth."
With a joyful heart and intention, his ten fingers joined in *añjali*,
the brahmin Śaila, having placed his outer robe over one shoulder, spoke.
"These five hundred young men stand here with palms joined in reverence;
O Sage, may we well receive the going-forth and full ordination."
Then the compassionate Teacher, the Great Seer who is full of pity,
said to them, "Come, monks," and that was their full ordination.
Śāriputra is of great wisdom; Maudgalyāyana possesses supernormal powers; and the elder Brāhmaṇa Kapphiṇa has attained the range of eloquence.
On the delightful bank of the Nadīsundarika, in a charming forest grove,
the elders, who were skilled in inspired eloquence, spoke to them there.
Having understood that Dharma from them and having delivered a discourse there that was in accordance with it,
they were before long liberated and established in the supreme goal.
Having attained their goal and being happy, they have realized nirvana in this very life;
filled with joy, they behold the Perfectly Awakened One, the Leader of the World.
They pay homage to the True Dharma, the supreme wealth, and to the training praised by the Victors; they honor heedfulness, meditative concentration, and the practice of renunciation.
Therefore, those here who desire their own welfare and long for greatness should go for refuge with reverence to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
For this indeed has been described as the refuge in the world by the Seer of Truth;
it bestows all happiness upon those who are afflicted and terrified.
One who seeks liberation should always honor the supreme, righteous majesty of the Buddha, the Son of Aditi, and the teaching of the King of Dharma.
The Kaineya Gāthās are completed.
Then the Blessed One, while wandering on a tour through the country of Kāśī, arrived at Kāśīpaṭṭa.
In that Kāśīpaṭṭa, there were two father and son who had previously been distinguished [as householders] and had now gone forth as monastics.
The son said:
"The Blessed One, along with the community of disciples, while wandering on tour through the country of Kāśī, has arrived here; the Blessed One and the community of monks are weary in body.
Suppose we were to invite the Blessed One together with the community of disciples to a drink of barley-gruel?
Why then do you prepare a beverage, or are you inviting the community of monks?"
"Go and invite the community of monks;
I shall prepare the rice gruel.
He then invited the community of monks.
He too, taking a mirror, went out into the street. There he saw the merchant with his hair and beard long; he showed him the mirror.
He said,
"Noble one, do you possess such skill even in this?
He replied:
"It exists.
Bring it down.
He brought it down.
The householder had begun his work when he fell asleep;
once the load was set down, he woke up and said:
"It has been brought down, noble one.
"Householder, it has been brought down.
Satisfied, he said:
"Noble one, I am exceedingly pleased. Tell me, what boon shall I grant you?
He replied:
"I have invited the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, to partake of a drink of gruel;
please give them the gruel.
He replied:
"Noble one, what is the use of this rice-gruel for you? I shall provide you with excellent solid and soft food;
go and invite [some]."
Having said, "May you be free from illness," he departed.

Then that householder, having prepared pure and excellent food— both solid and soft— as previously described, sat down on the seat prepared before the community of monks, and there the excellent food was served.
The monks reflected:
"We have been invited with coarse food,
yet this meal is exquisite."
"How shall we accept it? they asked, and so they did not accept it.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"If one has been invited with coarse food but receives something refined, it may be consumed;
no remorse should be felt in this matter."
The Blessed One reflected:
"Whatever disadvantage arises because monks carry finished wares,
therefore a monk must not display his craft."
"One should not provide such an article for one of that same category;

if one provides it, one incurs an offense, except for the case of former physicians providing a sheath for their instruments, former barbers providing a vessel, and needle-makers who have gone forth providing a needle-case.
The Blessed One, while wandering on a tour through the Malla country, arrived at Pāpā.
He was staying in the Jalūkā forest grove at Pāvā.
At Pāvā lived a high official among the Mallas named Roca,
who was the maternal uncle of the Venerable Ānanda.
He was extremely faithless.

The wicked Mallas heard that the Blessed One, while wandering on a tour through the Malla country, had arrived at Pāpā and was staying there in Pāpā in the Jalūkāvana grove. Having heard this, they began to converse among themselves.
"Gentlemen, it is heard that the Blessed One, while wandering on a tour through the Malla country, has arrived at Pāvā and is staying in Pāvā in the Jalūkā forest grove.
If each one of us were to feed the community of monks headed by the Buddha, the others would find no opportunity.
Therefore, let us establish a formal agreement in every respect."
"No one among us is to feed the community of monks headed by the Buddha alone;
we shall feed them all together.
Whoever among you feeds [the Sangha] alone shall be fined sixty kārṣāpaṇas by the community."
Then all the Pāpeya Mallas, having gathered together, approached the place where the Blessed One was.
Having approached and bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
As the Pāpeya Mallas were seated to one side, the Blessed One instructed, inspired, and gladdened them with a discourse on the Dharma, as previously described, and then remained silent.
Then the Mallas of Pāpā rose from their seats, draped their upper robes over one shoulder, and extending their joined palms toward the Blessed One, addressed him thus:
"May the Blessed One, together with the community of monks, accept our invitation for a meal tomorrow at our home.
The Blessed One accepted the invitation of the Mallas of Pāpā by remaining silent.

Then the Mallas of Pāpā, understanding through the Blessed One’s silence that he had consented, rejoiced and delighted in the Blessed One’s words; they bowed their heads at the Blessed One’s feet, rose from their seats, and departed.
The Mallan chief minister Roca remained right there.
The Venerable Ānanda said to him,
"Roca, have you become a person of faith?
He replied:
"I have not become a believer; rather, a formal agreement was made by the community,
as before, up to the point that one shall be fined sixty kārṣāpaṇas."
"You have approached the Blessed One for a vision out of fear of punishment?
"It is so, venerable Ānanda.
Then the Venerable Ānanda [addressed] Roca...
Taking the Malla chief Roca with him, he approached the Blessed One;
having approached, he said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, this Mallan chief Roca has no faith in the Buddha, nor does he have faith in the Dharma or the Saṅgha."
"It would be well if the Blessed One were to teach the Dharma to him in such a way that he might gain faith in the Buddha, gain faith in the Dharma, and gain faith in the Saṅgha.
The Blessed One consented to the Venerable Ānanda by remaining silent.

Then the Blessed One gave such a teaching of the Dharma to Roça, the chief minister, that upon hearing it, Roça, the chief minister of the Mallas, gained faith in the Buddha, gained faith in the Dharma, and gained faith in the Saṅgha.
Then Roca, the chief minister of the Mallas, rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and extending his joined palms toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"May the Blessed One consent to take a meal at my home tomorrow, together with the community of monks.
"I have already been invited by the Mallas of Pāpā for that very first meal, O Roca."
"May the Blessed One grant me his consent; I shall act in such a way that the Mallas of Pāpā will give their permission.
If it pleases you, and if the Mallas of Pāpā grant permission, then I shall grant my consent to you."
Then Rocaka, the chief minister of the Mallas, bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, rose from his seat, and departed for Pāpā, where the Mallas of Pāpā resided.
Having arrived, he addressed the Mallas of Pāpā as follows:
"Gentlemen, please wait until I have first fed the Blessed One and the community of monks."
"Afterwards, it will not be difficult for you as well to feed the Blessed One and the community of monks.
They said:
"We invited the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, for that very first [meal], so we do not grant permission. He said,
"If you do not grant permission, I shall distribute one type of solid food and one type of drink."
Thereupon, those who were faithful said,
"Sirs, this man is faithless;
we grant that it is so, provided that the offering has been dedicated by him to the Saṅgha."
They gave their permission.
Then he summoned the artisans and said to them, "Sirs, prepare such foodstuffs that one portion alone will suffice; I shall provide all the necessary utensils."
He provided various utensils combined with diverse fragrant substances;
with these, he prepared a variety of foods filled with many kinds of fragrant ingredients,
such that a single portion was sufficient for each individual.
Then, on that very night, the Mallas of Pāpā prepared pure and excellent food, both hard and soft, and as before, they sat down on seats arranged in front of the community of monks.
Then Roca, the chief minister of the Mallas, began to distribute the snacks and the drinks.
The monks did not consume [the food] due to remorse.
The Blessed One said,
"The donor should be looked upon."
The monks looked upon the Pāpeya Mallas and said,
"Noble ones, we have been observed by Rocana, the high official of the Mallas."
"Please accept them.
Then, the Malla chief Roca distributed solid foods,
and by that alone, the monks' needs were fully satisfied.
The Blessed One, having given the instruction regarding the alms-offering, departed.
That food did not come to be consumed by the Pāpeya Mallas.
On another day, the monks entered for alms-food.
The brahmins and householders said to them, "Come, O Buddha! Come, O Dharma! Come, O Saṅgha! Accept this.
Out of remorse, the monks did not accept it.
The Blessed One said:
"You should ask them: 'Are you giving this to me, or to that Blessed One who is the foremost of bipeds?
If they say, 'To that Blessed One who is the foremost of bipeds,' [then you should give it to him]."
It should not be accepted.
However, if they say,
"You alone are our Buddha," then it should be accepted.
No regret should be felt in this matter.
Thus it should be said regarding the Dharma: "He who is the foremost among those free from passion. Regarding the Saṅgha, it should be said: "He who is the foremost among the assemblies."
This should be applied in detail.
The setting was in Śrāvastī.
A certain householder invited the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, to a steam-bath house (jentāka).
Now at that time, the venerable Svāti was newly arrived, young, recently ordained, and had only recently entered this Dharma and Vinaya.
He reflected:
"It has been said by the Blessed One: 'By those who have given little, and by those who have given much, and by those who have given what is excellent...'"
"Those who have performed the preparatory service with joyful minds, and those who have rejoiced with clear hearts—
all of them shall partake in the merit.
What if I were now to perform the preparatory service?"
He began to split some wood when, from the hollow of a certain rotten log, a venomous snake emerged and bit him on the big toe of his right foot.
Overwhelmed by the poison, he fell to the ground, drooling saliva, distorting his face, and rolling his eyes.
Seeing him thus distressed, the brahmins and householders gathered around.
They said,
"Sirs, whose son is this? and others replied:
"Of such-and-such a person," they replied,
"he has gone forth among the Śākya-son ascetics who are without a protector."
"If he had not gone forth, his kinsmen would have provided him with medical treatment.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said,
"Having consulted a physician, medical treatment should be performed.
The monks then consulted a physician.
He said,
"Noble lady, please give me some unusual food.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said,
"It should be given according to the physician's instruction.
The monks did not know what kind of food was meant by "altered food."
They questioned the physician, who said, "Noble ladies, your Teacher himself— the Blessed One, who is all-knowing and all-seeing— he alone will know."
The monks informed the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said: "Monks, 'altered food' refers to feces, urine, ash, and clay."
Therein, the dung consists of the droppings of very young calves and their urine;
the shade is provided by five trees:
the *kāñcanaka*, the *kībala*, the *aśvattha*, the *udumbara*, and the *nyagrodha*.
"One should remove four finger-breadths of soil from the ground and then lift it up"— this is called "eating with a modification.
Then the monks gave the food modified in this way to the Venerable Svāti,
yet even so he did not recover his health.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Ānanda, will you be able to learn and master the Mahāmāyūrī spell from me and [bestow it] upon the monk Svāti?"

"May the Blessed One speak so that I may hear it for the sake of providing protection, rescue, guardianship, the neutralization of poison, the avoidance of punishment, the destruction of poison, the binding of boundaries, and the binding of the earth. Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke this Mahāmāyūrī vidyā:
Homage to the Buddha, homage to the Dharma, homage to the Saṃgha.
It is as follows: Amale, Vimale, Nirmale, Maṅgale, Hiraṇye, Hiraṇyagarbhe, Bhadre, Subhadre, Samantabhadre, Śrībhadre, Sarvārthasādhani, Paramārthasādhani, Sarvānarthapraśamani, Sarvamaṅgalasādhani.
Manase / Mānase / Mahāmānase.
O Acyute, O Adbhute, O Atyadbhute, O Muktā, O Mocanī, O Mokṣaṇī, O Araje, O Viraje, O Amṛte, O Amare,
O Amarāṇī, O Brahmā, O Brahmasvarā, O Pūrṇā, O Pūrṇamanorathā, O Muktā, O Jīvatī! May there be protection from all calamities, fears, and diseases, Svāhā!

"So be it, Venerable Sir," replied the venerable Ānanda. Having received and mastered the Mahāmāyūrī spell from the Blessed One, he performed a rite of well-being for the monk Svāti. He became free from poison, restored to his former state.
The monks, filled with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts.
“It is wonderful, Blessed One, how much the Mahāmāyūrī vidyā has been beneficial and of great service!
Monks, it was not only now; even in the past, when I had entered upon an unfavorable rebirth and my body was fallen into ruin, the Mahāmāyūrī vidyārājñī was likewise beneficial and of great service.”
Listen to that:
Once upon a time, monks, on the southern slope of Himavat, the king of mountains, there lived a peacock king named Suvarṇāvabhāsa.
Having performed a morning benediction by means of this Mahāmāyūrī spell, he dwelt throughout the day with a protective rite for well-being.
Having performed this auspicious rite, he dwells during the night under that auspicious protection.

At a later time, together with many forest peahens, he goes from grove to grove, from park to park, and from mountain slope to mountain slope; he is excessively inflamed by sensual passion, greedy for sense-pleasures, fettered, and infatuated.
Intoxicated by liquor, utterly bewildered and unconscious,
while wandering about, he entered a certain mountain cleft out of faith;
there, for a long time, he was bound with peacock-nooses by adversaries, enemies, and harmful beings who were seeking an opportunity to strike him down.
He too, being situated there in the midst and bewildered, regained his mindfulness and brought this very Mahāmāyūrī vidyā to mind:
*tadyathā amale vimale nirmale maṅgalye hiraṇye hiraṇyagarbhe bhadre subhadre samantabhadre śrībhadre sarvārthasādhani paramārthasādhani sarvānarthapraśamani sarvamaṅgalyasādhani*.

O Manasī, Mānasī, Mahāmānasī; O Acyutā, Adbhutā, Atyadbhutā; O Muktā, Mocanī, Mokṣaṇī; O Arajā, Virajā, Amare, Amṛte, Amarāṇī; O Brahmā, Brahmasvarā, Pūrṇā, Pūrṇamanorathā, Vimuktā; O Jīvatī, protect me from all calamities, svāhā!
Having cut his peacock snares, he fled.
What do you think, monks? He who was the king of peacocks named Suvarṇāvabhāsa at that time and on that occasion—was he anyone else?
Even then, my Mahāmāyūrī spell was beneficial and of great service; even now, my Mahāmāyūrī spell is beneficial and of great service.
Behold, venerable sir, how far the Blessed One’s protection through knowledge has been performed for the monk Svāti!
It is not only now; listen also to how it was in the past.
Long ago, monks, in the city of Vārāṇasī, a certain young kṣatriya who was a snake-charmer was bitten by a serpent;
he passed away,
but the snake-charmer restored him to health by means of his spells.
"What do you think, monks? He who was that snake-charmer at that time, on that occasion, was I.
He who was that boy at that time, on that occasion, was the monk Svāti.
The Bhaiṣajyavastu is finished."
